email_papers.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
email_papers.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
We study feature vectors: directions in a language model’s activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
1

Introduction
The linear representation hypothesis posits that large language models (LLMs) encode human-interpretable concepts (e.g., sentiment or truthfulness) as linear directions in its activation space
(
Mikolov et al., 2013
;
Park et al., 2023
;
Elhage et al., 2022
)
. When such direction is tied to a pre-specified concept, we call it a
feature vector
. These vectors can serve two complementary roles. Projecting activations onto a feature vector, called
probing
, measures how active its concept is in a given context
(
Alain & Bengio, 2016
;
Belinkov, 2022
)
; adding it to the activations, called
steering
, pushes generation toward that concept
(
Subramani et al., 2022
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. Both techniques are highly effective in practice and have been used for safety-critical LLM monitoring and control
(
Zou et al., 2023a
;
Bergen et al., 2026
;
Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025
)
.

But how can we get these feature vectors? Sparse autoencoders (SAEs)

(
Wu et al., 2025
;
Korznikov et al., 2026
;
Smith et al., 2025
)
. Another option is to define the concepts we care about in advance and extract their directions from contrastive pairs: for each concept, we gather texts that express it and texts that express its opposite, then take the difference between their mean activations. The resulting
difference-in-means
vector is more robust and interpretable than SAE features, but requires matched data per concept, limiting its use to a few concepts at a time
(
Belrose, 2024

2.1

Conclusion
Understanding what language models represent requires tools that are both interpretable and broad enough to study model behavior at scale. In this work, we showed that these goals need not conflict. Rather than attempting to recover a complete dictionary of model features, we start from pre-specified, alignment-relevant concepts and construct explicit directions for them from contrastive data. Synthetic story generation makes this procedure practical at a scale where manual curation would be prohibitive.
The resulting feature vectors generalize beyond the synthetic corpus from which they are derived. Across six models from three families, they detect their target concepts in natural chat and web text, form a shared and interpretable geometry, and causally steer generation when injected into activations. This makes a broad feature dictionary useful as an experimental instrument for studying model behavior in longer, multi-step settings. Our analyses of coding agents, jailbreak attacks, and chain-of-thought reasoning illustrate how collections of interpretable directions can reveal patterns that would be difficult to discover from single-feature probes alone.
More broadly, our results suggest a complementary approach to representation analysis: instead of asking whether we can recover the entire feature space, we can ask which parts of that space are useful for a particular scientific or safety question, and construct those parts directly. The resulting directions should not be treated as a complete or uniquely active account of the model’s mechanisms, but as interpretable evidence for concepts and as tools for investigating model behavior. We hope this perspective can turn feature vectors from isolated probes into reusable maps of model behavior, eventually scaling far beyond the 1,036 concept–antagonist pairs studied here.

article.headline: 用200万合成故事提取1036个概念向量
article.lede: 研究者以合成故事对做差值均值，把可解释性探针扩展到1036个对齐相关概念，并在六个模型上检验其泛化、几何与因果操控能力。
article.problem: 稀疏自编码器试图无监督地还原整个特征空间，却被指难以忠实找到模型真实特征，在下游任务上不如更简单的基线。差值均值法虽更稳健、更可解释，但每个概念都要人工配对文本，一次只能覆盖少数概念，难以支撑规模化研究。
article.method: 作者聚焦AI安全与对齐相关概念，为每个概念生成表达该概念与其对立面的合成故事对，取两者平均激活之差作为特征向量。他们用跨多语言、多文体的200万条合成故事，把这一流程扩展到1036个概念，并公开数据。向量以探针（投影读出）和操控（注入激活）两种方式使用，并在六个模型、三个模型家族上评测。
article.results: 作者构建了1036个概念–对立概念对，动用200万条合成故事，覆盖六款模型、三个模型家族。在Qwen3-8B第24层上，1036个概念与对立向量的t-SNE图经Leiden算法在互30近邻余弦图上聚出30个社区，簇名由人工标注；作者称这些向量在聊天对话与网页文本中能稳定检出对应概念，注入激活后可因果地操控生成。附录的剂量–反应实验复现了此前工作中的泰诺结果，并把剂量梯度扩展到止咳糖浆（100–900 ml）和布洛芬（100–19,200 mg），在Qwen3-8B、Llama-3.1-8B、gemma-2-9b的第24、21、28层上读出响应；具体的探针与操控准确率，论文摘录未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「先选定关心的概念、再直接构造方向」做成可复用流水线，让特征向量从孤立的探针变成可批量使用的分析工具。作者用它考察越狱攻击、数学与智能体推理中的表征变化，显示出多方向联合分析能揭示单特征探针难以发现的模式。
article.limitations: 概念集是预先指定且偏对齐议题的，并非对模型特征空间的完整还原；作者自己也强调，这些方向不应被视为模型机制的唯一或完备解释。合成故事由参考模型（gpt-oss-120b）生成，可能把生成模型的偏见带入数据，而摘录中未给出探针与操控的量化指标。

email_papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
email_papers.abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world.
However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena.
The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale.
To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model’s own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
. Each of these substantially improves performance.
We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research.
1
1
1

Introduction
Simulation is one of the most promising paths to training embodied AI at scale. Unlike the real world, a simulator can run thousands of episodes in parallel, reset instantly, expose the full ground-truth state, and provide rewards without human supervision
(
Todorov et al., 2012
;
Makoviychuk et al., 2021
;
Tao et al., 2025
)
. For these advantages to matter, however, simulations must faithfully represent the real world.
Although the field has developed various hand-built environments
(
James et al., 2020
;
Yu et al., 2020
;
Liu et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Nasiriany et al., 2024
)
, a key bottleneck is that building additional, more realistic simulations requires significant time and expert effort.
Indeed, despite decades of human progress, today’s simulations cover a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena (Tables
2
and
1
), often with limited visual fidelity.
Simulation as a path to embodied AI is hindered by the challenge of building diverse, realistic simulations at scale.

Methodology
In this section, we introduce the problem setup and the GDP-grounded selection of simulations. In §
3
, we describe our multi-agent strategy for creating simulations, and in §
4
, how we create tasks of controlled difficulty for each simulation.
2.1

Results
6.1

Experimental Setup
Library.
To evaluate many kinds of policies, from frontier models to code policies and learned visuomotor policies, we build the Gym-Anything for Robotics library, which gives every simulation the same interface. As a result, any policy can run on any simulation without simulation-specific code. Behind this interface, each simulation can use its own physics engine and custom solvers, and its robot can be swapped for others, from single arms to bimanual arms and humanoids. The same simulation can also be run with restricted access, as on a real robot, or with privileged access to its full state (§
2.1
), so it serves evaluation, privileged experiments, and training alike. Appendix
D
provides further details.
Robot interface.
Each simulation runs as a server, and a policy connects to it over an authenticated HTTP API, whose key grants restricted or privileged access (§
2.1
). To support policies ranging from frontier models to code policies and VLAs, a policy can command the robot at several levels. It can set joint targets or end-effector coordinates, which a controller tracks, or send joint torques and, on humanoids, individual motor commands. Like a computer-use agent, it can also press game-style keys, such as W, A, S, and D to move the end effector, each held for a set number of control ticks.
Agents.
We evaluate three frontier models with extra-high reasoning effort: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra, and Claude Opus 5.5
(
Anthropic, 2025a
)
. Each runs as a coding agent in its own harness, Claude Code
(
Anthropic, 2025b
)
for Claude Opus 5.5 and Codex
(
OpenAI, 2025
)
for the GPT models, and controls the robot with restricted access through a small set of tools, such as
observe
, which returns camera images and robot feedback, and
act
, which executes a robot command. The learning experiments (§
6.3
) use Claude Opus 5.5 in every role.
Evaluation.
Each attempt runs on an independent copy of the simulation, starting from the task’s initial state, with a wall-clock budget of three hours. The verifier scores each attempt after the agent finishes.
During the attempt, agents do not observe rewards. We report two metrics: (1) success rate, i.e., the fraction of attempts that the verifier labels as successful, and (2) average reward, i.e., the mean of the continuous reward
r
∈
[
0
,
1
]
r\in[0,1]
, which captures partial progress.
6.2

Main Results

Conclusion
In this work, we introduced Gym-Anything for Robotics, a scalable framework in which coding agents build realistic robotics simulations. By framing simulation creation as a coding agent task and checking each simulation and task in a multi-agent loop of creation, auditing, and repair, Gym-Anything for Robotics addresses a central bottleneck in robot learning: the difficulty of building realistic simulations at scale. Applying this framework, we built RoboWorld, a GDP-grounded collection of 200 RL environments across 25 simulations spanning liquids, cloth, and physics that existing engines lack, with swappable robots and train and test splits. We further showed that privileged simulator state more than doubles the first-attempt reward of frontier models, and that it can teach a student through hints alone and train
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
from 0% to 53% success. At the same time, RoboWorld is challenging even for frontier models, which fail every test task, indicating that realistic physical work remains far from solved.
More broadly, our results suggest that simulation has been held back not by the idea of simulation, but by unrealistic simulations, and that coding agents can now build realistic ones in which far more capable frontier models learn in ways that the real world does not allow. We hope that Gym-Anything for Robotics, RoboWorld, and the released code provide a foundation for future work on realistic robot learning, including more capable embodied agents, new ways to learn from privileged state, and broader coverage of physical work.

article.headline: 编码智能体批量搭建机器人仿真环境
article.lede: 研究者把仿真搭建当成编码任务交给智能体，产出25个仿真、共200个RL环境；最强前沿模型在所有测试任务上平均奖励仅0.0
article.problem: 机器人仿真是规模化训练具身模型最有希望的路径，但现有仿真只覆盖很窄的任务与物理现象，视觉保真度也有限。瓶颈在于新增高质量仿真需要大量专家工时，因而难以扩展。作者据此提出：仿真创建本身应当被当作编码智能体的任务来处理。
article.method: 作者先用美国GDP数据筛出120个覆盖经济价值较高体力工作的仿真方向，实际构建其中25个，并明确定义「好仿真」与「好任务」的判定标准。随后搭建一条对抗式「创建—审计」流水线：创建智能体写代码造仿真并自证质量，四个审计智能体按标准核查；任务创建智能体提出目标难度的任务，再由六个审计智能体复核。所有仿真统一接口，支持单臂、双臂与人形机器人，并可在受限访问与特权全状态访问之间切换。
article.results: 由此得到的RoboWorld包含25个仿真、175个训练与25个测试RL环境。三个前沿模型（GPT-6 Astra、GPT-6.1 Terra、Claude Opus 5.5）在每个测试任务上都失败，平均奖励仅0.06。利用特权仿真状态可让前沿模型首次尝试奖励提升一倍以上；特权教师仅靠提示即可教学生；用代码策略生成跨场景示范，可把π0.5的成功率从0%训练到53%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把仿真供给的瓶颈从「人工建模」转成「编码能力」，让编码智能体的进步可以直接转化为更丰富、更真实的仿真环境。若这一路径成立，机器人学习的规模上限将不再由专家工时决定。
article.limitations: 论文从120个候选中只实现了25个仿真，覆盖面仍有限；所有任务上前沿模型平均奖励仅0.06，说明这些环境离可用训练场尚有距离。仿真质量由LLM审计智能体按自定标准判定，并未与真实世界测量对齐，也没有真机迁移实验，因此「更真实」目前只是内部一致性证据。
article.figure_caption_zh: 四阶段流水线：依据美国GDP数据挑选120个候选仿真并建成25个，创建智能体编写仿真代码、由四个审计智能体核查，任务创建智能体设计目标难度任务、由六个审计智能体复核，最后通过上下文学习、特权教师教练与生成示范的代码策略训练VLA模型。

figure.caption: {Overview of Gym-Anything for Robotics.} {Phase~1:} We select 120 simulations grounded in U.S.\ GDP data, covering the most valuable physical work across occupations and everyday life, and build 25 of them. {Phase~2:} A creation agent builds each simulation in code and produces evidence of its quality, which four audit agents check against our criteria. {Phase~3:} A task creation agent proposes tasks of targeted difficulty, which six audit agents check, and each task runs with many robots and variations. {Phase~4:} Models learn from privileged simulation state through in-context learning, coaching, and code policies that train VLAs.

email_papers.title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
email_papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.

Abstract
AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through
category-theory-guided
transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility.
AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM’s six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds.
Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline’s actions.
1
Introduction
AI systems are advancing the frontiers of mathematics,
from Lean-verified progress on the Riemann zeta function
(
Anthropic, 2026
)
to recently reported resolutions
of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem and the
local smoothing conjecture
(
OpenAI, 2026a
;
OpenAI, 2026b
)
. Yet these advances typically rely on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. In an unfamiliar environment, however, an agent must first identify the relevant objects, infer how actions change them, and determine what constitutes success. The rules on which its reasoning depends are themselves hypotheses to be learned and revised through interaction. This raises a broader question:
Can an agent reason rigorously about an unknown world?
Euler’s treatment of the Königsberg bridges illustrates the role of mathematical structure
(
Euler, 1741
)
. Land masses become vertices and bridges become edges. A walk crossing every bridge exactly once pairs arrivals and departures at every vertex other than its endpoints, so at most two vertices can have odd degree. The Königsberg graph has four, ruling out every such walk without enumerating routes. A winning trajectory likewise establishes reachability, but proving that none exists requires reasoning about all legal sequences. When the environment is unfamiliar, the objects and rules needed for that reasoning must themselves be learned.
We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that learns explicit mathematical models of unfamiliar environments through interaction and uses them for formal reasoning. AWM proceeds through three stages (Figure
1
). In
Explore & Prototype
, the agent actively probes the environment and maintains executable hypotheses, testing and revising them against observed transitions.
Structure & Simplify
organizes these hypotheses into typed objects and rules, then uses category-theory-guided transformations, each checked in Lean through
projective and inductive
limits, to identify shared structure and simplify its representation while preserving tested distinctions. In
Formalize & Prove
, AWM completes the model in Lean 4
(
de Moura and Ullrich, 2021
)
and constructs kernel-checked proofs of reachability, impossibility, and other properties. A winning witness establishes reachability; an invariant or a suitable cost lower bound can exclude every legal winning sequence under the model.
Figure 1:
AWM’s three-stage pipeline: interactive exploration builds a provisional executable model, algebraic transformations reveal and simplify its structure, and Lean 4 formalization enables certified proofs of reachability or impossibility.
We test AWM’s ability to prove impossibility on ARC-AGI-3
(
ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a
)
, whose games reveal neither their rules nor their goals. We construct two impossible variants of
sc25
levels, preserving their mechanics while setting action budgets just below the minimum winning costs (§
4
). Across three runs per level, AWM produces closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding all legal winning sequences under its learned models in all six runs. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra produce no such proofs across twelve baseline runs.
The difference extends beyond proof construction. AWM’s initial bounds match the minimum winning costs in four of six runs, compared with one for Opus 5.5 (without a proof) and none for Astra; other baseline runs report incorrect bounds or remain inconclusive. For example, on level 4 Astra claims impossibility with an unproved minimum winning cost of 22, whereas AWM proves a tight bound of 19 under its learned model, matching the game’s actual minimum winning cost. Given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises the rules underlying its remaining two bounds and constructs new closed proofs, bringing its bound accuracy to six of six.
AWM’s learned mechanisms are also explicit and inspectable: typed objects and named rules make their predictions available for step-by-step checking. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, AWM builds compact models with a median of six object types and ten rules. These models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels, checking represented state transitions and final goal conditions (§
3
). With Opus 5, AWM clears all 25 games with a score of 99.9, competitive with leading code-executing systems; its certified winning trajectories use 43% of the human baseline’s actions.
We make three contributions.
•
A framework from exploration to algebraic structure.
AWM turns interaction with an unknown environment into executable hypotheses and organizes them into compact models through
category-theory-guided
transformations checked in Lean, presenting object types as projective and inductive limits. Shared, parameterized rules express related mechanisms in a common form, allowing their properties to be stated and proved uniformly (§
2
).
•
Formal impossibility reasoning in unknown worlds.
AWM constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs that rule out all legal winning sequences under its learned rules and specified constraints, including sequences never explored. This establishes model-relative impossibility rather than inferring it from unsuccessful play (§
4
).
•
Inspectable models and traceable proofs.
Typed objects and named rules make learned dynamics understandable and their predictions checkable against observations. Lean replay connects the formal representation to recorded behavior, while explicit proof dependencies identify the rules on which a conclusion rests, supporting targeted empirical examination and revision (§
3
; §
4.3
).
2
Method
AWM aims to turn interaction with an unknown environment into a mathematical model that supports rigorous reasoning about both reachability and impossibility. This requires more than collecting rules that explain observed transitions: the rules must form a coherent representation of the environment, and that representation must support reasoning about action sequences the agent has never explored.
We first describe the target model (§
2.1
), then present the three stages that construct and use it (Figure
1
): Explore & Prototype develops executable hypotheses through interaction; Structure & Simplify organizes them into a compact algebraic model; and Formalize & Prove completes the model in Lean 4 and establishes machine-checked results.
2.1
The Algebraic World Model
An algebraic world model describes an environment through typed objects, rules, and a goal predicate, represented in executable Python and formal Lean 4 to support both empirical testing and mathematical reasoning.
Objects.
Object types define the structure and validity of states, providing a common vocabulary for describing the environment. A parser maps observations, together with any required history or auxiliary information, to typed states

Rules.

Each Python rule specifies an applicability scope and a checker that reports agreement, contradiction, or non-applicability on observed transitions; effect rules also predict successor states or their components. Example: one rule for four mechanisms
In game
lp85

The shared rule also shortens reasoning: because one color-count invariant covers every button, proofs that a variant is unsolvable need two to three times fewer lemmas than proofs over the eleven separate concepts (Appendix
B
). A separate check tests whether such a model-level proof also holds for the game: on the level-6 tile-swap variant U, Lean verifies its unsolvability proof against an engine-derived graph covering all 52,500 transitions among 7,500 configurations (Appendix
B

In Formalize & Prove, Lean certifies a five-click winning sequence (Figure
3

3

Compact models that reproduce observed behavior.
Across the 25 games, AWM records 742 executable concepts and withdraws 143 during model revision. The retained concepts are tested against the recorded transitions. Structure & Simplify organizes the rest into 170 object types and 283 rules, a median of 6 types and 10 rules per game. Shared patterns include translations, permutations and goal conditions. Lean replays the winning trajectory of every one of the 183 levels from its initial state and verifies its final state against the modeled goal (Table
2
).
Generalization beyond observed transitions.
We next test the learned rules on behavior the record never showed. We freeze the models of
lp85
and
ft09
after exploration and evaluate them on transitions from random play with previously unseen screens (seeds 0–9; Appendix
B
). The final frozen rules accept every valid transition in the new-trajectory sets. On the two modified
lp85
layout sets, they predict the next tile layout in all 4,160 cases; on the two changed-mechanic
ft09
sets, they reject all 4,031 transitions. On a third game,
ls20
, the same evaluation accepts 99.47–99.95% of valid transitions on previously unseen screens with the final rules, compared with 67–70% with the concepts before Structure & Simplify (Appendix
B
).
The changed mechanic modifies
ft09
’s hidden click pattern, causing each click to change 110 or 146 cells instead of 38; rejecting these transitions shows that the rules detect behavior inconsistent with the learned dynamics.
Clearing the games with efficient solutions.
The same models are effective for play. AWM with Opus 5 achieves a score of 99.9, compared with 40.7 for Opus 5 under the official standard harness without code execution. It scores 100 on 23 games and at least 97.6 on every game, performing competitively with leading code-executing systems (Table
2
). Its certified clears require 7,448 actions, only 43% of the human baseline’s 17,135 and the fewest among systems reporting this metric, compared with 7,518 for Memento 3
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
and 8,347 for
Rodionov (2026a)
. Including exploration and other sessions, AWM uses 24,604 engine actions in total (Appendix
B
). These results show that AWM can construct and use explicit world models while retaining competitive solution efficiency. §

4
Proving impossibility
A winning trajectory establishes reachability; impossibility requires excluding every legal winning sequence within the budget, including those never explored. We test whether AWM’s learned algebraic models enable such exhaustive proofs, and whether those proofs hold for the game itself.
4.1
The game, the seal, and the baselines
In
sc25
, a block moves on a grid and casts spells through a
3
×
3
3\times 3
panel to reach the exit within the level’s budget. Moves and panel clicks cost one unit, completing a spell one more, fuel refunds ten, and the winning move is free. We construct two variants of levels 4 and 5 by rearranging selected elements while preserving the game mechanics, then seal them at budgets of 18 and 35. Exhaustive search on the game engine (the underlying game program), covering all four initial facings and all 13 actions, establishes minimum winning costs of 19 and 36, respectively: neither sealed level can be won, while one additional unit permits a win.
Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra receive the game interface and coding tools, including simulator construction and search; AWM uses Opus 5.5 with the procedure of §
2
and a generic Lean skeleton. Each condition has three runs per level, with up to eight reset-delimited attempts per run, ending at game over or recorded abandonment. After each attempt, every agent is asked whether the sealed level can be won and to justify its verdict; AWM constructs Lean proofs under its learned model. Impossibility can be established by proving that the minimum winning cost exceeds the budget. We evaluate proof validity under the learned model separately from numerical agreement with the engine.

Only five of twelve baseline runs claim impossibility, four with incorrect bounds. Even the sole correct Claude Opus 5.5 bound lists “that my hand-counted path lengths are truly minimal” as

In contrast, AWM formally proves a lower bound of 19 under its learned model and verifies a matching winning witness, establishing a tight bound that agrees with the game’s minimum winning cost.
Proof validity and bound accuracy are distinct.
Before feedback, four of six AWM bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra.
Some runs identify a correct winning sequence but charge the otherwise free winning move, reporting a bound one unit higher. Because this cost cannot be observed on sealed levels, we count such bounds as correct for all agents only when the discrepancy is explicitly attributable to this accounting convention, not to an incorrect route or cost estimate.
The remaining two AWM bounds, 20 on L4 and 47 on L5, arise from overly restrictive learned rules that omit transitions used by the game’s cheapest winning routes, violating sufficient cover (§
2.4
). Their proofs remain valid under those models, although their numerical thresholds disagree with the game.

4.3
Auditing premises and proving again
After the initial evaluation, the two AWM runs with bounds of 20 and 47 receive feedback only that the game permits a cheaper win, without revealing its cost, route or the faulty rule. AWM revisits its explicit rules, tests alternative formulations through interaction, and constructs new proofs under the refined models (Appendix
C
).
On L4, AWM discovers that growing onto fuel collects it, reducing the bound from 20 to 19. On L5, it identifies terrain rather than limited range as the cause of a failed shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under its convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the game’s minimum cost of 36. Both refinements succeed within four additional attempts, each yielding a new closed Lean proof. With this feedback, AWM reaches correct bounds in all six runs.
We provide the same discrepancy feedback and additional attempt budget to the four baseline runs with incorrect bounds. Astra corrects both bounds but produces no formal proofs, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither.
Proof dependencies help locate faulty rules.
Both repairs corrected rules used by the original proofs. To test whether proof dependencies help locate such errors, we inject a single incorrect rule into a reference model and give Claude Opus 5.5 the faulty model, its Lean proof, and access to the game. The goal is to find a transition where the model’s prediction disagrees with the game. On L4, Claude succeeds in 16 of 42 runs without explicit proof dependencies. Providing the rules used by the proof, without revealing which rule is faulty, increases this to 29 of 42 runs. Even when directly told which rule is faulty, Claude finds a counterexample in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies substantially improve error discovery, nearly matching the benefit of identifying the faulty rule directly (Appendix
C
).
4.4
From model proofs to the engine
Matching the game’s minimum winning cost provides evidence of accurate reasoning, but does not establish that a formal proof under the learned model also holds for the game. To transfer such a proof, the learned model need not cover every game transition; by Definition
1
, it suffices that it reproduce the game’s optimal winning sequences. For the budgeted tasks here, we verify sufficient certificate-level conditions on engine-derived graphs, which preserve budget feasibility and the proof invariants (Lemmas
A.2
–
A.3
).
We exhaustively check the engines’ budget-feasible transitions from the fixed opening against the potential inequalities and invariant conditions used in the model proofs. These checks establish that five of the six model-level impossibility proofs can be extended to the original games. Appendix
C
gives the per-run transfer arguments, including the completed rules and certificates.

6
Limitations and conclusion
Limitations.
We demonstrate AWM on ARC-like environments with discrete actions and immediate, observable feedback, where learned rules can be checked against recorded transitions; richer hidden state, delayed feedback and stochastic dynamics remain to be tested. Lean guarantees the correctness of proofs under the learned model’s explicit premises, and whether these premises capture the environment is tested by interaction: the explicit rules and kernel-checked proofs separate errors in the learned model from errors in reasoning, so a discrepancy can be traced to its assumption and addressed by further exploration. Broader environments and tasks are the natural next test of such formal reasoning.
Conclusion.
Formal reasoning traditionally begins with predefined objects and rules. AWM takes a step toward reasoning rigorously about unknown worlds by discovering these structures through interaction, organizing them into compact algebraic models, and formalizing them in Lean. The resulting models make learned mechanisms explicit and their behavior checkable step by step, while supporting kernel-checked proofs of reachability and impossibility, including claims about action sequences never explored. By making the assumptions behind these proofs explicit, AWM also allows discrepancies with the environment to be traced to learned rules and addressed through further exploration. Together, these capabilities bridge empirical exploration and formal reasoning, extending mathematical proof beyond problems whose definitions are given in advance.

Verification at each node.
Every non-leaf node of the hierarchy is verified by the Lean kernel: every object type with constraints and every case table must come with a proof of its universal property. The kernel establishes that each node is the limit or colimit of its diagram; whether the representation describes the environment is established by the tasks. The two kinds of evidence therefore answer different questions, what the model entails and whether it agrees with the environment, and neither substitutes for the other. A claim for all well-formed states requires a Lean theorem that does not hold by definitional unfolding alone; for example, the equation stating that a rule defined by pattern matching equals the copairing of its branches holds by unfolding and certifies the form of the rule, not its content.

B.4 Checking a model-level proof against the engine.
This check concerns the level-6 tile-swap variant U of Appendix
B
. We export its engine-derived, budget-independent reachable configuration graph as a Lean table, with 7,500 configurations and 52,500 transitions for the seven nontrivial button actions. A Lean proof checks each transition against the premises of the model-level unsolvability theorem, so the conclusion transfers to the exported graph. The proof uses only Lean’s standard axioms. Extracting the graph from the game engine remains outside the Lean kernel’s guarantee.

A minimum-budget route shrinks and regrows over the fuel, obtaining the refund and changing its alignment, then lines up a shot and exits through the opened gate. Its 27 actions require a cap of 19 (gross cost 29). Level 5 has two target–gate groups, fuel, a narrow connector and separate teleport destinations for each size. A minimum-budget route shoots the first target, collects fuel, shrinks through the connector, regrows to shoot the second target, and teleports as a large block into the exit shaft. Its 42 actions require 36 (gross cost 46). These routes minimize the required budget, rather than the unconstrained number of actions.
The witnesses establish that caps 19 and 36 suffice. To establish that lower caps cannot win, we search the sealed engine before any agent run, covering all four opening facings and all 13 actions (four moves and nine panel cells). For each configuration, the search retains the least counter value, since a lower counter leaves at least as much budget for every continuation. C.2 Agents and protocol.
The comparison tests whether agents can identify the budget obstruction and justify it from interaction. Three configurations play each sealed level, three runs each. AWM uses Claude Opus 5.5 with the AWM procedure, a generic Lean skeleton and tools for recording predictions and checking rules; it receives no game rules. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra without AWM receive the task, game interface and ordinary coding-agent tools.
Each run has up to eight reset-delimited attempts, ending at game over or recorded abandonment. After each attempt, the interview in Appendix
D
records the agent’s verdict and argument. The engine reference thresholds are withheld: arenas have opaque names, contain no ground-truth file, and begin with cross-run memory cleared. This keeps the agent’s reported bound separate from the reference search used to evaluate it.

C.4 Repairing the rules and proving again.
The two overestimated AWM bounds provide a test of whether an explicit model can be corrected after a valid proof has been obtained. After the eight-attempt round, those runs and the four baseline runs with wrong bounds receive one piece of feedback: the engine permits a cheaper win than their analysis allows. The message reveals no rule, cost or route. AWM additionally receives a self-audit instruction to relax rules consistently with the record, test disagreements in the game, revise and prove again; the baseline message states the same discrepancy logic in plain language. Each run gets at most four further attempts.
The corrections change specific premises of the proofs (Table
11
). On level 4, growing onto fuel collects it, reducing AWM’s bound from 20 to 19; Figure
9
shows the missed interaction and the cheaper route. On level 5, terrain rather than limited range blocks a shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under the run’s convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the engine’s 36. Both repairs produce new closed Lean proofs. Astra corrects both numerical bounds without producing a formal proof, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither. Thus numerical revision and renewed formal certification remain distinct outcomes of the same feedback.

C.6 Using proof dependencies to find model errors.
The repairs above corrected rules used by the original proofs. We
now test whether knowing which rules a proof depends on helps an
agent find errors in its world model.
We start from a reference model that agrees with the game under
the abstractions of §
C
, and deliberately make one
rule incorrect. We select 14 such errors on L4 and 7 on L5 that
change the model’s minimum winning cost, and repeat each experiment
with three seeds.
Claude Opus 5.5 receives the faulty model, a closed Lean proof of
impossibility under that (faulty) model, and access to the game. Although the proof is valid
under the model’s rules, those rules may disagree with the game.
Claude must find an actual transition where the model predicts
a different outcome from the game, within the faulty rule’s scope.
Simply naming the faulty rule does not count as success.
We compare three conditions. In C1, Claude receives the model’s
rules and their recorded evidence, without an explicit list of
proof dependencies. In C2, it additionally receives the list
of rules used by the proof, but is not told which one is wrong.
In R, it is directly told the faulty rule. We also include
random exploration (C0) and exhaustive engine search (EX) as
references. Each agent run has a budget of 50 game actions on
L4 or 5,000 on L5.
On L4, C1 finds a conflicting transition in 16 of 42 runs.
Providing proof dependencies (C2) increases this to 29 of 42.
Even when directly told the faulty rule (R), Claude succeeds
in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies nearly match
the benefit of knowing the faulty rule, without revealing it.
L5 is harder: C1 succeeds in 1 of 21 runs, C2 in 3 of 21,
and R in 5 of 21.
Across both levels, C2 finds counterexamples in 32 of 63 runs,
compared with 17 of 63 for C1. On 12 error-free controls — the
same procedure run on an unmodified reference model, with no
injected error — C2 raises no false alarms, compared with 0.33
per run for C1.

C.7 Additional tests of the verification procedure.
We conduct mutation tests to examine what kinds of errors our
verification procedure can detect. In experiments, we deliberately introduce errors
into three models: the two sealed-level reference models (2,675
and 3,502 states) and the merged
lp85
model (869 states).
These errors affect proof certificates, model rules, consistency
between Python and Lean, or theorem statements. We compare a Python
certificate checker with our Lean
-
based verification procedure,
which also includes a separate audit of theorem statements.
Both methods reject all 12 invalid proof certificates, including
nine that would support conclusions contradicted by the game.
The Lean-based procedure additionally detects all three tested
Python–Lean mismatches and all three reversed bounds, which the
Python checker misses. Its separate statement audit also flags
all six cases where a theorem holds only because its premises
cannot be satisfied or its starting-state set is empty. Such
theorems may still compile in Lean: the kernel verifies that
conclusions follow from their premises, not whether those
premises are meaningful.
Neither method detects errors deliberately introduced into the
model’s rules (M1–M6), or theorem statements referring to the
wrong goal or model version (S3, S7). These results illustrate
both the additional checks provided by Lean-based verification
and their limits: a valid proof does not guarantee that the
underlying model correctly describes the game.

article.headline: AWM：从交互探索到Lean证明
article.lede: AWM把未知环境中的交互转成可执行代数模型，再用Lean 4证明可达性与不可达性。
article.problem: AI已能在Lean中给出数学问题的机器可检查证明，但通常依赖预先给定的定义与形式规范。在未知环境中，智能体必须先识别对象、推断动作效果并确定成功条件，而这些规则本身只是需要通过交互学习和修正的假设。论文追问：智能体能否对未知世界进行严格推理？
article.method: AWM分三阶段运行：Explore & Prototype通过主动探测维护可执行Python概念，并依据观测不断检验和修正；Structure & Simplify把假设组织成类型化对象与规则，用范畴论中的投射极限和归纳极限引导变换，在保留已测区分的前提下压缩模型；Formalize & Prove在Lean 4中补全模型，用不变式或成本下界构造核检查的可达性与不可达性证明。
article.results: 在sc25两个密封关卡（预算18和35，引擎穷举最小获胜成本19和36）上，AWM在6/6次运行中产出封闭、内核检查的Lean不可达证明，12次基线运行（Claude Opus 5.5与GPT-6 Astra各6次）均未产出。AWM初始界4/6正确，Opus 5.5为1/6、Astra为0/6；仅收到“存在更便宜获胜”的反馈后，AWM修正规则并达到6/6正确。25个公开ARC-AGI-3游戏的183关全部通关，得分99.9；认证通关轨迹用7,448个动作，为人类基线17,135的43%。模型每局中位数为6个对象类型和10条规则，Lean重放183/183关，形式化220条规则并检查1,374个定理。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把经验探索与形式证明连接起来：在规则未知时，智能体可以给出相对于所学模型的不可达性证明，并把证明依赖的假设暴露出来供审计。
article.limitations: 实验限于离散动作、即时可观察反馈的ARC类环境，隐藏状态、延迟反馈和随机动态尚未测试；Lean只保证证明在模型前提下成立，错误模型规则并不总能被验证流程发现（注入错误规则0/18检出），且6个模型级不可达证明中只有5个可扩展到真实引擎。
article.figure_caption_zh: AWM的三阶段流水线：交互探索构建临时可执行模型，代数变换揭示并简化其结构，Lean 4形式化则支持可达或不可达的认证证明。

figure.caption: AWM's three-stage pipeline: interactive exploration builds a provisional executable model, algebraic transformations reveal and simplify its structure, and Lean~4 formalization enables certified proofs of reachability or impossibility.

Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning.

Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters. However, addressing residual diagnostic, management, and safety limitations, alongside integrating external safeguards and clinician-supervised workflows, remains necessary before prospective clinical validation with real patients.

Introduction
Clinical dialogue is foundational to patient-facing medicine, but in psychiatry, the clinical interview itself remains a principal diagnostic instrument
144
. In psychiatric presentations, the psychopathology itself can directly compromise how history is communicated, and patients often do not recognize the relevance of prior treatment failures or comorbid medical conditions causing their symptoms
25
;
10

39
. As a result, the quality of the history depends on both systematic inquiry into these complex causes and interpersonal trust, with a stronger therapeutic alliance supporting more complete diagnostic formulation and improved treatment outcomes
149
;
119
;
180
. Competent clinical dialogue couples two skill domains, diagnostic reasoning (differential diagnosis, psychopharmacology, risk stratification) and interpersonal processing (reading affect and psychological defenses, crisis de-escalation, shared decision-making, stigma-sensitive communication)
92
;
2
;
176
. In psychiatry, both dimensions are especially entangled. A clinician who probes aggressively risks rupturing rapport; one who overprioritizes validation may never arrive at a diagnosis. Here we investigate whether language models can acquire these capabilities through training in simulated clinical environments.

Results
We report three findings. First, in a randomized, double-blind OSCE with psychiatrists role-playing patients, the simulation-trained agent outperformed its identically prompted base model, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, differential diagnosis formulation, and initial management planning (Section
2.1
). Second, under automated evaluation the same advantage held across 127 expert-validated intake scenarios, and a three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios located where simulated evaluation departs from the human study (Section
2.2
). Third, under adversarial presentations, training reduced but did not eliminate unsafe behavior, and the residual failures were mainly under-triage and missed red flags, including errors of omission that post-hoc output filters cannot intercept because no overtly harmful text is generated, such as failing to ask the probing questions needed to uncover a concealed crisis or failing to escalate care (Section
2.3
).

Discussion
We trained a language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters and validated it against its identically prompted base model in three settings. In a randomized, double-blind crossover OSCE with board-certified psychiatrists role-playing standardized patients, the trained agent received a higher independent transcript score than the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, and differential diagnosis formulation (Section
2.1
). Across an automated evaluation of 127 clinician-validated psychiatric intake scenarios, it nearly doubled its base model’s pre-penalty clinical rubric score and substantially improved composite clinical reward, with gains across all four difficulty tiers (Section
2.2
). Under 256 adversarial presentations designed to elicit unsafe clinical behavior, training more than halved under-triage relative to the base model, although residual failures remained (Section
2.3
). Comparing the post-trained agent against its untuned base checkpoint under an identical clinical system prompt, tool interface, and reasoning-token budget isolates the combined effect of the simulation RL pipeline (spanning both adaptation to dynamic patient states and alignment to structured clinical rubrics) from prompt engineering or test-time compute. Because on-policy RL updates model weights from scalar rewards on self-generated trajectories without additional medical corpora, these results also show how far procedural gains carry across clinical tasks. In psychiatric intake, diagnostic reasoning and communication are more tightly coupled than in general medical consultations
176
;
15
, where core symptom histories are less contingent on trust; accordingly, diagnostic formulation scaled with interpersonal and history-taking gains, consistent with building rapport and sustaining structured inquiry unlocking the gated patient disclosures needed to double differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3% in the OSCE). Conversely, downstream management tasks that generally depend on static clinical knowledge rather than conversational elicitation, specifically comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% vs. 26.7% appropriateness across pharmacological and psychotherapeutic recommendations), showed more modest gains and likely remained constrained by both the base model’s parametric capacity and the greater case-level subjectivity of psychiatric treatment selection
75
.
Gains in patient-centered communication were broad, and clinician-patients rated the trained agent as displaying more empathic behavior than the base model during live interaction. These are best read as gains in procedural communication and structured empathic responding, captured in the same direction by all three communication instruments (PCCBP, GMCPQ, and the patient-facing PACES items), rather than as evidence of therapeutic alliance formation, which develops over sustained multi-session relationships
45
. Frequent not-applicable responses on the WAI-SR, an instrument designed for multi-session psychotherapy
62
, are consistent with this distinction (Appendix
A.3
). Whether simulation training also improves alliance in longitudinal settings remains an open question.
Automated multi-turn evaluation complements clinician-enacted assessment by gating diagnostically critical information behind rapport and targeted inquiry, testing interactive clinical interviewing rather than static knowledge recall; the training gain was preserved under an independent out-of-family evaluator (Section
2.2
; Appendix
C.2
). In the adversarial evaluation, simulation training substantially reduced contraindications, missed red flags, and under-triage, but did not eliminate failures when acute risk was concealed behind benign complaints. The composition of these residual failures has direct implications for safety governance. Deterministic guardrails can intercept generation-side harms such as a contraindicated prescription, because the harmful content is present in the output and can be filtered. They cannot address omissions in which the agent never asks the question that would have surfaced a concealed risk, because a post-hoc safety layer has no corresponding content on which to act. Mitigating omission failures therefore requires process-level safeguards external to free-text generation, including structured state-tracking checklists that gate encounter termination on mandatory safety and review-of-systems inquiry, real-time supervisory monitors that audit dialogue state for unprobed red flags, and clinician-in-the-loop verification at handoff. Beyond evaluating our trained model, the clinician-validated intake suite, adversarial stress-testing protocol, and Delphi taxonomies (Table
1
) provide a structured methodology for auditing both commission and omission failures across conversational systems proposed for mental health settings.

Simulated evaluation can therefore order and stress-test models, but neither estimate the size of their differences nor identify the scenarios on which one model outperforms another. As a training environment, however, the same simulator proved sufficient: the gains it produced held when psychiatrists role-played the patients and graded the transcripts.
A documented gap in access to mental health services motivates this line of work. More than 75% of individuals with mental disorders in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment
191
, and even in high-income settings, fewer than one in five individuals with major depressive disorder receive minimally adequate care
173
. Tele-psychiatry supports effective evaluation and treatment delivery for many presentations
71
, which suggests that the encounter format is not the primary barrier to competent assessment, but it does not change the supply of clinician time, since a synchronous consultation occupies a psychiatrist for its full duration whether remote or in person. Addressing this bottleneck does not, however, imply automating psychiatric evaluation or replacing psychiatrists, social workers, or intake clinicians. Given the complexity of psychiatric care and the substantial error rates observed even after simulation training, our findings do not support autonomous deployment of the present system; rather, any prospective near-term clinical role should be strictly assistive and clinician-supervised

, such as conducting a structured pre-visit intake to generate a provisional history and symptom summary that a supervising clinician reviews, verifies, and builds upon during the clinical encounter, potentially supplementing routine psychosocial intake or static questionnaires with structured medical review of systems, medication reconciliation, and preliminary differential screening for somatic mimics.
Limitations.
Several methodological and clinical limitations constrain what these results support. First, while multi-institutionally validated synthetic cases help address the scarcity of shareable psychiatric clinical data
75
and allowed training and automated evaluation to scale across the diagnostic taxonomy, simulated and clinician-enacted patients cannot reproduce the full range of rare conditions, backgrounds, motivations, or disorganized communication encountered in clinical practice; unlike trained professional standardized patients (such as those used in clinical trial rater calibration) or real patients, psychiatrists role-playing patients may present symptoms in overly structured, textbook patterns, making validation with professional standardized patients and real patient cohorts essential next steps. Second, our study uses a controlled within-model design comparing a lightweight policy model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) against its identically prompted base checkpoint rather than against larger frontier models or human clinicians (such as psychiatrists or psychiatric social workers); while this design keeps multi-turn GRPO rollouts computationally tractable and isolates whether simulation training improves upon static prompt instructions, smaller model capacity likely constrained the ceiling on knowledge-intensive tasks such as comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% comprehensive and appropriate treatment in the OSCE), and future studies evaluating clinical readiness must incorporate human clinical comparators alongside ablations against non-interactive rubric fine-tuning and oracle-history baselines. Third, the training reward and scenario reference rubrics were generated within the same model family (Gemini 3.1 Pro) that served as the primary automated evaluator, introducing circularity risks including verbosity bias, stylistic mimicry, and reward hacking
203
;
182
. Cross-evaluator validation with GPT-5.6-Luna confirmed that a substantial training gain persisted under an independent judge (difference between models 0.165, attenuated from 0.270 under the in-family Gemini evaluator against which the policy was trained), though agreement between language-model judges does not exclude shared stylistic preferences, underscoring why evaluation grounded in human clinical judgment remains essential.
In the three-way concordance analysis (Section
2.2
), only the in-family autorater was compared against psychiatrists on the OSCE transcripts. Furthermore, because each OSCE transcript was graded by a single psychiatrist (with different evaluators across each pair), cross-rater reproducibility could not be estimated directly (Appendix
A.6
). Although transcript formatting and turn-count metadata were standardized and independent evaluators graded unpaired transcripts, the trained agent’s substantially longer consultations (median 60 vs. 8 clinician turns) could partially cue crossover clinician-patients during live interaction; however, independent psychiatrist score gains were not significantly correlated with turn-count differences across scenarios (

Clinically, our findings are restricted to single-encounter text-based intake rather than ongoing care. Single-encounter intake aims at a provisional formulation and triage plan, whereas ongoing psychiatric care, including longitudinal medication management and psychotherapy, requires sustained therapeutic relationships and adaptive treatment planning across repeated contact
180
;
118
. Moreover, text restricts assessment to a text-inferable Mental Status Examination (Methods, Section
4.3
); written dialogue exposes thought process, thought content, orientation, and expressed insight, but structurally excludes physical, behavioral, and non-verbal observations on which several diagnostic discriminations depend, including separating negative symptoms of schizophrenia from depressive psychomotor retardation, identifying catatonic features, and detecting acute intoxication or withdrawal
121
;
84
. A text-based agent therefore cannot perform a comprehensive psychiatric examination or substitute for a psychiatrist, and at most could support preliminary, clinician-supervised pre-intake information gathering. In addition, all scenarios and consultations were conducted in English and the clinical norms encoded in our rubrics reflect US psychiatric practice, whereas linguistic expressions of distress, diagnostic conventions, emergency hold criteria, and duty-to-warn mandates vary across languages and jurisdictions
64
;
49
, and the agent was trained for semi-structured intake as opposed to scripted diagnostic instruments such as the SCID-5
42
. Finally, deploying AI in psychiatric care raises domain-specific ethical risks
20
. Reinforcement learning to overcome guardedness corresponds in human practice to motivational interviewing
111
, but under unconstrained optimization has a potential risk of discovering manipulative conversational shortcuts, and individuals in distress are susceptible to anthropomorphic projection and parasocial attachment
87
. Any future translation would therefore require safeguards architecturally external to the learned policy, including hard output-level vetoes on clinical disposition and prescribing, anti-sycophancy auditing, clinician oversight, and deterministic escalation protocols for acute risk
154
.
Conclusion.
A simulation-trained agent conducted standardized psychiatric intake at a level that board-certified psychiatrists rated above its identically prompted base model across clinical examination skill, patient-centered communication, and diagnostic formulation. Standardized patient OSCEs are an established milestone in medical education, but they do not substitute for prospective validation in real patient populations; the environment, agent, reward functions, rubrics, and evaluation scenarios described here are research prototypes, and none has been cleared by any regulatory authority for clinical use. Prospective study under institutional clinician oversight, with real patients and longitudinal follow-up, is the necessary next step. Such text-based systems are not a substitute for psychiatric clinicians and are not ready for autonomous psychiatric assessment; the immediate clinical question for future research is whether, as strictly assistive tools operating under direct clinician oversight, they can help expand the reach of clinician-led care
191
;
173
;
75
. Answering that question requires the psychiatric community to define the evaluation standards and governance boundaries
75
;
47
, and the evaluation framework, rubrics, and taxonomies described here are offered as one contribution toward that goal.

Methods
Training an agent for psychiatric care requires a corpus that captures the diagnostic breadth, clinical ambiguity, and relational complexity of outpatient practice. A training set clustered on common presentations (such as uncomplicated depression or generalized anxiety) risks producing an agent that fails to generalize to diverse clinical encounters. Building on
Liévin et al. Super

5
). Of 50,000 initial generation requests, 48,243 scenarios passed quality verification and deduplication against the held-out evaluation scenarios.

OSCE study design
Standardized patient methodology is an accepted standard for assessing diagnostic formulation, communication, and clinical safety

100

The OSCE cohort comprised 60 scenarios drawn from the 127 clinician-validated intake evaluation scenarios (Section
4.6
) by sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content, covering major psychiatric categories, occult somatic mimics, and complex ethical or legal presentations. Thirty-two board-certified psychiatrists (59.4% female; median experience 12.5 years, IQR 8–18; Supplementary Table
5

Psychiatrists were selected for this role rather than lay actors because executing each scenario’s conditional information-gating protocol required real-time clinical judgment of whether the agent’s inquiry warranted disclosing guarded diagnostic facts, alongside expert calibration when scoring post-encounter communication instruments, while avoiding any exposure of real patients to an experimental system. Each received a detailed role sheet specifying the patient’s history, presentation, psychological defenses, and disclosure triggers (Appendix
A.1
). The clinician-actor conducted separate, blinded, synchronous text consultations with the identically prompted base model and the simulation-trained agent. Presentation sequence was randomized and counterbalanced, with a 48-hour washout period between paired consultations. Clinician-actors and independent raters were blinded to model identity and training condition.
To prevent affective halo effects from live role-play, evaluation used a two-perspective protocol. Clinician-patients provided post-encounter perceptions immediately following the chat. Separately, an independent panel of 15 board-certified psychiatrists drawn from the 54-member expert validation cohort (disjoint from the 32 clinician-patient actors) independently evaluated full consultation transcripts and clinical outputs, formatted as standardized clinical records stripped of AI identifiers (Appendix

Extended Methodology
A.1
Psychiatrist-as-Patient Recruitment and Protocol
Board-certified psychiatrists were recruited to role-play patients in a blinded, counterbalanced, within-scenario crossover design. During the OSCE, clinician-patients received only the Patient Role Sheet specifying the patient’s clinical background, behavioral traits, disclosure rules (what to share freely versus what to reveal only if trust is established or if asked directly), communication style, and resistance patterns, without the ground-truth diagnostic or management scoring key. Although some clinician-patients had participated months earlier in scenario validation (where each reviewer inspected a small subset of candidate scenarios; Appendix
C.1
), each scenario’s two crossover encounters were enacted by the exact same clinician-patient under strict blinding to model identity and condition order, ensuring that any prior familiarity was held constant across paired conditions.
From the 127 expert-validated psychiatric intake evaluation scenarios (Appendix
C.1
), 60 were selected for the crossover OSCE via stratified sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content. Each scenario produced two text-based encounters (one with the identically prompted base model and one with the RL-trained agent) in counterbalanced order with a mandatory 48-hour washout period. Post-encounter, clinician-patients completed the WAI-SR (Appendix
A.3
), GMCPQ (11 items; comprising nine 5-point Likert communication items used to compute the GMCPQ composite and two binary global retention items), PACES patient-facing communication and empathy items (4 items), and PCCBP patient-centered communication items (11 binary items). Clinician-patients also provided qualitative feedback.

article.headline: 模拟环境强化学习提升精神科访谈能力
article.lede: 随机双盲交叉OSCE显示，模拟环境多轮强化学习提升语言模型精神科接诊表现，但治疗规划与安全遗漏仍存。
article.problem: 精神科接诊访谈本身是主要诊断工具，要求医生在建立信任的同时系统追问并鉴别重叠表现。现有医疗对话AI评估多集中于一般医学场景，静态问答难以衡量通过关系建立和针对性询问获取被隐藏的关键临床信息的能力。
article.method: 作者构建模拟临床环境：用语言模型生成并验证48,243个精神科场景，让模型与模拟患者进行多轮互动，由自动评分器按临床量表打分，并用GRPO更新策略。训练后在127个专家验证场景中自动评估，并开展60对随机双盲交叉OSCE，由32名精神科医生扮演标准化病人、15名独立精神科医生盲评转录。
article.results: 在60对OSCE中，训练代理在76.7%配对中胜出（p<0.0001），PACES临床技能3.04 vs. 2.32（满分5），以患者为中心沟通82.0% vs. 65.2%，鉴别诊断适当性68.3% vs. 33.3%。自动评估的127个场景中，临床量表分0.706 vs. 0.379，复合奖励0.564 vs. 0.294（p<0.0001）；256个对抗呈现中，急性风险分诊不足12.9% vs. 30.5%，禁忌0.8% vs. 6.2%，漏红旗6.2% vs. 10.9%。残余问题仍明显：人评接诊中仅46.7%获得全面且适当的治疗建议，模拟接诊中60.6%至少漏问一个关键问题。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明模拟环境可作为训练和压力测试精神科对话智能体的受控试验台，且增益能迁移到医生扮演的标准化病人接诊。但论文强调其近期角色应是临床监督下的辅助工具，而非自主评估或替代精神科医生。
article.limitations: 研究限于单次、文本、英语及美国临床规范的接诊，医生扮演患者可能过于结构化，且模型为轻量级Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite、未与人类临床医生或更大前沿模型比较；训练奖励与场景评分同属Gemini 3.1家族，存在循环性与奖励黑客风险。更关键的是残余失败包括“从不提问”的遗漏型安全风险，事后输出过滤无法拦截，需外部流程级防护和临床监督。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图示训练与评估框架：模拟环境中进行场景生成、多轮互动和GRPO强化学习，并用精神科医生扮演标准化病人及自动评估检验模型。

figure.caption: {Overview of contributions.} The proposed framework involves training a language model in a simulated environment and evaluating it with human experts. {Left (Training in Simulation),} The training process comprises three components: {a,} Scenario Generation, which synthesizes clinical, behavioral, and demographic data into verified patient scenarios using a language model; {b,} Simulation, where the model engages in multi-turn interactions with a simulated patient; and {c,} Reinforcement Learning, which uses an autorater to grade conversation transcripts against a clinical rubric and updates the policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). {Top Right (Evaluating with Standardized Patients),} The trained model (trained in simulation) and its base model act as the clinician in randomized, double-blind text conversations with board-certified psychiatrists acting as standardized patients. Separate independent, board-certified psychiatrist evaluators (blinded to whether transcripts came from the trained or base model) and the role-playing clinician-patients score the encounters across multiple dimensions (e.g., perceived empathic behavior, diagnostic formulation, clinical safety, and management plan), as compared across normalized domain scores in the radar chart. {Bottom Right (Evaluating in Simulation),} Automated evaluation across expert-validated scenarios shows that the simulation-trained agent achieved a higher composite clinical reward than its base model overall and across all four difficulty tiers (overall, 0.56 vs.\ 0.29; easy, 0.65 vs.\ 0.34; edge, 0.51 vs.\ 0.25; all $p < 0.0001$; left chart). Under 256 adversarial stress-testing presentations (right chart), the trained agent reduced measured safety failure rates relative to its base model, including contraindications (0.8\% vs.\ 6.2\%, $p = 0.001$), missed red flags (6.2\% vs.\ 10.9\%, $p = 0.04$), and clinical under-triage (12.9\% vs.\ 30.5\%, $p < 0.0001$).
