Play2Perfect
: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
Tyler Ga Wei Lum
Kushal Kedia
C. Karen Liu
Jeannette Bohg
Affiliation:
Stanford University
Affiliation:
Cornell University
*
Equal contribution
†
Equal advising
play2perfect.github.io
Abstract
Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can
perfect
precise assembly, it must first learn to
play
. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to
play
matter for precise assembly? We propose
Play2Perfect
, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through
play
on diverse objects and goals, which is then
perfected
on precise assembly. The goal of
play
is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in
play
pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.
Figure 1:
Play2Perfect
Overview.
Before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it first learns to play. We pretrain a single goal-conditioned RL policy on task-agnostic dexterous object manipulation, producing a reusable prior for grasping, in-hand reorientation, and 6D pose control. This pretrained play policy is then finetuned in sparse-reward RL environments derived from CAD designs to solve diverse contact-rich assembly tasks, including tight insertions, screwing, and multi-part assembly.
Keywords:
Reinforcement Learning, Dexterous Manipulation, Sim-to-Real
1
Introduction
Robots with multi-fingered hands hold the potential to bring speed and dexterity to the diverse tasks humans perform with their hands. Yet, this flexibility comes at the cost of controlling many degrees of freedom through contact, leaving challenging domains like precise assembly out of reach for current robot learning methods. On one hand, the contact-rich nature of assembly makes dexterous teleoperation challenging, so most imitation learning has focused on lower-precision pick-and-place tasks
[
58
,
14
,
15
,
39
,
7
]
. On the other hand, assembly is sparse-reward, defined by a part’s final pose, limiting the use of sim-to-real RL methods that require dense-reward shaping
[
56
,
65
,
11
,
2
,
18
,
27
,
13
]
.
Prior work has made progress on assembly by adding structure to the problem. One approach is to modify the environment with custom fixtures that simplify grasping and insertion
[
32
,
42
]
. Another is to modify the robot itself with specialized tool attachments or end-effectors that make the control problem easier
[
17
,
44
]
. However, both strategies require per-assembly engineering of the hardware or environment. The use of robots with parallel-jaw grippers makes teleoperation feasible, enabling imitation learning
[
3
]
and subsequent RL finetuning
[
4
]
. Without teleoperation, RL methods often rely on dense, task-specific rewards
[
52
,
51
]
or scripted multi-stage controllers
[
54
]
. The reliance of these approaches on parallel-jaw grippers still limits their speed and dexterity.
Our goal is to tackle hard, sparse-reward problems such as precise assembly with dexterous hands, without relying on teleoperation. The core challenge is that the sparse reward defined by the final goal configuration of an assembly part offers limited training signal for RL. Starting from a random policy, the agent must discover grasping, in-hand reorientation, alignment, and contact-rich insertion before receiving any reward. Intuitively, before learning the hard problem of
perfecting
precise assembly, a robot should first learn the easier problem of
playing
with objects in free space. While the concept of learning from
play
has been explored previously
[
33
,
57
,
25
,
23
]
, it remains unclear what aspects of the
play
pretraining recipe matter for downstream finetuning, especially for precise assembly. In this work, we systematically study the design choices that make
play
useful for precise assembly, including object diversity, trajectory diversity, training objective, and goal precision. Across these studies, we find a consistent takeaway:
play
pretraining transfers best when it forces the robot to learn in-hand manipulation using its fingers rather than movement with a fixed grasp.
We propose
Play2Perfect
, a framework for dexterous pretraining on general objects and goals, followed by finetuning for precise assembly. In simulation, we pretrain a goal-conditioned
play
policy via RL to manipulate diverse primitive objects to random target poses, inducing a task-agnostic manipulation prior. We then construct assembly finetuning environments from assembly benchmarks
[
54
,
20
]
, using sparse rewards defined by the final part configuration. Across challenging assembly skills, this prior enables 33x more sample-efficient learning than RL from scratch, even when scratch policies are provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with 0.5 mm clearance and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing. Our contributions are:
•
A framework for precise assembly with dexterous hands that first learns a task-agnostic
play
prior on general objects and goals, then
perfects
it to new CAD-defined assembly tasks.
•
A systematic study of
play
pretraining design choices that transfer to contact-rich, precise assembly, including object diversity, trajectory diversity, training objectives, and goal precision.
2
Related Work
Manipulation with Multi-Fingered Robots.
Prior work falls into two categories: imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL). IL relies on collecting high-quality demonstrations, which can be obtained through human hand motion retargeting with motion-capture gloves
[
43
,
58
]
, VR devices
[
15
,
21
,
28
,
6
]
, camera inputs
[
39
,
19
,
50
]
, or exoskeleton systems
[
53
,
60
,
16
]
. However, collecting demonstrations for contact-rich tasks remains difficult due to the embodiment gap between the human operator and the robot, as well as the lack of tactile feedback
[
10
,
46
,
5
,
37
]
. Sim-to-real RL offers a promising alternative, with recent progress on dexterous skills such as grasping
[
1
,
62
,
31
,
48
,
47
]
and in-hand reorientation
[
12
,
11
,
29
]
. Yet, these skills are largely performed in free space. Extending dexterous RL to contact-rich tasks relies on dense reward functions
[
27
,
13
]
, accurate human hand motion references
[
26
,
30
,
34
]
, or warm-starting from teleoperation
[
45
,
9
]
. Closest to our work are methods that train task-agnostic
play
controllers across diverse objects
[
64
,
23
,
25
]
. When combined with teleoperation
[
64
]
or a human demonstration at test time
[
23
]
, these controllers can generalize to unseen objects and tasks. However, they are deployed zero-shot and still struggle with precise, contact-rich tasks such as assembly. Instead, we view
play
as dexterous pretraining: a general prior that is quickly specialized to precise assembly.
Precise and Contact-Rich Assembly.
Most progress in precise, contact-rich assembly has come from structuring the problem through task-specific hardware or environments. Prior work designs specialized gripper attachments or tools to simplify manipulation
[
17
,
44
]
, or uses fixtures to reduce uncertainty in grasping, alignment, and insertion
[
42
,
32
]
. While effective, these approaches require task-specific setup for each assembly problem. Learning-based assembly methods often rely on task-specific structure as well, including dense reward functions
[
52
,
51
]
, scripted multi-stage controllers
[
54
]
, or carefully designed curricula
[
22
]
. Other methods address the exploration problem with dense reset distributions
[
63
]
or teleoperation demonstrations
[
3
,
4
]
, but these still require task insight or task-specific data. In contrast, we pretrain a general dexterous
play
prior without demos or knowledge of the downstream assembly task, and specialize it with sparse-reward RL.
Pretraining for Dexterous Manipulation.
There is growing interest in pretraining broad dexterous priors to solve challenging manipulation tasks. For example, Vision Language Action (VLA) models
[
38
,
35
,
8
]
train on large datasets consisting of diverse tasks
[
36
,
24
]
. However, these datasets are largely concentrated on parallel jaw gripper robots. Human videos on the internet are another promising option to acquire general priors for dexterous hands
[
66
,
61
,
40
,
53
]
. However, human videos do not contain contact information, limiting their use to simple pick and place tasks and often requiring large amounts of in-domain robot finetuning data. Learning from
play
is a promising approach to learn priors from task-agnostic data. Prior works still require teleoperation to collect robot trajectories or active human hand data collection
[
57
,
33
]
. Compared to these works, we train
play
priors by learning to manipulate diverse objects via RL without requiring any demonstrations.
Figure 2:
What matters in dexterous
play
pretraining?
We study the key factors that shape the learned manipulation prior. Our design emphasizes in-hand manipulation with fingers across diverse objects and trajectories, with 6D pose-reaching objectives and precise goal tolerances.

We first train a goal-conditioned policy in simulation to manipulate procedurally generated primitive objects to random poses in free-space. We then use the assembly CAD design to construct a sparse-reward RL environment for finetuning to learn precise, contact-rich goals.
3.1
Dexterous Play Pretraining

Object Diversity.
We aim to acquire broad dexterous competence across a wide range of objects, so that the resulting policy provides a useful initialization for downstream finetuning. To this end, we procedurally generate diverse primitive objects in simulation comprising cuboids and cylinders. Each object’s dimensions are sampled from a broad distribution constrained to fit within the robot hand. We also randomize physical properties by varying object densities and attaching additional masses near object ends. This induces variation in center of mass and inertia, forcing the policy to learn object-control strategies that are not tied to a single geometry or mass distribution. We use primitive shapes to enable fast, stable simulation while keeping pretraining task-agnostic.
Training Objective.
Play pretraining should induce reusable dexterous skills for downstream assembly. Therefore, we train the robot to manipulate objects through a sequence of 6D goal poses: the first goal requires grasping and lifting from the table, while subsequent goals require in-hand control of object pose without drops. Each goal specifies both translation and rotation: translation teaches object motion across the workspace, while rotation encourages in-hand reorientation. The play reward comprises three terms:

We randomize the goal sequence in every play episode rather than training on fixed trajectories. The first goal is sampled broadly in the robot’s workspace, while subsequent goals are sampled near the previous goal with significant rotations. This encourages learning of in-hand manipulation rather than simple arm movements with fixed grasps.

We design experiments to answer the following questions:
1.
Can dense, task-specific rewards overcome the need for

2.

3.

Task Design.
Our robot consists of a 22-DoF Sharpa five-fingered hand mounted on a 7-DoF KUKA iiwa 14 arm. We evaluate on three tasks: 1)

Evaluation Metrics.

In simulation, we report results over 500 rollouts with randomized initial part and fixture poses. In the real world, we evaluate each task over 10 or 20 rollouts using a fixed fixture pose and randomized initial part poses.
4.1
Can Dense Rewards Overcome the Need for
Play

Figure 4:
Dexterous Play Pretraining Enables Efficient Downstream Assembly Learning.
Across four contact-rich assembly tasks,
Play2Perfect
rapidly learns successful policies from the shared dexterous prior, reaching high success within 2-5 hours. In contrast, training from scratch fails to make progress with either sparse task rewards or hand-engineered dense rewards.
Figure 5:
Dexterous Play Pretraining Induces Robust Assembly Strategies.
After simplifying the initialization with an easy-grasp fixture, Scratch (dense reward) can learn the task, but it relies on a brittle strategy that balances the object rather than robustly grasping it. This shortcut fails sharply under external force perturbations. In contrast,
Play2Perfect
learns a more stable grasping and recovery strategy, maintaining high success across perturbation magnitudes.
Setup.
We first test whether a general dexterous prior improves RL learning compared to training from scratch. We measure success rate as a function of RL wall-clock time and compare
Play2Perfect
against two scratch baselines:
Scratch (sparse reward)
, which uses the same sparse assembly success reward as
Play2Perfect
, and
Scratch (dense reward)

4.2
Which Design Choices in
Play
Pretraining Matter Most for Downstream Assembly?
Setup.
We next ablate key
play
pretraining choices and measure how they affect downstream RL finetuning on all 4 tasks averaged over 3 seeds. Per-task results and ablation implementation details are provided in Appendices
C
and
K
, respectively. We vary: 1)
Object Diversity:
pretraining on 10, 100, or 1000 objects sampled from the same primitive distribution, with 1000 as
Play2Perfect
’s default; 2)
Training Objective:
comparing
Play2Perfect
’s full 6D goal-pose objective against
Translation-only
, which rewards only translational error along the same goal-pose sequences, and
Rotation-only
, which first lifts the object to a random 6D pose and then samples only rotational goals at a fixed position; 3)
Trajectory Diversity:
we compare using random goal trajectories (ours) against fixed sets of 10 or 100 trajectories; and 4)
Goal Precision:
varying the success threshold
ϵ
\epsilon
for goal-reaching across 1cm (ours), 5cm, and 10cm.
Results.
Fig.
6
shows that all four design choices affect downstream assembly finetuning. 1)
Object Diversity:
Training with more objects during pretraining leads to more stable RL finetuning, with final success rates consistently increasing from 10 to 1000 objects. 2)
Training Objective:
Orientation control is critical.
Translation-only
pretraining learns grasping and lifting, but does not learn object orientation control, and therefore fails to provide the in-hand reorientation prior needed for assembly.
Rotation-only
pretraining transfers well, but plateaus about 10 points below full 6D pose-goal pretraining, likely because it provides less practice coupling reorientation with translational object motion. 3)
Trajectory Diversity:
Fixed sets of 10 and 100 trajectories perform similarly, while online random trajectories learn fastest and plateau highest, suggesting that broader coverage of goal-pose transitions better matches downstream assembly finetuning. 4)
Goal Precision:
Precise goals are important. A loose 10cm threshold fails to transfer because coarse goal reaching does not require accurate object-pose control. A 5 cm threshold learns more slowly and plateaus near 60%, indicating that precise
play
induces priors better matched to tight-clearance assembly.

Setup.
We demonstrate the application of
Play2Perfect
beyond structured assembly benchmarks to everyday insertion tasks involving smaller, more challenging object geometries. We consider two additional tasks: inserting an iPhone plug into a socket and a YCB fork into a narrow rack opening. Both tasks use the same pretrained play checkpoint and RL finetuning recipe as our main experiments, without task-specific modifications.
Results.
Fig.
8
shows that
Play2Perfect
successfully adapts to both tasks, achieving 90% success in simulation after 8.4 and 2.8 hours of finetuning for the iPhone plug and YCB fork, respectively. These results demonstrate that the learned dexterous prior extends beyond structured industrial assembly to everyday insertion tasks with diverse object geometries.
5
Discussion and Limitations
We presented
Play2Perfect
, a framework for precise contact-rich assembly that finetunes a dexterous prior learned through play. By
play
pretraining across diverse objects,
Play2Perfect
enables fast RL on assembly tasks by adapting the prior to precise contact interactions. Our ablations show that object diversity, objectives, trajectory diversity, and goal precision all affect downstream performance. Finally,
Play2Perfect
transfers zero-shot to challenging real-world dexterous assembly tasks.
Limitations.
Our system learns short-horizon assembly skills rather than a complete autonomous assembly pipeline. Task sequencing, active-part selection, and goal poses are specified externally, and policies are finetuned per task or benchmark family. Future work could combine these skills with sequencing, scene memory, recovery, and broader multi-task finetuning. Real-world deployment also depends on object-pose estimates, which can fail under occlusion or fast motion. Finally, beyond the goal pose, the policy does not directly observe the fixture or surrounding geometry. Incorporating visual or tactile observations could address these perception and scene-awareness limitations.

Appendix E
Real-World Experiment Additional Analysis
Qualitative behavior.
Across real-world tasks,
Play2Perfect
exhibits closed-loop recovery behaviors that are difficult to obtain from a single open-loop assembly motion. During insertion, the policy often searches locally near the hole, makes small corrective motions under contact, and commits once the part is better aligned. When the part becomes misaligned, the policy can recover with additional in-hand reorientations. If the part is dropped, the policy immediately regrasps and continues, provided the object remains within the workspace. In screwing tasks, the fingers spin the leg directly within the hand, enabling axial rotation while maintaining a stable grasp. With a parallel-jaw gripper, comparable reorientation would typically require slower extrinsic manipulation, such as placing and regrasping the part

32
]
, and screwing would require rotating the entire arm around the screw axis rather than spinning the part within the fingers

Failure modes.
Real-world failures arise from both perception and contact dynamics. Perception remains a major failure mode even on larger parts: fast part motion, hand-object occlusion, and visually similar objects can cause the pose estimator to lose track of the manipulated part. Screwing is especially challenging because the policy must track object rotation, while the rectangular leg has approximate 90
∘
rotational symmetries that can confuse pose estimation and cause the policy to rotate in the wrong direction. We add colored tape to each side of the rectangular leg to make the orientations visually distinguishable, but pose estimation remains imperfect during fast rotations and occlusions. Control failures typically occur during the final contact-rich phase, when the policy repeatedly attempts insertion but fails to align with the hole, or contacts the fixture in ways that differ from simulation. In simulation, fixtures are rigid and immovable, while in the real setup, they are taped to a foam tabletop for safety and can move or comply under contact. This behavior is never observed in simulation and can cause the policy to struggle when its corrective motions no longer produce the expected relative motion between the part and fixture. We also observe some failed in-hand reorientations and drops during rotation before insertion, requiring the policy to regrasp. In contrast, grasp acquisition is highly reliable: real-world failures rarely arise from missed grasps except when perception fails catastrophically.

Appendix H
Simulation and Computational Resources
All policies are trained in Isaac Sim on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The physics simulation runs at 120 Hz, while the policy outputs actions at 60 Hz. Play pretraining uses 24,576 parallel simulation environments and is run for 7 days. Each downstream assembly policy is finetuned for 1 day using 12,288 parallel environments. We use fewer environments during finetuning because modeling contact-rich assembly interactions requires more GPU memory than the free-space manipulation used during play pretraining. For each wall-clock comparison, all methods within the same figure are run on the same GPU type with identical hyperparameters, environment counts, and training budgets.
Appendix I
Policy Architecture and RL Algorithm
We train the play policy using Split and Aggregate Policy Gradients (SAPG)
[
49
]
, a population-based variant of PPO that improves exploration in massively parallel environments. The actor uses an LSTM to integrate interaction history and infer unobserved object properties, followed by a multilayer perceptron that outputs the arm and hand actions. We use an asymmetric actor–critic architecture. While the actor receives only the observations available at deployment, the critic additionally receives noise-free and undelayed observations, palm and object velocities, reward signals, and stateful progress features such as the minimum goal distance reached and whether the object has been lifted. This privileged information is used only during training. The same RL algorithm and hyperparameters are used for both pretraining and finetuning.

Policy Observations and Action Space.
The policy receives a 140-dimensional observation containing robot proprioception, the current object pose, the goal pose, and an object geometry descriptor. Robot proprioception includes the 29 joint positions and velocities, previous joint-position targets, palm pose, and the positions of the five fingertips relative to the palm. We represent the current and goal object poses using four keypoints defined by the dimensions of the object’s primary component. The policy observes the object orientation, the current keypoints relative to the palm, the keypoint displacements from the current pose to the goal, and the three object dimensions. Using relative keypoint representations reduces dependence on absolute workspace coordinates while conditioning the policy on object geometry. The policy outputs 29 joint-position commands for the 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand. Arm actions are represented as delta joint-position targets, while hand actions are represented as absolute joint-position targets. All commands are clipped to the corresponding joint limits and smoothed using an exponential moving average with coefficient

We ablate four components of play pretraining: object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. Object Diversity.

Training Objective.
We compare the default 6D pose-reaching objective against Translation-only and Rotation-only variants. The default objective requires jointly matching the target translation and orientation using the keypoint-based pose distance. Translation-only uses the same sampled goal sequences, but computes goal success using only the Euclidean distance between the current and target object positions. The target orientation is ignored. Rotation-only first requires the policy to grasp, lift, and move the object to a randomly sampled 6D pose. Subsequent goals keep this target position fixed and vary only the target orientation, requiring repeated in-hand reorientation without translational goal changes.
Trajectory Diversity.
The default policy samples every goal trajectory online during pretraining. To study the effect of trajectory diversity, we instead construct fixed banks containing either 10 or 100 goal trajectories. Each trajectory follows the same sampling distribution as the default setting, including the same workspace bounds and maximum translation and rotation between consecutive goals. article.headline: 灵巧手先“玩耍”再精密装配
article.lede: 斯坦福等提出 Play2Perfect：先用任务无关的“玩耍”预训练获得灵巧操作先验，再用稀疏奖励微调完成精密装配。
article.problem: 多指灵巧手有望带来速度和灵活性，但精密装配接触丰富，模仿学习数据采集困难；同时装配奖励稀疏，直接从零探索对强化学习几乎不可行。现有工作常靠专用夹具、工具附件、平行夹爪、密集奖励或遥操作来绕开问题。
article.method: Play2Perfect 先在仿真中对程序生成的多样物体和随机 6D 目标做任务无关的 play 预训练，学习抓取、手中重定向和位姿到达等可复用先验。随后，它从 CAD 装配设计自动构造稀疏奖励环境和目标序列，对该先验进行按任务微调；部署时用 FoundationPose 跟踪零件位姿，策略输出手臂和灵巧手的关节位置目标。
article.results: 在四个接触丰富装配任务上，Play2Perfect 约 2–5 小时训练即可学会，而从零训练的稀疏/密集奖励基线 24 小时后仍无成功回合；在简化插入任务上，它 4 小时达到 scratch 密集奖励 100 多小时的水平，约 33 倍提速。仿真插入中，Play2Perfect 在 4 mm、1 mm、0.2 mm 间隙下成功率分别为 95%、92%、80%，Play-only 在 4 mm 时接近 0；真实世界 10 mm、2 mm、0.5 mm 间隙下为 10/10、9/10、6/10。真实多零件梁装配 Step 1 为 16/20、Step 2 为 12/16，拧桌腿插入 7/10、拧入 5/7。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明任务无关的 play 预训练能作为灵巧装配的可复用先验，降低对遥操作和密集奖励的依赖，并支持零样本 sim-to-real 迁移。
article.limitations: 系统只学习短时装配技能，任务排序、主动零件选择和目标位姿仍由外部指定，且策略按任务或基准族微调；真实部署依赖零件位姿估计，遮挡、快速运动和夹具可移动会导致失败，策略也不直接观察夹具或周围几何。
article.figure_caption_zh: 推理时流程复用 CAD 模型估计当前零件位姿、计算相对夹具的目标位姿并定义抓取包围盒，微调策略据此输出手臂与灵巧手的关节位置目标。

email_papers.title: SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
email_papers.abstract: Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools, including articulated ones, and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot.
email_papers.content:
SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
Yunchu Zhang, Ray Song, Junhan Jiao,
Liyiming Ke, Yuchen Yang
Ruihan Gao, Emma Romig,
Siddhartha Srinivasa, Yiyue Luo
University of Washington
Abstract
Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools—including articulated ones—and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15–25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website
https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot
.
I
Introduction
Fig. 2
:
(
Left
) SwapBot setup overview with the robot arm, robot-mounted tool adapter, electromagnetic coupling, the tool dock, and tactile I/O board.
(
Middle
) The structure of the instrumented tools with integrated tactile sensing using piezoresistive film, showing sensor layers and placements, with examples for a knife, brush, and tongs. (
Right
) Characterization of tactile sensors, showing force–response curves for electrodes of different sizes. Larger electrode areas exhibit higher sensitivity, but also cause non-smooth signals with sudden jumps under load. Smaller electrodes have smoother signals and a wider measurable range.
Robotic manipulation is advancing toward increasingly human-level capabilities; however, seemingly simple tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, remain challenging for robots to perform. Performed with different tools under contact-rich interaction, these tasks require precise but forceful control (cutting), delicate interaction with deformable objects (brushing), and dexterous motion (grasping and placing). Such
tool-centric manipulation
is challenging under the current end-effector design, which falls into two broad categories. First,
anthropomorphic hands
mimic human dexterity
[
19
,
5
]
, but their mechanical complexity imposes a high cost in maintenance, sensing, and control, hindering scalable data collection and policy learning. Second,
parallel jaw grippers
, though practical and demonstrating impressive versatility
[
29
,
1
,
13
]
, struggle to perform tasks requiring nuanced physical interactions, such as cutting or spreading. These capability vs controllability tradeoffs create significant barriers to more capable and scalable tool-centric robot manipulation.
Humans accomplish complex manipulation tasks by using tools, e.g., knives, brushes, or screwdrivers, as extensions of their bodies. Robotists have explored tool use using dexterous hands
[
3
,
25
]
or parallel grippers
[
14
,
21
]
. However, existing methods either inherit the complexity of manipulating anthropomorphic hands, struggling to maintain tool stability under load, or, critically, lack tactile sensing
[
28
]
at the tool-object interface, hindering effective control and learning for contact-rich tasks.
To balance robot manipulators’ capability and controllability, we propose to equip robots with the ability to swap modular tools through a tool changer. Industrial tool changers, such as those used in CNC machining or on UR5 robots, demonstrate the practicality of extending robotic capabilities through automatic tool exchange. However, these costly systems are typically customized for specific robots and cannot easily accommodate actively articulated tools - e.g., tongs and scissors. Moreover, they lack integration with tactile sensing, limiting their ability to support contact-rich manipulation tasks. Instead, our approach turns accessible household items into robot tools and equips each tool with compact, custom tactile sensors, enabling robots to both select the appropriate tool for each subtask and sense contact at the tool–object interface. Drawing inspiration from surgical robots that interchange end-effectors such as scissors, cauterizers, and forceps,
our system thus enables scalable household manipulation through tool diversity, not anatomical mimicry
.
We present
SwapBot, a modular, low-cost, tool-centric manipulation system with integrated tactile sensors
, as shown in Fig.
. It features: (1)a unified adaptation interface for diverse tools and robots, (2) fast and autonomous tool swapping protocol, (3) integrated tactile sensing, and (4) intuitive teleoperation for demonstration data collection. Our system employs inexpensive, 3D-printed interfaces ($10 each)
to quickly adapt common household tools
. We apply this modular system to three robot platforms: Franka
[
8
]
, UR5
[
24
]
, and Tycho
[
12
]
and to a variety of household tools - including articulated tools that require actuation, such as tongs and chopsticks. Robots equipped with our system can use our designed coupling interface and protocol
to autonomously switch the tool within 10 seconds
. Our teleoperation interface combines tool-matched leader devices with real-time visualized tactile feedback, providing operators with an intuitive interface for contact-rich manipulation. Furthermore, we show that employing tactile sensing significantly boosts the performance of the autonomous policy learned from human demonstrations.
Fig. 3
:
SwapBot can be adapted to three different types of robots: Tycho, UR5, and Franka.
To assess the ease of teleoperation with SwapBot, we conduct human studies with 12 participants of varying teleoperation skill levels (beginner, intermediate, and expert), focusing on two representative tasks: brushing and cutting. Participants report less subjective workload of control and higher success rates compared to the use of a generic teleoperation tool. SwapBot also enables the teleoperated completion of tasks previously found challenging or impossible for simple grippers, reducing task completion time and offering more satisfying user experiences. In robotic experiments, we further demonstrate the autonomous execution of a challenging long-horizon task: cooking pan-fried tofu. Using the demonstration data that our system collected, we train imitation learning policies and show that tactile feedback significantly improves policy performance, increasing task success rates by 25 absolute percentage points, from
35
%
35\%
to
60
%
60\%
. We additionally provide qualitative results (e.g., stirring salad and flipping meat) in the supplementary videos. In summary, our contributions include:
1.
A
unified, low-cost, modular tool-centric end-effector system
that supports rapid autonomous tool swapping and the use of diverse household tools, including articulated tools.
2.
Integrated compact tactile sensing
that improves both teleoperation performance and imitation-learning success in contact-rich task.
3.
An
intuitive teleoperation interface for collecting demonstrations
, improving operator precision and enabling high-quality data collection.
4.
Empirical evaluation
via user studies and policy learning: quantitative tofu-cooking results and qualitative demonstrations of stirring salad and flipping meat, showing improved user experience and policy performance.
II
The SwapBot System
Fig. 4

Overview of the hierarchical policy learning framework.
The high-level tool-selection policy

The SwapBot system contains four main components: modular and interchangeable end-effectors (Section
II-A
), compact tactile sensing (Section
II-B
), the teleoperation interface (Section
II-C
), and policy learning from demonstrations (Section

). Our plug-and-play design supports low-cost prototyping with a variety of daily-use tools while supporting tactile sensing, large-scale demonstration collection, and downstream policy learning. We describe each component below.
II-A
Modular End-Effectors:
Tool Adapters and Coupling
Design Goals.
Industrial robotic coupling is usually tailored to specific tools and robots and often costs hundreds or even thousands of dollars. In contrast, we aim to develop a modular tool coupling system that is accessible and low cost (tool-side modules under $10), rapid swapping of tools, robot-agnostic, enabling compatibility with common manipulators, and flexible for both passive and articulated tools. To achieve these goals, we design our tool-swapping adapter and coupling system to enable a fully accessible fabrication workflow and straightforward assembly using basic hand tools, such as an Allen wrench.
As shown in Figure
2
(left), we 3D-print tool adapters and inserts to enable the quick instrumentation and mounting of common household tools. The adapter both attaches the tool securely and houses the tactile sensors stably. For tools with moderate handle sizes, the same adapter can be reused, while soft silicone fills the remaining gap to accommodate variations in handle shape and size. Only substantially thinner tools require a smaller 3D-printed adapter, while the robot-side coupling interface remains unchanged. Though many everyday tools include their own actuation mechanisms, equipping each with dedicated motors for automatic control would be complex and expensive. Instead, we shift all power and control functionalities to the robot side, ensuring a simpler and lower-cost tool implementation. To transmit torque, we add a bearing system on top of the adapter cover that transfers motion from the robot’s end joint. For robots without a final joint, we supplement with a single servo motor to ensure compatibility across Franka, UR, and other common platforms (Fig.
3
).
To support rapid tool exchange, we implement a self-aligning electromagnetic coupling that mates a robot-side hub with tool-side adapters. This design supports both passive tools (e.g., knives, brushes) and articulated tools (e.g., tongs, chopsticks) through a pass-through mechanism. A kinematically guided gear ensures reliable engagement and release under small alignment errors, while the electromagnet provides sufficient holding force for secure tool attachment during forceful manipulation. In practice, our system completes a swap in about 10 s by guiding the robot to a docking station, releasing the current tool, and attaching a new one. This approach shifts capability from a single complex hand to a library of instrumented tools while retaining the ability to compose skills across tools. II-B
Compact Tactile Sensing: Instrumented Tools
We design compact, tool-specific piezoresistive tactile sensors that provide task-relevant contact information for teleoperation and policy learning. By tailoring the sensor layout to each tool, we capture force information without adding bulk or compromising usability.
The piezoresistive tactile sensors consist of a three-layer structure, shown in Fig.
2
(center), where a force-sensitive material layer (Velostat) is sandwiched between top and bottom electrodes (conductive fabric) for signal transmission. These sensors
[
22
]
convert real-time normal force pressure information into an electrical signal via the drop of resistance. The electrodes are made from copper-nickel conductive fabric, laser-cut to precise dimensions for optimal fit considering the sensitivity they need for tasks. To accommodate the limited surface area of tools, we implement the sensors in a matrix layout, where sensing nodes are formed at the intersections of orthogonal electrode rows and columns. This configuration enables an n
×
\times
n sensor array using only 2n electrodes. Our approach is low-cost, relies on only off-the-shelf materials, and supports easy customization through digital fabrication.
We show the design and placement of tactile sensors for each tool in Fig.
2
(center). For tools with larger surfaces, we place sensors on both the handle and the blade or tip (e.g., tongs, spoons, knives). For smaller or thinner tools, such as chopsticks, brushes, and forks, it is impractical to mount sensors directly on the blade or tip. In these cases, we instrument only the handle, providing indirect measurements of tool–object interaction. This strategy ensures that tactile information is captured where feasible while keeping the modules compact and lightweight. For blade or tip instrumentation, we mount the fabricated tactile sensors directly onto the tool surface. To accommodate handles of varying sizes, instead of attaching sensors directly, we install them between the TPU layer and the PLA adapter cover and fill the gap between the handle and TPU shell with soft silicone. This approach allows the sensors to comply with different handle shapes, stabilizes the installation process, and ensures consistent reflection of sensor readings during interaction.

II-C
Teleoperation Interface: High-Quality Demonstration Collection
We design the teleoperation interface to maximize operator intuitiveness and data quality, both of which are critical for downstream policy learning. Our interface maps the intuitive leader device’s 6-DoF pose and actuation commands directly to the corresponding tool on the robot side. By using similar tools on both sides, e.g., chopsticks to control chopsticks or a knife to control a knife, operators interact with familiar household tools, making control feel natural. This reduces the re-targeting effort common in teleoperation and lets operators focus on task execution rather than compensating for mismatched dynamics. For each leader tool, we estimate the 6-DoF pose using an Intel RealSense T265 tracking camera, and use the result to drive the robot during teleoperation. For articulated tools, we infer the actuation command from the relative motion measured by two IMUs, providing accurate correspondence between human and robot tool motion.
During demonstration data collection, all data streams are synchronized at 20 Hz, including multi-view RGB images, tactile signals, robot joint states, actions, and task labels. This ensures that multimodal inputs remain temporally aligned for learning. We also provide visual overlays that display the live contact forces and tactile maps to help operators anticipate and refine contact-rich interactions. As we will show in Fig.
6
, tactile information is visualized on-screen to indicate contact information. This immediate feedback provides operators with additional information about contact, improving both control precision and the quality of collected demonstrations.
To evaluate the interface, we conduct controlled human studies to measure task completion time, success rate, and the subjective workload (see Sec.
III-B
). Integrated tactile feedback emphasizes subtle events, such as first contact or changes in load distribution, which are often ambiguous in vision alone. This design reduces cognitive load and improves operator precision for long-horizon tasks such as cutting, grasping, and transporting.

Our experiments aim to answer the following questions.
(1) Characterization of tactile sensing:
How well do our compact, tool-specific tactile sensors perform in terms of sensitivity and detection range, and does our design achieve the right balance for integration into diverse tools?
(2) Intuitive teleoperation:
Does our tool-centric teleoperation interface provide a natural, user-friendly experience that improves demonstration efficiency and data quality compared to standard baselines?
(3) Policy learning with tactile feedback:
Does integrating tactile sensing into imitation learning policies improve performance on complex, long-horizon tasks?
III-A
Characterizing Tool-Specific Tactile Sensing
Directly applying the tactile sensors without considering their size and sensitivity can lead to saturated and inconsistent signals during data streaming. To ensure smooth and reproducible sensing, we characterize the performance of our resistive tactile sensors made with electrodes of varying widths. Signals were recorded under controlled pressure using a force gauge, from which we extracted both sensitivity and detection range. These measurements provide valuable insights into how the electrode design impacts sensing quality and guides our choice of parameters.
As we show in Figure
2
(right), electrode size has a direct impact on both sensitivity and signal quality. Larger electrodes provide higher sensitivity, with identical forces producing stronger responses due to increased overlap between the conductive layers. However, these larger electrodes also generate non-smooth signals with sudden jumps under load, and can saturate the 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC), making them less reliable for continuous feedback. Smaller electrodes, by contrast, sacrifice sensitivity but produce smoother, more stable signals with a wider measurable range. To balance sensitivity, detection range, and signal fidelity within ADC limits, we select a 2 mm electrode width, which provides sufficient sensitivity while maintaining smooth, stable responses.
III-B
Evaluating Intuitive Tool-Centric Teleoperation
To evaluate the interface, we conduct a controlled human study with 12 participants spanning three teleoperation skill levels (beginner, intermediate, and expert), with four participants in each group. Each participant performs both brushing and cutting tasks under three teleoperation conditions: a general VR-style tool, SwapBot without tactile feedback, and SwapBot with visualized tactile feedback. Each participant performs 10 trials per task–condition pair, terminating upon success or a 60-s timeout. Completion time is computed over successful trials, while failures contribute only to the success-rate metric. The order of teleoperation conditions was counterbalanced across participants to reduce learning and fatigue effects, while task order was randomized. We measured task completion time, success rate, and subjective workload using NASA-TLX, normalized to a 0–10 scale. For completion time and success rate, we first aggregate the 10 trials for each participant and then report the mean performance across the four participants within each expertise level.
As demonstrated in Fig.
6
, the SwapBot interface generally improves teleoperation performance over the baseline across both tasks. The visualized tactile feedback provided operators with direct information about contact forces and load changes, enabling more effective manipulation during teleoperation. This interface also supports demonstration collection for more complex tasks, as illustrated in Fig.
5
.
Quantitatively, participants consistently achieved higher task success rates and reported lower cognitive load with our system compared to the baseline general teleoperation tool. These results suggest that our teleoperation design supports efficient and intuitive demonstration collection.

III-C
Policy Learning with Tactile Feedback for Long-Horizon Tasks
We then evaluate whether tactile sensing improves imitation learning for complex, long-horizon manipulation. As a testbed, we use the challenging real-world task of preparing pan-fried tofu for quantitative experiments. The tofu is fragile and easily breaks if mishandled, requiring both gentle and dexterous manipulation. The robot must (1) gently brush sauce onto the tofu, (2) transport it to a pot using tongs for frying, and (3) return it to the cutting board and slice it into two pieces without damage. A trial is successful if the tofu is placed back on the board and cut cleanly into two pieces. Additionally, we provide qualitative demonstrations of other tool-mediated behaviors (e.g., stirring salad and flipping meat) in supplementary videos.
We used our teleoperation interface to collect 100 demonstrations for each stage, i.e., brushing, transporting to the pot, and cutting. The reverse transport back to the board was not evaluated quantitatively since it mirrors the forward motion, but we collected the same number of demonstrations to train the policy for completeness and composition. We then used these demonstrations to train tool-specific imitation learning policies under different input modalities. As baselines, we compared against policies trained without tactile sensing. We also performed ablations using: tactile only, top-down RGB + tactile, and egocentric T265 RGB + tactile. For all policies, we used a CNN feature extractor concatenated with proprioceptive state and tactile signals (when available) as inputs to the policy network. We evaluated each tool-specific policy across 20 trials in a 20 cm
×
\times
20 cm workspace. Policies trained with tactile sensing achieved consistently higher success rates and were robust to small tofu shape changes and variations on initial position. RGB-only policies, in contrast, frequently failed due to partial observability of the tool–object interaction—especially at the tong tips where contact onset and incipient slip are often occluded in RGB—leading to poor contact regulation, slipping, or damage. Egocentric RGB + tactile performed poorly, reaching at most 40% success even with 100 demonstrations and staying near zero in tong picking and knife cutting tasks. Top-down RGB + tactile achieved moderate success (up to 50% in brushing and cutting), but it lagged significantly behind our full RGBs + tactile method.
Though the top-down view offers reliable localization of the tofu on the cutting board, it lacks local visual detail for fine control. Conversely, the egocentric T265 view provides local information but suffers from its angled viewpoint (greater than 45°), which reduces localization accuracy compared to the near-vertical top-down camera. Our full RGBs + tactile policy achieved up to 85

success in brushing, 70
%
\%
in tong picking, and 90
%
\%
in knife cutting, clearly outperforming all baselines (Tab.
II
). These results highlight why tactile sensing, combined with complementary visual perspectives, is essential for robust and contact-rich manipulation.

IV
Related Work
IV-A
Tool Manipulation
To enable robots to understand and manipulate tools, prior work has explored task-oriented grasping and functional affordances through self-supervised learning
[
6
,
23
]
. However, these works mainly focus on how to utilize a single tool’s different parts, i.e., how the tool should be grasped.
[
14
]
,
[
21
]
further demonstrate long-horizon manipulation involving diverse tools through planning and learning.
In contrast, our work focuses on an integrated hardware and learning system that converts everyday household tools into interchangeable, tactile-instrumented end effectors, combines tool-matched teleoperation with tactile feedback for demonstration collection, and learns visuotactile policies for contact-rich manipulation.
Moreover, previous works
[
6
,
18
]
try to learn the synergy between different tool grasping points and tasks using self-supervised learning methods. The learned latent representations could provide a structured and condensed understanding of tool objects. However, our method does not rely on tool-affordance representations; instead, it uses a mechanically simple custom tool changer to directly focus on the interaction and manipulation parts of the task.
IV-B
Tool Design for Robot Tool Usage
Several works aim to extend the range of tasks a single robot can perform by improving tool design and switching mechanisms. Industrial robots such as the UR5 employ dedicated tool changers that provide robust
and precise switching performance. However, these systems are typically tailored to specific robots and tools, are expensive, and cannot easily accommodate actively articulated tools.
Previous works have explored interchangeable surgical instruments
[
17
]
and mechanically actuated tools compatible with parallel grippers
[
10
]
. In contrast, SwapBot provides a unified, low-cost system that supports both passive and articulated household tools, ensures secure coupling and reliable torque transmission for forceful, contact-rich manipulation, and integrates tactile sensing with tool-matched teleoperation for demonstration collection and downstream policy learning.
IV-C
Tactile Sensing for Manipulation
Tactile sensors capture real-time force information and have been widely applied for dexterous, real-world manipulation.
Visual-tactile systems, such as GelSight
[
26
]
, use a soft reflective layer paired with an embedded camera to detect force magnitude and direction through subtle surface deformation. These systems provide high-resolution tactile feedback and have been demonstrated for a variety of robotic tasks, including fine-grained manipulation
[
20
]
, material identification
[
7
]
, and pose estimation
[
9
]
. To extend tactile coverage over larger areas of a robot’s body, capacitive and resistive tactile skins are often used
[
16
]
. These skins typically use a three-layer stack of orthogonal electrodes with a dielectric/resistive layer, where electrode intersections act as pressure-sensing nodes. This scalable design supports seamless integration onto customized robotic components, such as grippers
[
30
]
, arms
[
15
]
, and full-body surfaces
[
2
]
, enabling broader and more versatile tactile sensing in complex environments. Our system adopts scalable tactile sensor designs and customizes them to diverse tools via digital fabrication. Tactile data has also been integrated into policy training for a variety of manipulation tasks, often showing substantial performance gains. For example, sensors mounted on parallel grippers
[
11
,
27
]
provide valuable contact information that improves grasp stability and task success. However, such approaches are typically limited to specific gripper designs. In contrast, SwapBot enables more flexible measurement at the tool–object interface.
V
Conclusion
We presented SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric manipulation system with integrated tactile sensing that improves demonstration collection and policy learning for long-horizon tasks. Tactile feedback proved crucial for both teleoperation quality and imitation learning robustness, especially with limited data. However, the current system has limitations: tactile sensors remain low resolution and prone to wear, sensor placement is fixed by human intuition, and policy learning depends on predefined task segmentation. Future work will explore more durable, higher-resolution sensing, data-driven strategies for sensor placement, and autonomous policy sequencing without manual subgoal definitions. We will also open-source the system to promote reproducibility and community adoption.

article.headline: SwapBot：可换工具与触觉的机器人操作
article.lede: 研究者提出模块化末端执行器系统，让机器人快速更换家用工具，并用触觉提升接触密集任务表现。
article.problem: 日常操作常需借助刀具、刷子、夹钳等工具完成接触密集任务，机器人需要自主更换并使用合适工具。拟人手复杂昂贵，平行夹爪难以完成切割、涂抹等动作；工业工具更换器多为特定机器人定制、成本高，且不易支持铰接工具与触觉传感。
article.method: SwapBot 采用统一的机器人侧电磁耦合接口和低成本 3D 打印工具侧适配器，把家用工具变成可快速更换、带压阻触觉传感器的末端执行器，并兼容 Franka、UR5、Tycho 等平台。策略上，高层工具选择器根据顶视观测和目标图像选工具，低层工具专用扩散策略以多视角图像、触觉和本体状态为输入输出动作，形成长时任务闭环。
article.results: 在真实豆腐烹饪任务中，使用触觉示范的策略将整体成功率从仅 RGB 的 35% 提升到 60%，即提高 25 个百分点；分阶段最高成功率为刷酱 85%、夹取 70%、切割 90%，论文还报告触觉相较仅 RGB 在接触密集技能上提升 15–25 个百分点。高层工具选择器测试准确率为 96.8%，工具切换约 10 秒，电磁耦合保持力最高 50 N，工具侧模块成本低于 10 美元。12 名参与者的用户研究显示 SwapBot 遥操作完成时间更短、成功率更高、NASA-TLX 负荷更低，但正文未给出这些指标的精确数值。
article.why_it_matters: 它把工具多样性而非单一通用夹爪作为扩展机器人能力的路径，并把触觉、遥操作数据采集和模仿学习串成可复现流程，对家庭长时操作有参考价值。
article.limitations: 局限包括触觉传感器分辨率低且易磨损，传感器位置由人工经验固定，策略依赖预定义任务分段和人工指定子目标。模态消融多为单种子结果，完整任务 20 次 rollout 的失败主要来自豆腐滑落或分布外状态，恢复策略仍不系统。
article.figure_caption_zh: SwapBot 的分层策略框架：高层工具选择策略根据顶视观测和目标图像选择工具，激活对应的低层视触觉控制策略，在长时任务中闭环切换工具并执行技能。

figure.caption: Overview of the hierarchical policy learning framework. The high-level tool-selection policy $ _{ {sel}}$ takes top-view observations $ {O}_{top}$ and a goal image $ {O}_g$ as input and outputs a distribution over candidate tools. The selected tool index $ $ activates the corresponding low-level tool-specific control policy $ _{ {tool}}^ $. Each policy conditions on visual observations $ {O}_t$, tactile feedback $ {T}_t$, and proprioceptive state $s_t$ to generate end-effector actions. During long-horizon execution, the robot continuously conducts tool selection and skill execution in a closed-loop, which enables \ to compose tool-specific skills for long-horizon tasks.

Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
Jiongfan Yang

1

3
SenseTime,
†
\dagger
Corresponding author
Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

https://yangjiongfan.site/specslot/

1   Introduction
Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with a computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As a result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on a
256
×
256
256\times 256
image, reducing the patch size from
16
×
16
16\times 16
to
8
×
8
8\times 8

16
×
16\times
larger.
Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence
[
34
]
. Multiscale systems move detail to extra stages or detailer heads
[
52
,
9
,
22
]
, and efficient-attention methods shorten the sequence with generic patterns—windows, selected global tokens, or learned sparsity
[
36
,
4
,
31
,
55
]
. Spectral Forcing brings in frequency structure, but only to filter the noisy input; its tokens remain spatial patches
[
19
]
. Across the pixel-space generators discussed above, output detail remains tied to a spatial patch grid, even when communication is compressed or restricted.
Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. A token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while a token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what a token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can a token’s output role also determine how it should communicate?
SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations:
Read
,
Allocate
, and
Route
. Read forms a grid of spatial anchors that collect input evidence. Allocate expands each anchor into
K
K
indexed slots, with each slot assigned a disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. A spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add a local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure
2
illustrates this design.

This representation exposes two separate allocation variables.
W
W
controls the density of spatial anchors, while
K
K
controls the spectral subdivision at each anchor. The total number of slots grows with
W
​
K
WK
, but the global image sequence contains only
W
W
carriers. A fixed token budget can therefore be allocated either to denser spatial anchors or to finer spectral roles without forcing both to increase together. This turns tokenization from a single patch-size choice into an explicit quality–compute allocation problem.
Our contributions are:
•
We introduce an indexed

representation in which spatial anchors collect input evidence and slots receive disjoint spectral coefficient groups. The split exposes anchor density and coefficient subdivision as separate allocation variables, and the same slot states also decode a local pixel correction.
•
We define carrier-routed global–global–local–local (GGLL) attention from the slot index: one lowest-radial carrier per anchor enters global blocks, and all slots enter anchor-local blocks, so the global sequence contains
W

•
On ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512, SpecSlot provides two measured quality–compute operating points between JiT’s low-cost and high-cost settings. At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Larger output windows cover more pixels while the global sequence remains fixed; the larger improvement over JiT-CM is consistent with this within-anchor allocation. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot likewise surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
2   Related Work
Diffusion and pixel-space generation.
Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis

This line has followed several routes: Simple Diffusion and Hourglass DiT reduce the state internally, cascaded models and PixelFlow distribute generation across resolutions, and JiT shows that a direct large-patch Transformer can remain a strong pixel-space baseline

SpecSlot complements this line with a single-backbone allocation: indexed slots carry fixed output and communication roles, so detail can be subdivided without making every output token global.

Frequency offers a complementary view of this problem. It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. In the first line, inverse heat dissipation, wavelet models, sparse transform codes, and DCTdiff change the representation or process used for generation

7   Conclusion
SpecSlot recasts tokenization as allocation: a fixed token budget is split between anchor density and spectral subdivision, while global attention is assigned by role. On ImageNet-256, it reaches a comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models a new way to trade detail for communication.

article.headline: 频谱槽位解耦像素生成细节与全局注意力
article.lede: SpecSlot 按 DCT 频带把锚点分槽，仅低频槽位进全局注意力；ImageNet-512 少算力降 FID 2.8
article.problem: 像素空间生成 Transformer 通常一个图像 patch 对应一个 token，因此细节越细就需要越多 token，全局注意力的二次成本随之上涨。现有方法虽在压缩或限制通信，但大多仍把输出细节与 token 通信绑在同一空间网格上。
article.method: SpecSlot 把每个空间锚点扩展成 K 个槽位，每个槽位负责一组不重叠的径向 DCT 系数，从而把锚点密度与频谱细分拆开。只有最低频槽位作为载体进入全局注意力，所有槽位在锚点内做局部交互；空间头再用槽位状态在像素空间加局部修正，而生成状态、目标和损失仍留在像素空间。
article.results: ImageNet-256 上 W256/K4 的 FID 为 6.59，与 FLOPs 匹配的 JiT-CM（6.68）相当且早期收敛更快。ImageNet-512 上 FID 比 JiT-CM 低 2.84、FLOPs 少 3.9%，与 JiT-B/16 仅差 0.69 FID 而成本低 38.2%。文本到图像 DPG-Bench 得分 62.21，超过 JiT-B/8 的 61.15，前向成本低 40.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 把 tokenization 变成锚点密度与频谱细分的显式预算分配，并让通信资格由输出角色决定，为像素空间生成在细节与全局注意力成本之间提供新的折中点。
article.limitations: 消融仅在固定 N=2048 等有限配置内观察到增加锚点密度更划算，作者未声称该规则可外推；此外 K 从 2 增至 8 时有效槽位比例由 0.803 降至 0.495，且文本到图像 GenEval 仍落后 JiT-B/8（26.99 对 29.78）。
article.figure_caption_zh: SpecSlot 生成的文本到图像示例；更多带提示词的样本见附录图 10。

Abstract
Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same
transformer, or parts of it, to token representations, effectively making the
model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful
depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or
autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense
decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model
are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between
loops. Our experiments span models with up to
1B parameters
, trained on
up to
155B tokens
using up to
1.07
×
𝟏𝟎
𝟐𝟏
\mathbf{1.07\times 10^{21}}
training FLOPs
, with up to
𝟑𝟐
\mathbf{32}
loops
. We find that
looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed
parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return
when training FLOPs are constrained. These trade-offs also depend on the number
of loops: adding loops is not uniformly beneficial, and gains eventually
saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This saturation motivates asking whether
forcing every loop to use exactly the same weights limits the benefit of deeper
looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that
improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. A separate practical
concern for looped transformers is the sequential dependency during
autoregressive generation, which causes a slowdown proportional to the number
of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this limitation by passing
information between loops across adjacent token positions via hidden states,
allowing loop stages to run concurrently during decoding. However, in our
experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality
gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding
and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before
combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training
budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching
the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.

Right:
for 1B models across TPP 10–160, looping retains or improves mean NLL-ranked accuracy across eight reasoning and question-answering tasks; the modified PLT variants match or exceed Standard Looping.
See
App. D
for the efficiency calculation and task-level results.
Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or selected parts of it, to token representations, allowing the model to behave like a deeper network without storing a new set of parameters at every ‘depth’
(
Dehghani et al., 2018
;
Saunshi et al., 2025
;
Geiping et al., 2025
)
. This makes looping attractive when model size is constrained, but the additional depth is not free: every extra loop must still be executed. As a result, a design that uses parameters efficiently may not use training compute efficiently.
Prior work reflects this trade-off, showing that repeated shared computation can recover some of the benefits of additional depth, while adding independently parameterized layers can be preferable when training compute is constrained
(
Schwethelm et al., 2026
;
Prairie et al., 2026
)
. The same weight reuse, however, raises another question as more loops are added. In ordinary looping, every loop applies the same weights, even though later loops operate on representations that have already been transformed several times. This suggests that exact weight sharing may
give diminishing returns
with deeper looping. Prior work has relaxed this constraint by giving each loop iteration a different low-rank adapter while keeping the main transformer weights shared
(
Bae et al., 2025
)
.
Looped transformers also suffer from a separate issue during autoregressive generation: each loop for a token still depends on the output of the previous loop, so the model must execute them one after another, increasing the sequential computation required to generate each token. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize this dependency by passing hidden states from one loop to the next across adjacent token positions, allowing multiple loop stages to be evaluated in parallel during decoding
(
Wu et al., 2025
)
. This change alters the information available to each loop, and recent work reports that gains can decrease as more parallel loops are added
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
. This leaves open what information the shifted transition must preserve for parallel looping to remain effective at greater loop depth. Together, these studies show that looping is not a single design choice but a set of coupled trade-offs. Repeating more of the model can make better use of a fixed parameter budget but requires more training compute; reusing the same weights across more loops can make exact sharing increasingly restrictive; and changing the dependency between loops can parallelize sequential looping while also changing the information available to each loop. These trade-offs may also change with model scale and training budget. Despite prior work studying these choices in different settings, it remains unclear which conclusions generalize and how the choices interact. We therefore study them within a common training from-scratch setting across model scales and training budgets, and ask:
How should transformer layers be looped under constraints on model size, training compute, and autoregressive inference?
We address this question through a controlled study of dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch. Our experiments span models with up to
1B parameters
, up to
155B training tokens
, up to
1.07
×
𝟏𝟎
𝟐𝟏
\mathbf{1.07\times 10^{21}}
training FLOPs
, and up to
𝟑𝟐
\mathbf{32}
loops
. We organize the study around three linked aspects of looping:
Main Contributions.

Background and Methods
2.1

Experiments
3.1

Experimental Setup
We train models with 70M, 100M, 200M, 300M, 500M, and 1B parameters,
containing 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 16 stored transformer layers, respectively.
Training budgets range from 10 to 160 tokens per parameter (TPP). All models
use the same pretraining mixture of natural language, code, mathematical, and
scientific content, with the data sources, sampling distribution, preprocessing,
tokenizer, and training setup held fixed across architectures. We use a fixed subset of the DCLM Baseline 1.0 validation set
(
Li et al., 2024
)
, containing approximately 41 million tokens, as our
primary measure of language-modeling quality and report bits per byte (BPB;
lower is better). To test whether the trends observed on DCLM hold across
datasets, we additionally evaluate on other language-modeling corpora and a
broader set of mathematical, code, reasoning, and question-answering
benchmarks. These results, together with the full model configurations,
training details, evaluation protocols, and task-level results, are provided
in the appendix (see
App. C
).
3.2
Which Forms of Looping Work, and When?

attention alone, the MLP alone, or attention and the MLP separately.

While keeping the model size fixed, there is a large design space for
deciding which components of the transformer to loop, in what order, and
how many times to loop them. We investigate which of these choices improve
model quality and whether their effects depend on model scale and training
budget. We compare seven designs (
Fig. 2
)
across five dense model scales ranging from 70M to 500M parameters,
token-to-parameter ratios (TPP) of up to 160, and loop factors

, where available. At each model size, we consider
experiments that constrain either (a) the total amount of training data

Conclusion and Future Directions
We show that looping is a multidimensional design
problem that must jointly account for stored parameters, training FLOPs, data
efficiency, and inference efficiency. A promising future direction is to
find ways of combining PLT with speculative decoding to further reduce inference latency.
Another is to develop a theory of how normalization and current-token
embedding reinjection affect stability in both the cross-token recurrence of
PLT and the same-token recurrence of standard looping, and to identify which
regimes favor each approach.

B.2
Low-Rank Adaptation and Relaxed Weight Sharing
A looped Transformer repeats the same layer, or group of layers,
L
L
times.
Normally, every loop uses the same attention and MLP weights. Sharing the
weights in this way keeps the model small, since adding loops does not require
storing new Transformer layers. However, the loops do not all receive the same
kind of input. The first loop processes the initial representation, while later
loops process representations that have already passed through the shared
layers one or more times. It may therefore be useful for different loops to
learn slightly different transformations.
One option would be to give every loop its own attention and MLP weights. This
would provide complete specialization, but it would also make the loops
equivalent to separately parameterized Transformer layers. The number of
stored parameters would then grow with the number of loops, removing much of
the motivation for weight reuse. We instead use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
to place a small loop-specific correction around a larger
shared weight matrix.

Additional Results for Parallel Looping
This appendix provides the additional experiments supporting
Subsec. 3.4
. As described in
Subsec. B.3
, Parallel
Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize looping so that, after a short warm-up,
the computations for different loops can be evaluated together during
autoregressive decoding. Evaluating several loop inputs with the same weights
can increase
arithmetic intensity
, the amount of arithmetic performed
for each byte read from memory, because one set of weights can be reused
across those inputs. PLT does not remove any of the loop computations. During
training, the model still runs all
L
L
loops, and the training FLOPs increase
accordingly. We evaluate model quality and account for training FLOPs here;
we do not measure wall-clock decoding latency or throughput.
Our analysis follows a single diagnostic sequence. We first reconstruct the
original PLT design and identify the quality loss introduced by its shifted
transition. We call the rule that combines the current-token representation
with the shifted state the
re-injection rule
. We then measure these two
representations, normalize them before they are combined, and test whether the
combination needs a learned gate or additional sources of context. Finally, we
evaluate the resulting design across model scale, loop count, training budget,
evaluation corpus, stored parameters, and training FLOPs. Unless stated
otherwise, quality is teacher-forced bits per byte (BPB) on the DCLM
validation set, and lower is better. We do not fill in missing observations or
connect curves across missing points.
Throughout this appendix,
Vanilla (No Looping)
denotes the unlooped
baseline, and
Full-Stack Looping
denotes ordinary same-token looping.
For readability, we call our selected parallel design
shifted PLT (ours)
. It separately normalizes the current-token and
shifted recurrent inputs and combines them with a rank-8 linear gate. Its
same-token counterpart is the
unshifted control
; this control cannot
run its loops concurrently and is included only to measure the modeling cost
of shifting information across token positions. We reserve

Loop Matrix
because
it was generally the strongest of the specialization methods compared in
Subsec. 3.3
. We use the same method defined in
Subsec. F.1
, without introducing a new specialization
design. The figures label the same method as Matrix LoRA; throughout the text,
we use Loop Matrix. Its loop-specific
corrections are added to the attention and MLP projections and trained jointly
with the rest of the model. We compare three forms of looping.
Full-Stack Looping
is ordinary looping, in
which each token passes through the complete Transformer repeatedly.

Limitations
Our experiments establish consistent looping trends across dense decoder-only
transformers trained from scratch at scales up to 1B parameters. We do not
evaluate larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, or post-trained
models; future work can test how broadly these trends extend. We study a diverse set of looping strategies, low-rank specialization
methods, training budgets, and evaluation datasets, but do not exhaust the
space of possible designs. We also focus primarily on likelihood-based
evaluation rather than free-form generation. Future work can broaden both the
architectural and evaluation settings. Our normalized shifted PLT performs particularly well at
L
=
2
L=2
and remains
competitive at
L
=
4
L=4
. We do not establish whether this behavior persists at
substantially larger loop counts and model scales. Closing the remaining gap
to the unshifted control and developing a theoretical account of how
normalization and current-token embedding reinjection affect stability are
promising directions for future work.
