article.lede: 在从头训练的稠密解码器上，如何循环、循环多少次、如何跨循环传信息，取决于参数、算力还是解码效率是瓶颈。
article.problem: 循环（looping）通过反复对同一组权重施加于token表示，在不增加参数的情况下让模型“变深”，因此当模型尺寸受限时很有吸引力。但每多一次循环就多一次实际计算，参数效率高不等于训练算力效率高；同时普通循环在自回归解码时存在串行依赖，而并行循环Transformer（PLT）虽然能并行解码，却改变了每个循环可见的信息。已有工作在不同设定下分别研究这些选择，哪些结论可推广、各选择如何相互作用仍不清楚。
article.method: 作者在统一的从头训练设定下做受控实验：稠密解码器模型规模70M至1B，数据量最高155B token、训练算力最高1.07×10²¹ FLOPs、循环次数最高32次，TPP（每参数token数）覆盖10至160。实验系统变化“循环什么、循环几次、循环之间如何传递信息”，包括全栈循环、中栈循环、逐层循环以及注意力与MLP分别循环，并用约4100万token的DCLM验证集BPB作为主要指标。作者还比较了循环专属低秩适配（Loop LoRA、Loop Matrix、Loop Softmax），并修正PLT：保留当前token嵌入，先将其与上一token隐藏状态分别归一化再组合（rank-8线性门）。
article.results: 固定参数量与数据预算时，全栈循环（Full-Stack Looping）总体质量最好，且在更大模型与更高TPP下优势更稳定；训练FLOPs受限时，中栈循环（Middle-Stack Looping）用更少的额外计算获得更大收益。循环次数并非越多越好：70M与100M的扫描延伸到L=32，BPB的边际下降随L增大而变小，并出现饱和、反转甚至不稳定（200M–500M只扫到L=8，1B只到L=4）。加入循环专属低秩适配可提升质量，且收益随循环数增加更明显（L=4时比L=2更清楚）。1B模型上，循环在八个推理与问答任务上保持或提高了平均NLL排名准确率。并行方面，作者发现在其复现中原始PLT配方并不能稳定保留普通循环的质量增益，而修正后的移位PLT（shifted PLT）通常优于普通全栈循环且保留并行解码；无移位PLT质量最强，但解码仍是串行的。
article.why_it_matters: 工程上，这篇论文提供了明确的选择规则：部署时受参数预算、训练算力还是解码时延约束，就应选不同的循环位置与循环方式；而作者对PLT的归一化与当前token重注入修正，让“并行解码不牺牲质量”更接近可用。
article.limitations: 实验只做到1B参数、稠密解码器、从头训练，未涵盖更大模型、MoE与后训练模型，评估也以BPB、teacher-forcing似然为主，而非自由生成的实际质量。修正版PLT主要在L=2、4上验证，更大循环数与更大规模是否成立未确定，作者也未测量实际解码延迟或吞吐。
article.figure_caption_zh: 300M与500M模型在DCLM上的BPB对比：无移位PLT质量最好但解码串行，移位PLT在保留并行解码的同时通常优于普通全栈循环，叠加Loop Matrix后该排序不变。

figure.caption: {Loop-specific specialization preserves the ordering among ordinary and parallel looping designs.} DCLM BPB for 300M and 500M models. The figure compares ordinary Full-Stack Looping, shifted PLT, and unshifted PLT with shared weights and with Loop Matrix. Unshifted PLT gives the strongest quality but remains sequential during decoding. Shifted PLT generally improves over Full-Stack Looping while retaining parallel decoding. Lower BPB is better.

Robotic Data Inoculation
Qiyang Li   Zhiyuan Zhou   Charles Xu   Sergey Levine
UC Berkeley
data-inoculation.github.io
Abstract
Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover.
Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it.
In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves
during data collection
to collect more useful data.
We propose
Data Inoculation (DI)
, a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make.
These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human’s continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, “inoculating” the dataset against the learner’s future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
Figure 1
:
Data inoculation (DI).
Left
: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human’s closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human’s corrective feedback, “inoculating” the dataset against such mistakes.
Right
: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.
1
Introduction
Modern robot learning systems have shown promise in acquiring complex manipulation skills (
e.g.
, shirt-folding
[
7
]
, tea/juice-making
[
28
]
) from demonstration data.
While there has been extensive recent research on the design of these models, the quality of the data the models are trained on is every bit as critical. Good data should have high coverage: it should contain a wide range of states to maximize the chance that the policy generalizes to the states that it actually visits at test time. In practice, coverage is determined by the scenes where data is collected and the behaviors of the teleoperators, which must strike a balance between consistency and variety. Improving data quality and coverage through task design and operator instruction is largely heuristic and ad hoc. Can we instead directly modify how the robot behaves
during
data collection to provide for more useful data?
Existing solutions largely sit at the two extremes of how the robot is being controlled. Aside from the human-driven teleoperation which exhibits obvious drawbacks above, a learned policy may control the robot autonomously and collect data. While this allows us to run RL online which improves the policy upon its own experience overtime, real-world exploration can be sample inefficient and unsafe. DAgger-style methods partially address this by using learned policy to drive the robot until it makes a mistake, where a human intervenes and corrects it, often through teleoperation. This is reactive: each intervention requires a failure to occur naturally, and rare failure modes may take many rollouts to appear, and for many tasks (
e.g.
, that require working with delicate objects that may break) failures cannot be corrected once they occur.
In this paper, we argue that autonomous policy rollout and human control should
not
be mutually exclusive, and a shared-control framework in which a learned agent and the human drive the robot together allows for better data collection. Our framework is simple: the human retains closed-loop teleoperation of the robot that supplies the demonstration signal as usual in the form of control commands, but these commands are perturbed by a residual policy, which is trained online on the growing dataset, in a way that mimics the mistakes a policy trained on the current data might make. We call this residual policy an
inoculative policy
because it exposes data collection to controlled, human-corrected “doses” of the learner’s expected mistakes, so that the policy learned from the collected data is already robust to them. The human can therefore correct policy-like deviations continuously throughout every data collection episode rather than only after a visible failure while ensuring safety because they are always in control of the robot. The resulting data collection strategy, which we call
Data Inoculation (DI)
(
Figure
1
), produce data that are favourable for downstream policy extraction—it contains near-failure states paired with actions that allow recovery from these states, which is exactly the good coverage data that would help behavior cloning (BC) to learn the recovery behavior directly but also help offline RL to learn better value functions.
Our main contribution is the new data collection strategy (DI). We evaluate DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks and show that DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of the policies extracted from both behavior cloning (BC) and offline RL. These results demonstrate the benefits of proactively
inoculating
data collection so that the policies become more robust at deployment time.
2
Related Work
Human-in-the-loop learning
methods address a common failure mode of imitation learning on passive data, where the learned policy may visit states different from the training distribution and suffers from compounding errors. They typically work by alternating between executing the current policy and collecting human correction data in the form of action re-labeling
[
21
]
or intervention trajectories
[
9
]
. Interventions can be triggered automatically by the model
[
30
,
2
,
18
]
or initiated by human
[
9
,
16
,
15
,
13
,
4
,
6
]
. In real-world robotics, intervention-based approaches are often more convenient and natural to human because the corrective trajectories are collected under human’s continuous, closed-loop control of the robot. However, this also comes with a limitation: once the control is switched to human, the trajectory may quickly go out of the learned policy’s state distribution. As a result, only the first few transitions right after the switching point provide direct supervision to the mistakes made by the policy.
In contrast, rather than using a binary switching from the learned policy’s distribution to the expert’s distribution after intervention, our method constructs a controlled distribution by combining human demonstrator actions with residual actions from an
inoculation policy
, allowing the human to provide corrections of the policy’s mistakes throughout a data collection trajectory.
Prior work trains assistive residual policies in simulation, using a model trained on a fixed set of demonstrations to approximate human control, then deploys them with human operators
[
23
,
22
]
.
In contrast, our method doesn’t depend on simulation and directly train the residual inoculation policy online as data accumulates. This also yields a broader range of corrective demonstrations as updates to the residual policy expose humans to different errors during its training.
Data perturbation
approaches broaden the distribution of observations
[
26
,
11
,
29
,
31
]
, actions
[
31
,
8
,
3
,
17
]
, or even environment and its dynamics
[
5
,
27
,
20
,
25
]
during training so that the model is robust. These approaches typically directly perturb either a simulator (
e.g.
, domain randomization) or previously collected data (
e.g.
, data augmentation), but do not directly interact with how a human demonstrator collects trajectories, which our method does. The closest line of work injects zero-mean Gaussian noises during data collection, exposing human demonstrator to random mistakes and thereby eliciting recovery behaviors
[
10
,
19
,
24
]

inoculation policy
trained online to approximate the mistakes that a policy learned from the growing dataset would likely make. This allows the collected trajectories to target policy-specific failure modes like DAgger-style approaches, rather than relying on symmetric random perturbations. Furthermore, while prior approaches mostly focus on improving imitation learning performance, we additionally demonstrate that our technique allows for improved offline RL performance and the quality of learned value functions.

In this section, we describe in detail how we use a residual policy in a shared-control framework to continuously inject controlled perturbations such that the collected data is favorable for downstream policy training.
We start by discussing how a residual policy alongside closed-loop human control can address the failure mode of vanilla human teleop data collection, and then detail how such a residual policy can be learned online during data collection with online RL.

Injecting purely random noises without any guidance inefficient, because perturbations along axes that barely influence task success (
e.g.

Intuitively, the data collection budget is best spent on the critical perturbation axes that influence the task success the most, and elicit recovery behavior as a consequence of these perturbations. However, finding informative perturbations is not simple as they are highly task-dependent and non-stationary, requiring a form of fast adaptation that vanilla zero-mean random noises (as often used in prior work
[

maximize task success

In particular, we train our inoculative policy using standard TD-based off-policy RL, concurrently with collection, on the growing dataset from the data collection itself. While the data collection loop runs on the robot at the normal control frequency, an asynchronous RL training loop updates

This answer is two-fold. First of all, when the inoculative policy is optimized using the same reward-maximizing objective as a downstream offline RL algorithm later uses for policy extraction, its deviations are expected to closely mirror those a downstream learned policy would produce. Furthermore, early in collection, the critic is barely trained and inaccurate which causes the residual policy to exploit the critic’s errors, steering the robot into suboptimal states that require explicit recovery behaviors. Experimental Setup
We empirically evaluate our method across three different challenging precise manipulation tasks in the real world. We first describe the experimental setup, then the results in
Section
6
.
Robot setup and tasks.
We evaluate our method on three real-robot tasks that require precise manipulation. We focus on these tasks because successful executions require precise control of the robot, making it a challenging testbed for data collection and policy learning.
We use a Franka robot arm with a Robotiq gripper and two wrist cameras attached near the end effector. We use a spacemouse to control the robot’s end effector position and rotation during data collection at a frequency of
10
10
Hz.
Illustrations of the three tasks are shown in
Figure
1
, and we describe them in detail below:
1.
t-cube
requires the robot to pick up two colored cubes and carefully balance them on top of another yellow cube, resulting in a T-shape
[
1
]
. While this seems like a simple pick and place task, this in fact requires very precise manipulation skills and is arguably the most demanding task of the three: the robot needs to stack the two top cubes diagonally on top of the yellow cube with the centers of the three cubes roughly aligned, and any misalignment would cause one or two of the top cubes to fall off.
2.
cable
is a precision insertion task where the robot needs to pick up a USB-C cable and insert it into a port hole on a desktop machine that is barely bigger than the cable itself. Without changing the difficulty of the task, we only use the side plate of the desktop machine for ease of task setup.
3.
keycap
tasks the robot to use a keycap puller to remove the Q keycap from a keyboard. The robot must pick up the tool, locate the Q key, position the puller over the keycap, and lock its two hooks onto both sides of the keycap. Successful removal requires precise, directionally controlled force rather than a large brute force pull, which could cause the keycap to fly off. The robot must therefore learn a sequence of small lateral wiggling motions to loosen the keycap before pulling it out and placing it on the table.
Data collection procedure.
Since data collection through tele-operation is unavoidably a subjective process and can vary across different operators and collection trials, we conduct experiments on all tasks and data collection strategies with multiple operators and trials, which we refer to as “seeds”. Before data collection, each operator spent time to practice on the task to achieve a sufficient level of expertise before collecting any data.

Discussion
In this paper we introduce Data Inoculation, a data collection strategy that trains a residual RL policy online to aid human teleoperated data collection in a shared-control framework. The residual inoculative policy perturbs the human’s control of the robot to a wider range of states and can elicit recovery demonstrations in critical phases of the task, and eventually lead to higher data collection success rate as the residual policy is trained. Data collected with DI also improves the success rate of downstream policy learning.
Our work serves as a step towards a new paradigm of robot learning where data collection is shared between humans and autonomous policies, each helping the other.
Several challenges remain and is promising for future work. First, our approach trains the residual policy from scratch using online RL, which offers near-random perturbations at the beginning of training. A natural next step is to develop mechanisms for directed exploration that can more quickly provide useful perturbations, such as boostrapping training from an existing offline dataset.
Second, our approach assume the human operator to be fully in-the-loop during data collection, which is expensive in human time. One interesting direction is to explore whether we can automate parts of data collection to be autonomous gradually during training and leave only important correction for human operators.

The robot must pick up the cable lying on the table and then insert it through a port hole on the side panel that is barely bigger than the cable head. The insertion is a contact-rich process where the robot must search locally and find the right motion that allows the USB-C to go through the port hole. An episode succeeds when the USB-C passes through the port hole and rests there without falling (with the arm away).
Task
keycap
. The scene contains a mechanical keyboard and a keycap-puller tool. The robot must pickup the keycap tool and remove a transparent “Q” keycap from the keyboard. This requires the arm to seat the tool’s two hooks on the opposite sides of the keycap, loosen the keycap, and then pull it off the switch. An episode succeeds when the keycap is detached and placed on the table.

article.headline: 用在线RL扰动遥操作，给数据集「接种」
article.lede: 伯克利提出 Data Inoculation：在人类遥操作时叠加一个在线训练的残差策略，让演示数据自带纠错片段。
article.problem: 机器人模仿学习的效果高度依赖演示数据的覆盖度：熟练操作者的遥操作轨迹往往又快又一致，状态分布狭窄，缺少从偏离状态恢复的示范，策略一旦出错就难以纠回。纯在线 RL 探索代价高且不安全，DAgger 式干预又必须等策略偶然失败才能获得纠正，对易损物体的任务甚至无法事后补救。论文要问的是：能否不改变任务与操作者指令，而是直接改造采集时机器人的行为，从而收集更有用的数据。
article.method: DI 采用共享控制框架：人类操作者保持闭环遥操作，每一步给出控制命令，一个残差「接种策略」在同一观测和该命令的基础上输出 L∞ 有界的扰动量，叠加后执行，人类随即对偏差做出纠正，扰动与纠正天然配对成恢复示范。该残差策略与数据采集异步并行，用同一份不断增长的数据以标准 TD 离线式（off-policy）RL 在线训练，优化目标与后续策略提取所用的奖励最大化一致；因此其扰动会模仿「用当前数据训出的策略」可能犯的错，早期评论家网络不准时的利用行为还会把机器人带到需要显式恢复的次优状态。实现上每 0.5 秒（10 Hz 下 5 个控制步）采样一次扰动并保持，评论家直接估计扰动后动作的价值，并用一个流匹配 BC 模型近似 TD 目标所需的「干净」人类动作。
article.results: 在三个真实 Franka 精细操作任务上，t-cube、cable、keycap 分别用 9、5、5 个采集种子，每个种子评估 20 次。BC 策略成功率由 clean 的 0.37/0.38/0.63 提升到 DI 的 0.66/0.50/0.72；离线 RL（BFN 取 N=4）由 0.35/0.42/0.81 提升到 0.67/0.59/0.84。随机噪声基线在 cable 上有提升（BC 0.48、RL 0.56），但在 t-cube 几乎无益（0.40/0.42），在 keycap 上反而拖累 BC（0.69 对比 clean 0.63 尚可，RL 0.67 明显低于 clean 0.81）。采集过程本身，DI 的初期成功率低于对照，约进行到全程四分之一时追平 clean 和 random，最终反超；残余动作幅度随训练持续下降。纠正行为分析显示，DI 的纠正集中在 t-cube 最关键的 place/release 阶段，而随机噪声的纠正多发生在较简单的 retreat 阶段。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「数据采集」本身当成可学习对象：人类负责安全与意图，学习策略负责生成有针对性的扰动，得到接近失败的状态，以及配套的恢复动作，这正是 BC 学恢复、离线 RL 学值函数都需要的覆盖度。相比 DAgger，它不必等真实失败发生，也不改动最终策略的算法。
article.limitations: 残差策略从零用在线 RL 训练，采集初期扰动近乎随机，t-cube 上 DI 的整体采集成功率 54.4% 仍低于 clean 的 57.7%（keycap 94.0% 对 95.8%，cable 94.2% 对 96.9%），且需要人类全程在环，人力成本高。keycap 上三种方法差距很小（RL 0.84 对 0.81），说明任务本身对精确恢复要求不高时收益有限；实验仅覆盖三个桌面操作任务、单一机械臂平台，跨任务泛化性尚未验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 左：采集时用在线 RL 训练残差接种策略，扰动人类的闭环遥操作命令；右：在三个需精细操作的真实机器人任务上，DI 提升 BC 与离线 RL 策略的成功率。

figure.caption: {dmc}{ {Data inoculation (DI). }} {Left}: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human's closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human's corrective feedback, ``inoculating'' the dataset against such mistakes. {Right}: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.

email_papers.content:
ScheduleGen: Demonstration Generation via Skill Scheduling for Multi-Arm Imitation Learning
Neel Jawale, Stephan Pleines, Soha Pouya, Yuke Zhu, Ajay Mandlekar, Caelan Garrett
NVIDIA  The University of Texas at Austin
†
Equal advising
Abstract
Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks
with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints.
The paradigm of training generalist robot policies from massive datasets is a promising approach to address general-purpose multi-arm manipulation, but the acquisition of large multi-arm manipulation datasets remains a bottleneck.
Automated demonstration generation can alleviate this burden by synthesizing new demonstrations from a handful of source demonstrations, but existing algorithms ignore multi-arm constraints and as a result often induce unsafe and unsuccessful behaviors.
We address this limitation by introducing ScheduleGen, an integrated planning & scheduling algorithm for multi-arm demonstration generation.
We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 simulation task variants, including seven externally authored RoboDojo tasks and settings inaccessible to prior systems; it achieves 79.6% mean data-generation success and trains policies with 65.5% mean success.
ScheduleGen policies outperform those trained on a state-of-the-art data generation baseline, and achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants through zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real transfer.
Videos and more at:
schedulegen.github.io
.
keywords
Imitation Learning, Demonstration Generation, Multi-Arm Manipulation, Planning and Scheduling
Figure 1:
ScheduleGen overview.
Top:
From a few source demonstrations, ScheduleGen adapts contact-rich skill demonstrations, plans collision-free connecting motions, and jointly schedules multiple arms to generate simulation data for multi-arm imitation learning that transfers to the real world.
Bottom:
ScheduleGen can handle long-horizon contact manipulation, challenging reset distributions, cluttered layouts, and multi-arm scenarios.
\abscontent
1
Introduction
Generalist robot policies
[
1
,
24
]
hold the promise of seamlessly solving a wide range of manipulation tasks across diverse robot embodiments. There is substantial interest in applying this paradigm to multi-arm embodiments, especially bimanual and humanoid robots, due to their ability to address a wider range of tasks compared to single-arm embodiments. Such embodiments make it possible to address tasks requiring multi-arm coordination and larger manipulation workspaces, and also have the potential to carry out tasks more efficiently due to simultaneous operation.
However, the predominant method for training generalist robot policies requires large-scale data collection, usually obtained through months of human teleoperation effort
[
8
,
16
]
. Collecting such datasets is already painful and costly for single-arm embodiments, but these problems are exacerbated in the multi-arm setting, due to the need for special teleoperation interfaces
[
29
,
32
,
5
]
, and the resulting increase in operator burden. It can furthermore be difficult to capture desirable multi-arm coordination characteristics due to the limitations of the teleoperation interface
[
15
]
.
Synthetic data generation in simulation is a compelling method to address this need. Prior methods allow for the generation of large-scale datasets with minimal human effort
[
21
,
6
]
but fail to address some key challenges of generating data for multi-arm scenarios.
Some works use planning-based approaches
[
22
,
4
,
6
]
, but contact-rich tasks remain difficult for such methods, and generating data for diverse multi-arm coordination characteristics remains challenging. DexMimicGen
[
15
]
is able to handle different contact-rich tasks, but the coordination behaviors that it can generate are entirely dictated by the human demonstrations used to seed the process, limiting data diversity. Furthermore, the absence of planning means that it cannot handle situations where arm-arm or arm-object collisions are prevalent, such as wide object distributions or cluttered workspaces.
To address these shortcomings, we present ScheduleGen, a multi-arm manipulation data generation method that can encompass diverse multi-arm coordination strategies, long-horizon and contact-rich manipulation, and a wide range of workspaces and embodiments, including challenging object initializations and cluttered scenes. Given a small set of annotated demonstrations, ScheduleGen preserves object-relative contact skills, replans collision-free transitions, and jointly schedules the arms under task and collision constraints.
The contributions of this paper are:
•
ScheduleGen, a new automated demonstration generation algorithm for multi-arm systems that integrates planning, scheduling, and demonstration adaptation.
•
ScheduleGen utilizes a novel planning formulation that first plans single-robot behavior to adapt object-centric skill demonstrations and then safely coordinates the robots by framing scheduling as a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) with constraints evaluated using GPU-accelerated collision checking.
•
We demonstrate ScheduleGen’s applicability to long-horizon contact-rich tasks, challenging resets, cluttered workspaces, and configurable coordination strategies across bimanual, four-arm, and humanoid systems. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 task variants across 3 simulation frameworks. On comparable tasks, ScheduleGen-trained policies outperform prior work DexMimicGen
[
15
]
. In zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real evaluation, the learned policies achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants.
Figure 2:
ScheduleGen methodology.
(a) Contact-skill segments
τ
ψ
\tau_{\psi}
are adapted to the initial state and connected by planned motion
τ
m
\tau_{m}
, producing partially ordered paths for each arm. (b) Collision checking identifies conflicting path segments. (c) ScheduleGen implicitly inserts waits to form a joint schedule that preserves task order, avoids collisions, and enforces synchronization when required. It minimizes makespan with optional soft costs, like summed robot execution times. (d) Scheduled motions are replayed across parallel simulation environments, and successful rollouts are retained as demonstrations.
2
Related Work
Imitation Learning from Human Demonstrations.
Manipulation demonstrations are often collected via robot teleoperation
[
31
,
20
]
, and
Behavioral Cloning (BC)
[
25
]
is a common method for training manipulation policies on such datasets.
Recent efforts have scaled this paradigm to months of demonstration data using large teams of human teleoperators
[
8
,
16
]
, and train expressive policy architectures on this data, resulting in capable generalist robot policies
[
1
,
24
]
.
However, data sourcing remains a key bottleneck for this paradigm.
The problem is exacerbated for bimanual robots and humanoids, which can require specialized teleoperation interfaces to support multi-arm teleoperation
[
29
,
32
,
5
]
.
Automated Demonstration Generation.
Synthetic data generation in simulation is a promising way to address the data bottleneck.
TAMP-based approaches
[
22
,
4
,
10
]
fully automate generation but are limited to single-robot prehensile manipulation.
MimicGen
[
21
]
and DexMimicGen
[
15
]
instead adapt a few teleoperated demonstrations to new initial states for single-arm and bimanual tasks, but adapting full demonstrations without accounting for collision or kinematic constraints limits their robustness to substantial initial-state variation.
SkillGen combines demonstration adaptation with motion planning to preserve contact-rich behavior while accommodating environmental and state changes
[
11
]
, but is limited to single-arm systems.
GLIDE
[
17
]
and HumanoidMimicGen
[
18
]
also incorporate motion planning and support some bimanual tasks, but independently planned arm motions compromise safety and success on complex bimanual tasks.
In contrast, ScheduleGen frames demonstration generation as a collision-aware scheduling problem to directly plan safe and efficient multi-arm manipulation.
Multi-Arm Manipulation.
Planning for multiple arms as a single composite robot can be intractable due to high-dimensional, combinatorial search spaces.
Multi-robot planners therefore factor the problem into interacting single-robot subproblems
[
7
]

5.2
ScheduleGen Features
ScheduleGen generates demonstrations across diverse tasks and robot embodiments.
Across 17 Isaac Lab variants, ScheduleGen achieves 61.1-98.0% data-generation success, exceeding 85% on 10 variants. All policies trained on this data reach 30-100% success (Fig.
3
). These results span bimanual YAM and DROID
[
16
]
, a four-arm DROID setup, and a GR1T2 humanoid. Data-generation success also remains high (75.5-100.0%) across seven RoboDojo tasks on X5 (Fig.
5
).
On four robosuite variants in MuJoCo, BC-RNN-GMM policies reach 60-100% success over 50 episodes from data generated at 24.7-84% success (Table
1
).
ScheduleGen generates collision-free demonstrations even in scenarios with inter-arm overlap, unlike prior work.
The Cross-Arm variants introduce overlapping arm workspaces and broader object resets while reusing the Normal task demonstrations. DexMimicGen transfers each arm independently, while the manually selected holds in DexMimicGen-Tuned apply fixed timing across resets. ScheduleGen instead replans connecting motions and schedules collision-free waits for each reset. Across the four bimanual Cross and Cross-Bin variants, it reaches 64-88% data-generation success and 70-86% policy success. Two-Arm Cube Stacking uses a state-based BC-RNN, while Four-Arm Cube Stacking uses state-based flow-matching policies. DexMimicGen generates no valid trajectories on these variants, while DexMimicGen-Tuned remains below ScheduleGen throughout (Fig.
3
).
ScheduleGen scales data generation and policy learning to multi-arm systems.
Four-Arm Cube Stacking uses motion-planned pick-and-place segments as source skills rather than teleoperation. ScheduleGen jointly schedules them across four arms, checking all six arm pairs while building a five-object tower on a table or in a narrow bin. We train a separate state-based flow-matching policy for each layout and reset distribution. Across eight settings, data-generation success is 63.4-95.1% and policy success is 30-90% (Fig.
3
). DexMimicGen is not applicable because its interface supports only bimanual generation.

ScheduleGen scales released demonstrations to externally authored tasks.
Agentic annotation converts five released RoboDojo demonstrations per task into seeds with per-arm contact boundaries, object-relative frames, and task constraints; ambiguous cases retain human review, and all annotations must pass replay and task-success checks. ScheduleGen then generates 500 successful training demonstrations per task at 75.5-100.0% success (89.1% mean). The resulting flow-matching policies complete all seven tasks under both conditions, averaging 47.9% success on held-out Nominal layouts and 25.0% under doubled pose perturbations over 20 episodes per task and condition (Fig.
5
).
5.3
ScheduleGen Analysis
ScheduleGen reduces the task-specific data collection and tuning needed for difficult layouts.
We separately collect Cross-Arm demonstrations for YAM Bowl and Dishware Stacking. Each set takes the operator about 20 minutes, with additional work for annotation and hold tuning. To generate 1,000 demonstrations, DexMimicGen reaches 32.1% and 11.2% data-generation success and 30% and 20% policy success evaluated over 50 episodes. ScheduleGen instead reuses the five Normal demonstrations, reaching 66.7% and 68.0% data-generation success and 80% and 76% policy success. Task-matched teleoperation alone therefore does not close the gap: ScheduleGen retains the contact skills while replanning and scheduling free-space motion for each reset.
Policies trained on ScheduleGen data outperform the best DexMimicGen baseline across tasks and embodiments.
Across nine variants supported by DexMimicGen, ScheduleGen policies improve success on eight and match the best baseline at 94% on Normal Two-Arm Cube Stacking. Policy success rises from 42-78% to 76-100% on Bowl and Dishware Stacking, 0-74% to 70-86% on the Cross-Arm and Cross-Bin cube variants, and 20-90% to 48-96% on Humanoid Nut Pouring. ScheduleGen policies also use fewer steps whenever a baseline policy succeeds (Fig.
3
).
ScheduleGen shortens RoboDojo trajectories by scheduling more arm motion in parallel.
Across the 3,500 trajectories used for policy training, ScheduleGen reduces mean execution length by 2.3-11.1% per task relative to the released RoboDojo trajectories, with a 7.5% average reduction across tasks. Both arms are active together for 31.5% of execution steps, compared with 15.5% in the released demonstrations. To measure scheduling alone, we also apply the scheduler to all 700 released trajectories while keeping their paths and task order fixed. It finds valid schedules for 98.3% of these trajectories and reduces total steps by 14.98%
without replanning or physics replay. The mean reduction per episode is 16.44% (Fig.
5
). Appendix
C.5
gives the per-task measurements.

5.4
Real-World Evaluation
We evaluate two transfer routes on the real YAM setup. In sim-to-real, policies are trained only on ScheduleGen simulation data. In real-to-sim-to-real, calibrated real demonstrations seed simulation data generation for Cube Stacking and Trash, and the resulting policies are returned to the same robot. All policies are trained in simulation without real-world fine-tuning. We use calibrated robot, camera, workspace, and object geometry, and randomize object pose, appearance, lighting, camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and background. Policies observe three RGB views and both arms’ joint and gripper states, and predict joint-position and gripper targets.

6
Conclusion
We presented ScheduleGen, an automated demonstration generation system for multi-arm imitation learning. It combines object-centric skill adaptation, motion planning, and joint scheduling to preserve contact-rich behavior while satisfying task order, synchronization, and collision constraints. Experiments across 28 simulation variants show that ScheduleGen supports diverse embodiments and challenging layouts, and trains policies that outperform prior bimanual methods on most comparable tasks. The learned policies also transfer to eight real-world variants without real-world fine-tuning. These results show that adapting both motion and coordination can reduce task-specific data collection while supporting long-horizon, contact-rich multi-arm manipulation.

A.1
Path Construction
Algorithm
2
processes skills in a topological order of their sequential precedence constraints, updating object poses for later skills. This order is used to construct the planning scene; the arms can still execute in parallel after scheduling.
The adapted state sequence defines the configurations used for planning and collision checking, while the adapted action sequence supplies the controller targets for replay. article.headline: ScheduleGen：多臂演示生成与调度
article.lede: NVIDIA 等提出 ScheduleGen，用规划与调度从少量示范生成多臂机器人训练数据，并验证真实迁移。
article.problem: 多臂机器人（双臂、人形、四臂）能并行完成复杂操作，但大规模示范数据采集成本高、遥操作接口负担重。现有自动演示生成方法往往忽略臂间碰撞与协调约束，容易产生不安全或失败的轨迹，尤其在接触丰富、杂乱场景和宽初始分布下。
article.method: ScheduleGen 先把源示范切分为以物体为参照的单臂技能，按新初始状态做技能适配，并用运动规划连接各段。随后把多臂执行顺序建模为带时序约束和碰撞约束的混合整数线性规划（MILP），用 GPU 加速碰撞检查，隐式插入等待以生成无碰撞的联合调度。生成轨迹在仿真回放成功后才保留为训练示范。
article.results: 在 28 个仿真任务变体上，ScheduleGen 平均数据生成成功率为 79.6%，训练策略平均成功率为 65.5%，并在可比任务上优于 DexMimicGen 基线。零样本 sim-to-real 与 real-to-sim-to-real 在 8 个真实世界变体上取得 50–80% 成功率；RoboDojo 七个任务生成成功率为 75.5–100.0%（均值 89.1%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把多臂协调纳入数据生成环节，减少为每个新布局重新遥操作采集示范的需要，并为双臂、四臂和人形平台的模仿学习提供可扩展的数据来源。
article.limitations: 调度公式未显式约束加速度，且若任一机械臂的起止状态发生碰撞，MILP 会不可行。真实世界评估每个变体仅 20 个回合，RoboDojo 策略在物体位姿扰动加倍时平均成功率降至 25.0%。

page_papers.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
page_papers.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
We study feature vectors: directions in a language model’s activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
1

Introduction
The linear representation hypothesis posits that large language models (LLMs) encode human-interpretable concepts (e.g., sentiment or truthfulness) as linear directions in its activation space
(
Mikolov et al., 2013
;
Park et al., 2023
;
Elhage et al., 2022
)
. When such direction is tied to a pre-specified concept, we call it a
feature vector
. These vectors can serve two complementary roles. Projecting activations onto a feature vector, called
probing
, measures how active its concept is in a given context
(
Alain & Bengio, 2016
;
Belinkov, 2022
)
; adding it to the activations, called
steering
, pushes generation toward that concept
(
Subramani et al., 2022
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. Both techniques are highly effective in practice and have been used for safety-critical LLM monitoring and control
(
Zou et al., 2023a
;
Bergen et al., 2026
;
Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 1:
Overview.
Left:

Right:

(

)

30

(

)

cluster names were assigned manually.
But how can we get these feature vectors? Sparse autoencoders (SAEs)
(
Bricken et al., 2023
;
Huben et al., 2024
;
Templeton et al., 2024
)
attempt to recover all atomic features a model might store, yet a growing body of evidence shows SAEs fail to faithfully find true model features and underperform simpler baselines on downstream tasks
(
Wu et al., 2025
;
Korznikov et al., 2026
;
Smith et al., 2025
)
. Another option is to define the concepts we care about in advance and extract their directions from contrastive pairs: for each concept, we gather texts that express it and texts that express its opposite, then take the difference between their mean activations. The resulting
difference-in-means
vector is more robust and interpretable than SAE features, but requires matched data per concept, limiting its use to a few concepts at a time
(
Belrose, 2024
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
.

2.1

Conclusion
Understanding what language models represent requires tools that are both interpretable and broad enough to study model behavior at scale. In this work, we showed that these goals need not conflict. Rather than attempting to recover a complete dictionary of model features, we start from pre-specified, alignment-relevant concepts and construct explicit directions for them from contrastive data. Synthetic story generation makes this procedure practical at a scale where manual curation would be prohibitive.
The resulting feature vectors generalize beyond the synthetic corpus from which they are derived. Across six models from three families, they detect their target concepts in natural chat and web text, form a shared and interpretable geometry, and causally steer generation when injected into activations. This makes a broad feature dictionary useful as an experimental instrument for studying model behavior in longer, multi-step settings. Our analyses of coding agents, jailbreak attacks, and chain-of-thought reasoning illustrate how collections of interpretable directions can reveal patterns that would be difficult to discover from single-feature probes alone.
More broadly, our results suggest a complementary approach to representation analysis: instead of asking whether we can recover the entire feature space, we can ask which parts of that space are useful for a particular scientific or safety question, and construct those parts directly. The resulting directions should not be treated as a complete or uniquely active account of the model’s mechanisms, but as interpretable evidence for concepts and as tools for investigating model behavior. We hope this perspective can turn feature vectors from isolated probes into reusable maps of model behavior, eventually scaling far beyond the 1,036 concept–antagonist pairs studied here.

article.headline: 用200万合成故事提取1036个概念向量
article.lede: 研究者以合成故事对做差值均值，把可解释性探针扩展到1036个对齐相关概念，并在六个模型上检验其泛化、几何与因果操控能力。
article.problem: 稀疏自编码器试图无监督地还原整个特征空间，却被指难以忠实找到模型真实特征，在下游任务上不如更简单的基线。差值均值法虽更稳健、更可解释，但每个概念都要人工配对文本，一次只能覆盖少数概念，难以支撑规模化研究。
article.method: 作者聚焦AI安全与对齐相关概念，为每个概念生成表达该概念与其对立面的合成故事对，取两者平均激活之差作为特征向量。他们用跨多语言、多文体的200万条合成故事，把这一流程扩展到1036个概念，并公开数据。向量以探针（投影读出）和操控（注入激活）两种方式使用，并在六个模型、三个模型家族上评测。
article.results: 作者构建了1036个概念–对立概念对，动用200万条合成故事，覆盖六款模型、三个模型家族。在Qwen3-8B第24层上，1036个概念与对立向量的t-SNE图经Leiden算法在互30近邻余弦图上聚出30个社区，簇名由人工标注；作者称这些向量在聊天对话与网页文本中能稳定检出对应概念，注入激活后可因果地操控生成。附录的剂量–反应实验复现了此前工作中的泰诺结果，并把剂量梯度扩展到止咳糖浆（100–900 ml）和布洛芬（100–19,200 mg），在Qwen3-8B、Llama-3.1-8B、gemma-2-9b的第24、21、28层上读出响应；具体的探针与操控准确率，论文摘录未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「先选定关心的概念、再直接构造方向」做成可复用流水线，让特征向量从孤立的探针变成可批量使用的分析工具。作者用它考察越狱攻击、数学与智能体推理中的表征变化，显示出多方向联合分析能揭示单特征探针难以发现的模式。
article.limitations: 概念集是预先指定且偏对齐议题的，并非对模型特征空间的完整还原；作者自己也强调，这些方向不应被视为模型机制的唯一或完备解释。合成故事由参考模型（gpt-oss-120b）生成，可能把生成模型的偏见带入数据，而摘录中未给出探针与操控的量化指标。

page_papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
page_papers.abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world.
However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena.
The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale.
To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model’s own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
. Each of these substantially improves performance.
We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research.
1
1
1

Introduction
Simulation is one of the most promising paths to training embodied AI at scale. Unlike the real world, a simulator can run thousands of episodes in parallel, reset instantly, expose the full ground-truth state, and provide rewards without human supervision
(
Todorov et al., 2012
;
Makoviychuk et al., 2021
;
Tao et al., 2025
)
. For these advantages to matter, however, simulations must faithfully represent the real world.
Although the field has developed various hand-built environments
(
James et al., 2020
;
Yu et al., 2020
;
Liu et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Nasiriany et al., 2024
)
, a key bottleneck is that building additional, more realistic simulations requires significant time and expert effort.
Indeed, despite decades of human progress, today’s simulations cover a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena (Tables
2
and
1
), often with limited visual fidelity.
Simulation as a path to embodied AI is hindered by the challenge of building diverse, realistic simulations at scale.

Methodology
In this section, we introduce the problem setup and the GDP-grounded selection of simulations. In §
3
, we describe our multi-agent strategy for creating simulations, and in §
4
, how we create tasks of controlled difficulty for each simulation.
2.1

Results
6.1

Experimental Setup
Library.
To evaluate many kinds of policies, from frontier models to code policies and learned visuomotor policies, we build the Gym-Anything for Robotics library, which gives every simulation the same interface. As a result, any policy can run on any simulation without simulation-specific code. Behind this interface, each simulation can use its own physics engine and custom solvers, and its robot can be swapped for others, from single arms to bimanual arms and humanoids. The same simulation can also be run with restricted access, as on a real robot, or with privileged access to its full state (§
2.1
), so it serves evaluation, privileged experiments, and training alike. Appendix
D
provides further details.
Robot interface.
Each simulation runs as a server, and a policy connects to it over an authenticated HTTP API, whose key grants restricted or privileged access (§
2.1
). To support policies ranging from frontier models to code policies and VLAs, a policy can command the robot at several levels. It can set joint targets or end-effector coordinates, which a controller tracks, or send joint torques and, on humanoids, individual motor commands. Like a computer-use agent, it can also press game-style keys, such as W, A, S, and D to move the end effector, each held for a set number of control ticks.
Agents.
We evaluate three frontier models with extra-high reasoning effort: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra, and Claude Opus 5.5
(
Anthropic, 2025a
)
. Each runs as a coding agent in its own harness, Claude Code
(
Anthropic, 2025b
)
for Claude Opus 5.5 and Codex
(
OpenAI, 2025
)
for the GPT models, and controls the robot with restricted access through a small set of tools, such as
observe
, which returns camera images and robot feedback, and
act
, which executes a robot command. The learning experiments (§
6.3
) use Claude Opus 5.5 in every role.
Evaluation.
Each attempt runs on an independent copy of the simulation, starting from the task’s initial state, with a wall-clock budget of three hours. The verifier scores each attempt after the agent finishes.
During the attempt, agents do not observe rewards. We report two metrics: (1) success rate, i.e., the fraction of attempts that the verifier labels as successful, and (2) average reward, i.e., the mean of the continuous reward
r
∈
[
0
,
1
]
r\in[0,1]
, which captures partial progress.
6.2

Main Results

Conclusion
In this work, we introduced Gym-Anything for Robotics, a scalable framework in which coding agents build realistic robotics simulations. By framing simulation creation as a coding agent task and checking each simulation and task in a multi-agent loop of creation, auditing, and repair, Gym-Anything for Robotics addresses a central bottleneck in robot learning: the difficulty of building realistic simulations at scale. Applying this framework, we built RoboWorld, a GDP-grounded collection of 200 RL environments across 25 simulations spanning liquids, cloth, and physics that existing engines lack, with swappable robots and train and test splits. We further showed that privileged simulator state more than doubles the first-attempt reward of frontier models, and that it can teach a student through hints alone and train
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
from 0% to 53% success. At the same time, RoboWorld is challenging even for frontier models, which fail every test task, indicating that realistic physical work remains far from solved.
More broadly, our results suggest that simulation has been held back not by the idea of simulation, but by unrealistic simulations, and that coding agents can now build realistic ones in which far more capable frontier models learn in ways that the real world does not allow. We hope that Gym-Anything for Robotics, RoboWorld, and the released code provide a foundation for future work on realistic robot learning, including more capable embodied agents, new ways to learn from privileged state, and broader coverage of physical work.

article.headline: 编码智能体批量搭建机器人仿真环境
article.lede: 研究者把仿真搭建当成编码任务交给智能体，产出25个仿真、共200个RL环境；最强前沿模型在所有测试任务上平均奖励仅0.0
article.problem: 机器人仿真是规模化训练具身模型最有希望的路径，但现有仿真只覆盖很窄的任务与物理现象，视觉保真度也有限。瓶颈在于新增高质量仿真需要大量专家工时，因而难以扩展。作者据此提出：仿真创建本身应当被当作编码智能体的任务来处理。
article.method: 作者先用美国GDP数据筛出120个覆盖经济价值较高体力工作的仿真方向，实际构建其中25个，并明确定义「好仿真」与「好任务」的判定标准。随后搭建一条对抗式「创建—审计」流水线：创建智能体写代码造仿真并自证质量，四个审计智能体按标准核查；任务创建智能体提出目标难度的任务，再由六个审计智能体复核。所有仿真统一接口，支持单臂、双臂与人形机器人，并可在受限访问与特权全状态访问之间切换。
article.results: 由此得到的RoboWorld包含25个仿真、175个训练与25个测试RL环境。三个前沿模型（GPT-6 Astra、GPT-6.1 Terra、Claude Opus 5.5）在每个测试任务上都失败，平均奖励仅0.06。利用特权仿真状态可让前沿模型首次尝试奖励提升一倍以上；特权教师仅靠提示即可教学生；用代码策略生成跨场景示范，可把π0.5的成功率从0%训练到53%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把仿真供给的瓶颈从「人工建模」转成「编码能力」，让编码智能体的进步可以直接转化为更丰富、更真实的仿真环境。若这一路径成立，机器人学习的规模上限将不再由专家工时决定。
article.limitations: 论文从120个候选中只实现了25个仿真，覆盖面仍有限；所有任务上前沿模型平均奖励仅0.06，说明这些环境离可用训练场尚有距离。仿真质量由LLM审计智能体按自定标准判定，并未与真实世界测量对齐，也没有真机迁移实验，因此「更真实」目前只是内部一致性证据。
article.figure_caption_zh: 四阶段流水线：依据美国GDP数据挑选120个候选仿真并建成25个，创建智能体编写仿真代码、由四个审计智能体核查，任务创建智能体设计目标难度任务、由六个审计智能体复核，最后通过上下文学习、特权教师教练与生成示范的代码策略训练VLA模型。

figure.caption: {Overview of Gym-Anything for Robotics.} {Phase~1:} We select 120 simulations grounded in U.S.\ GDP data, covering the most valuable physical work across occupations and everyday life, and build 25 of them. {Phase~2:} A creation agent builds each simulation in code and produces evidence of its quality, which four audit agents check against our criteria. {Phase~3:} A task creation agent proposes tasks of targeted difficulty, which six audit agents check, and each task runs with many robots and variations. {Phase~4:} Models learn from privileged simulation state through in-context learning, coaching, and code policies that train VLAs.

page_papers.title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
page_papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.

AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM’s six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds.
Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline’s actions.
1
Introduction
AI systems are advancing the frontiers of mathematics,
from Lean-verified progress on the Riemann zeta function
(
Anthropic, 2026
)
to recently reported resolutions
of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem and the
local smoothing conjecture
(
OpenAI, 2026a
;
OpenAI, 2026b
)
. Yet these advances typically rely on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. In an unfamiliar environment, however, an agent must first identify the relevant objects, infer how actions change them, and determine what constitutes success. The rules on which its reasoning depends are themselves hypotheses to be learned and revised through interaction. This raises a broader question:
Can an agent reason rigorously about an unknown world?
Euler’s treatment of the Königsberg bridges illustrates the role of mathematical structure
(
Euler, 1741
)
. Land masses become vertices and bridges become edges. A walk crossing every bridge exactly once pairs arrivals and departures at every vertex other than its endpoints, so at most two vertices can have odd degree. The Königsberg graph has four, ruling out every such walk without enumerating routes. A winning trajectory likewise establishes reachability, but proving that none exists requires reasoning about all legal sequences. When the environment is unfamiliar, the objects and rules needed for that reasoning must themselves be learned.
We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that learns explicit mathematical models of unfamiliar environments through interaction and uses them for formal reasoning. AWM proceeds through three stages (Figure
1
). In
Explore & Prototype
, the agent actively probes the environment and maintains executable hypotheses, testing and revising them against observed transitions.
Structure & Simplify
organizes these hypotheses into typed objects and rules, then uses category-theory-guided transformations, each checked in Lean through
projective and inductive
limits, to identify shared structure and simplify its representation while preserving tested distinctions. In
Formalize & Prove
, AWM completes the model in Lean 4
(
de Moura and Ullrich, 2021
)
and constructs kernel-checked proofs of reachability, impossibility, and other properties. A winning witness establishes reachability; an invariant or a suitable cost lower bound can exclude every legal winning sequence under the model.

The difference extends beyond proof construction. AWM’s initial bounds match the minimum winning costs in four of six runs, compared with one for Opus 5.5 (without a proof) and none for Astra; other baseline runs report incorrect bounds or remain inconclusive. For example, on level 4 Astra claims impossibility with an unproved minimum winning cost of 22, whereas AWM proves a tight bound of 19 under its learned model, matching the game’s actual minimum winning cost. Given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises the rules underlying its remaining two bounds and constructs new closed proofs, bringing its bound accuracy to six of six.
AWM’s learned mechanisms are also explicit and inspectable: typed objects and named rules make their predictions available for step-by-step checking. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, AWM builds compact models with a median of six object types and ten rules. These models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels, checking represented state transitions and final goal conditions (§
3
). With Opus 5, AWM clears all 25 games with a score of 99.9, competitive with leading code-executing systems; its certified winning trajectories use 43% of the human baseline’s actions.
We make three contributions.
•
A framework from exploration to algebraic structure.
AWM turns interaction with an unknown environment into executable hypotheses and organizes them into compact models through
category-theory-guided
transformations checked in Lean, presenting object types as projective and inductive limits. Shared, parameterized rules express related mechanisms in a common form, allowing their properties to be stated and proved uniformly (§
2
).
•
Formal impossibility reasoning in unknown worlds.
AWM constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs that rule out all legal winning sequences under its learned rules and specified constraints, including sequences never explored. This establishes model-relative impossibility rather than inferring it from unsuccessful play (§
4
).
•
Inspectable models and traceable proofs.
Typed objects and named rules make learned dynamics understandable and their predictions checkable against observations. Lean replay connects the formal representation to recorded behavior, while explicit proof dependencies identify the rules on which a conclusion rests, supporting targeted empirical examination and revision (§
3
; §
4.3
).
2
Method
AWM aims to turn interaction with an unknown environment into a mathematical model that supports rigorous reasoning about both reachability and impossibility. This requires more than collecting rules that explain observed transitions: the rules must form a coherent representation of the environment, and that representation must support reasoning about action sequences the agent has never explored.
We first describe the target model (§
2.1
), then present the three stages that construct and use it (Figure
1
): Explore & Prototype develops executable hypotheses through interaction; Structure & Simplify organizes them into a compact algebraic model; and Formalize & Prove completes the model in Lean 4 and establishes machine-checked results.

An algebraic world model describes an environment through typed objects, rules, and a goal predicate, represented in executable Python and formal Lean 4 to support both empirical testing and mathematical reasoning.

Example: one rule for four mechanisms
In game
lp85
, buttons move colored tiles, and a level is won when every slot holds its matching color. During Explore & Prototype, the agent discovers eleven concepts describing four button mechanisms: belts, stars, hubs, and panels (Figure
3

The shared rule also shortens reasoning: because one color-count invariant covers every button, proofs that a variant is unsolvable need two to three times fewer lemmas than proofs over the eleven separate concepts (Appendix
B
). A separate check tests whether such a model-level proof also holds for the game: on the level-6 tile-swap variant U, Lean verifies its unsolvability proof against an engine-derived graph covering all 52,500 transitions among 7,500 configurations (Appendix
B

In Formalize & Prove, Lean certifies a five-click winning sequence (Figure
3

3

Across the 25 games, AWM records 742 executable concepts and withdraws 143 during model revision. The retained concepts are tested against the recorded transitions. 4
Proving impossibility
A winning trajectory establishes reachability; impossibility requires excluding every legal winning sequence within the budget, including those never explored. We test whether AWM’s learned algebraic models enable such exhaustive proofs, and whether those proofs hold for the game itself.

sc25

3
×
3
3\times 3
panel to reach the exit within the level’s budget. Moves and panel clicks cost one unit, completing a spell one more, fuel refunds ten, and the winning move is free. We construct two variants of levels 4 and 5 by rearranging selected elements while preserving the game mechanics, then seal them at budgets of 18 and 35. Exhaustive search on the game engine (the underlying game program), covering all four initial facings and all 13 actions, establishes minimum winning costs of 19 and 36, respectively: neither sealed level can be won, while one additional unit permits a win.
Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra receive the game interface and coding tools, including simulator construction and search; AWM uses Opus 5.5 with the procedure of §

After each attempt, every agent is asked whether the sealed level can be won and to justify its verdict; AWM constructs Lean proofs under its learned model. Impossibility can be established by proving that the minimum winning cost exceeds the budget. We evaluate proof validity under the learned model separately from numerical agreement with the engine.

Proof validity and bound accuracy are distinct.
Before feedback, four of six AWM bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra.
Some runs identify a correct winning sequence but charge the otherwise free winning move, reporting a bound one unit higher. Because this cost cannot be observed on sealed levels, we count such bounds as correct for all agents only when the discrepancy is explicitly attributable to this accounting convention, not to an incorrect route or cost estimate.

4.3
Auditing premises and proving again
After the initial evaluation, the two AWM runs with bounds of 20 and 47 receive feedback only that the game permits a cheaper win, without revealing its cost, route or the faulty rule. AWM revisits its explicit rules, tests alternative formulations through interaction, and constructs new proofs under the refined models (Appendix
C
).
On L4, AWM discovers that growing onto fuel collects it, reducing the bound from 20 to 19. On L5, it identifies terrain rather than limited range as the cause of a failed shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under its convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the game’s minimum cost of 36. Both refinements succeed within four additional attempts, each yielding a new closed Lean proof. With this feedback, AWM reaches correct bounds in all six runs.
We provide the same discrepancy feedback and additional attempt budget to the four baseline runs with incorrect bounds. Astra corrects both bounds but produces no formal proofs, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither.
Proof dependencies help locate faulty rules.
Both repairs corrected rules used by the original proofs. To test whether proof dependencies help locate such errors, we inject a single incorrect rule into a reference model and give Claude Opus 5.5 the faulty model, its Lean proof, and access to the game. The goal is to find a transition where the model’s prediction disagrees with the game. On L4, Claude succeeds in 16 of 42 runs without explicit proof dependencies. Providing the rules used by the proof, without revealing which rule is faulty, increases this to 29 of 42 runs. Even when directly told which rule is faulty, Claude finds a counterexample in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies substantially improve error discovery, nearly matching the benefit of identifying the faulty rule directly (Appendix
C
).
4.4
From model proofs to the engine
Matching the game’s minimum winning cost provides evidence of accurate reasoning, but does not establish that a formal proof under the learned model also holds for the game. To transfer such a proof, the learned model need not cover every game transition; by Definition
1
, it suffices that it reproduce the game’s optimal winning sequences. For the budgeted tasks here, we verify sufficient certificate-level conditions on engine-derived graphs, which preserve budget feasibility and the proof invariants (Lemmas
A.2
–
A.3
).
We exhaustively check the engines’ budget-feasible transitions from the fixed opening against the potential inequalities and invariant conditions used in the model proofs. These checks establish that five of the six model-level impossibility proofs can be extended to the original games. Appendix
C
gives the per-run transfer arguments, including the completed rules and certificates.
5
Related work
Executable world models.
Code world models are learned from interaction for planning
(
Tang et al., 2024
)
, refined by generation, testing and repair
(
Dainese et al., 2024
)
or composed from programmatic experts
(
Piriyakulkij et al., 2025
)
; theory-based agents explore and plan with learned theories
(
Tsividis et al., 2021
)
, and TheoryCoder-2 learns reusable abstractions for hierarchical planning
(
Ahmed et al., 2026
)
. Such models are central to recent ARC-AGI-3 agents
(
Rodionov, 2026b
;
Courtis et al., 2026
;
Rodionov, 2026a
)
: Twin does not act until its simulator reproduces every observed transition
(
Skoutnev et al., 2026
)
, and Tycho finds that a closer match does not by itself yield better play
(
Lehmann et al., 2026
)
. The closest work, Memento 3, compiles a natural-language rulebook into code and accepts an update only if an LLM judges it faithful and replay is exact
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. Yet a code world model can pass a sampled-transition check at 100% accuracy and still lose because it misses a key rule
(
Aguilar Martín, 2026
)
. AWM instead abstracts its rules into a shared structure, tests them beyond the record, and proves reachability and impossibility, checking the proofs’ premises against the game.
Certified impossibility.
Unsolvability certificates let an independent checker confirm that a planning task has no plan
(
Eriksson et al., 2017
)
, in the spirit of certifying algorithms
(
McConnell et al., 2011
)
, and certificate checking has been formally verified for temporal planning
(
Wang and Abdulaziz, 2025
)
; all start from a supplied model. Impossibility transfers from an abstraction that covers every environment transition, with preserved initialization and goals
(
Clarke et al., 1994
)
; Definition
1
requires only that the model reproduce the optimal winning sequences; action-model learning gives conditions under which learned models support such transfer
(
Aineto and Scala, 2024
)
. AWM learns its model from interaction; Lean checks every deduction from that model, and interaction checks the model’s rules against the game.
Formal reasoning.
Neural provers produce Lean proofs at olympiad level
(
Achim and others, 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Hubert et al., 2026
;
Ren et al., 2025
)
, AI systems have produced Lean proofs of open Erdős problems
(
Sothanaphan, 2026
;
Tsoukalas and others, 2026
)
, and autoformalization translates informal statements into formal ones
(
Wu et al., 2022
)
. There the objects of proof are given mathematics; AWM must first infer the dynamics and costs its proofs quantify over, which makes the fidelity of its formal model an empirical question.
Large-scale AI-assisted software verification proves properties of compiled programs relative to machine semantics and theorem statements, and can expose bugs during proof construction
(
Lucas et al., 2026
)
. That work also studies Claude-generated x86 semantics; AWM learns the objects, action rules and goals of an unfamiliar interactive environment.
6
Limitations and conclusion
Limitations.
We demonstrate AWM on ARC-like environments with discrete actions and immediate, observable feedback, where learned rules can be checked against recorded transitions; richer hidden state, delayed feedback and stochastic dynamics remain to be tested. Lean guarantees the correctness of proofs under the learned model’s explicit premises, and whether these premises capture the environment is tested by interaction: the explicit rules and kernel-checked proofs separate errors in the learned model from errors in reasoning, so a discrepancy can be traced to its assumption and addressed by further exploration. Broader environments and tasks are the natural next test of such formal reasoning.
Conclusion.
Formal reasoning traditionally begins with predefined objects and rules. AWM takes a step toward reasoning rigorously about unknown worlds by discovering these structures through interaction, organizing them into compact algebraic models, and formalizing them in Lean. The resulting models make learned mechanisms explicit and their behavior checkable step by step, while supporting kernel-checked proofs of reachability and impossibility, including claims about action sequences never explored. By making the assumptions behind these proofs explicit, AWM also allows discrepancies with the environment to be traced to learned rules and addressed through further exploration. Together, these capabilities bridge empirical exploration and formal reasoning, extending mathematical proof beyond problems whose definitions are given in advance.

Our interactive website presents the models, tests, Lean proofs,
and links to official replays for all 25 public games:
https://ephemeral6.github.io/awm-site/
.
The Lean model of
lp85
, our running example, is also
included in the supplementary materials (

),
together with scripts for building the project and auditing
its axioms.
The website also provides the results and supporting materials
for the sealed-level experiments, with per-run results reported
in Appendix

.
Statement on AI use
The agents studied in this paper are LLM agents, so AI use is part of the method. Generative
AI was also used to draft and edit the text and to write the analysis scripts. All
reported numbers come from script outputs over the recorded runs, not from
model-generated text. The Lean proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, independently of
any model.

Verification at each node.
Every non-leaf node of the hierarchy is verified by the Lean kernel: every object type with constraints and every case table must come with a proof of its universal property. The kernel establishes that each node is the limit or colimit of its diagram; whether the representation describes the environment is established by the tasks. The two kinds of evidence therefore answer different questions, what the model entails and whether it agrees with the environment, and neither substitutes for the other. A claim for all well-formed states requires a Lean theorem that does not hold by definitional unfolding alone; for example, the equation stating that a rule defined by pattern matching equals the copairing of its branches holds by unfolding and certifies the form of the rule, not its content.

The comparison tests whether agents can identify the budget obstruction and justify it from interaction. Three configurations play each sealed level, three runs each. Each run has up to eight reset-delimited attempts, ending at game over or recorded abandonment. After each attempt, the interview in Appendix

C.4 Repairing the rules and proving again.
The two overestimated AWM bounds provide a test of whether an explicit model can be corrected after a valid proof has been obtained. After the eight-attempt round, those runs and the four baseline runs with wrong bounds receive one piece of feedback: the engine permits a cheaper win than their analysis allows. The message reveals no rule, cost or route. AWM additionally receives a self-audit instruction to relax rules consistently with the record, test disagreements in the game, revise and prove again; the baseline message states the same discrepancy logic in plain language. Each run gets at most four further attempts.
The corrections change specific premises of the proofs (Table
11
). On level 4, growing onto fuel collects it, reducing AWM’s bound from 20 to 19; Figure
9
shows the missed interaction and the cheaper route. On level 5, terrain rather than limited range blocks a shot, reducing the bound from 47 to 37 under the run’s convention of charging the winning move, equivalent to the engine’s 36. Both repairs produce new closed Lean proofs. Astra corrects both numerical bounds without producing a formal proof, while Claude Opus 5.5 corrects neither. Thus numerical revision and renewed formal certification remain distinct outcomes of the same feedback.

C.6 Using proof dependencies to find model errors.
The repairs above corrected rules used by the original proofs. We
now test whether knowing which rules a proof depends on helps an
agent find errors in its world model.
We start from a reference model that agrees with the game under
the abstractions of §
C
, and deliberately make one
rule incorrect. We select 14 such errors on L4 and 7 on L5 that
change the model’s minimum winning cost, and repeat each experiment
with three seeds.
Claude Opus 5.5 receives the faulty model, a closed Lean proof of
impossibility under that (faulty) model, and access to the game. Although the proof is valid
under the model’s rules, those rules may disagree with the game.
Claude must find an actual transition where the model predicts
a different outcome from the game, within the faulty rule’s scope.
Simply naming the faulty rule does not count as success.
We compare three conditions. In C1, Claude receives the model’s
rules and their recorded evidence, without an explicit list of
proof dependencies. In C2, it additionally receives the list
of rules used by the proof, but is not told which one is wrong.
In R, it is directly told the faulty rule. We also include
random exploration (C0) and exhaustive engine search (EX) as
references. Each agent run has a budget of 50 game actions on
L4 or 5,000 on L5.
On L4, C1 finds a conflicting transition in 16 of 42 runs.
Providing proof dependencies (C2) increases this to 29 of 42.
Even when directly told the faulty rule (R), Claude succeeds
in only 30 of 42 runs. Thus, proof dependencies nearly match
the benefit of knowing the faulty rule, without revealing it.
L5 is harder: C1 succeeds in 1 of 21 runs, C2 in 3 of 21,
and R in 5 of 21.
Across both levels, C2 finds counterexamples in 32 of 63 runs,
compared with 17 of 63 for C1. On 12 error-free controls — the
same procedure run on an unmodified reference model, with no
injected error — C2 raises no false alarms, compared with 0.33
per run for C1.
