C.7 Additional tests of the verification procedure.
We conduct mutation tests to examine what kinds of errors our
verification procedure can detect. In experiments, we deliberately introduce errors
into three models: the two sealed-level reference models (2,675
and 3,502 states) and the merged
lp85
model (869 states).
These errors affect proof certificates, model rules, consistency
between Python and Lean, or theorem statements. We compare a Python
certificate checker with our Lean
-
based verification procedure,
which also includes a separate audit of theorem statements.
Both methods reject all 12 invalid proof certificates, including
nine that would support conclusions contradicted by the game.
The Lean-based procedure additionally detects all three tested
Python–Lean mismatches and all three reversed bounds, which the
Python checker misses. Its separate statement audit also flags
all six cases where a theorem holds only because its premises
cannot be satisfied or its starting-state set is empty. Such
theorems may still compile in Lean: the kernel verifies that
conclusions follow from their premises, not whether those
premises are meaningful.
Neither method detects errors deliberately introduced into the
model’s rules (M1–M6), or theorem statements referring to the
wrong goal or model version (S3, S7). These results illustrate
both the additional checks provided by Lean-based verification
and their limits: a valid proof does not guarantee that the
underlying model correctly describes the game.

article.headline: AWM：从交互探索到Lean证明
article.lede: AWM把未知环境中的交互转成可执行代数模型，再用Lean 4证明可达性与不可达性。
article.problem: AI已能在Lean中给出数学问题的机器可检查证明，但通常依赖预先给定的定义与形式规范。在未知环境中，智能体必须先识别对象、推断动作效果并确定成功条件，而这些规则本身只是需要通过交互学习和修正的假设。论文追问：智能体能否对未知世界进行严格推理？
article.method: AWM分三阶段运行：Explore & Prototype通过主动探测维护可执行Python概念，并依据观测不断检验和修正；Structure & Simplify把假设组织成类型化对象与规则，用范畴论中的投射极限和归纳极限引导变换，在保留已测区分的前提下压缩模型；Formalize & Prove在Lean 4中补全模型，用不变式或成本下界构造核检查的可达性与不可达性证明。
article.results: 在sc25两个密封关卡（预算18和35，引擎穷举最小获胜成本19和36）上，AWM在6/6次运行中产出封闭、内核检查的Lean不可达证明，12次基线运行（Claude Opus 5.5与GPT-6 Astra各6次）均未产出。AWM初始界4/6正确，Opus 5.5为1/6、Astra为0/6；仅收到“存在更便宜获胜”的反馈后，AWM修正规则并达到6/6正确。25个公开ARC-AGI-3游戏的183关全部通关，得分99.9；认证通关轨迹用7,448个动作，为人类基线17,135的43%。模型每局中位数为6个对象类型和10条规则，Lean重放183/183关，形式化220条规则并检查1,374个定理。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把经验探索与形式证明连接起来：在规则未知时，智能体可以给出相对于所学模型的不可达性证明，并把证明依赖的假设暴露出来供审计。
article.limitations: 实验限于离散动作、即时可观察反馈的ARC类环境，隐藏状态、延迟反馈和随机动态尚未测试；Lean只保证证明在模型前提下成立，错误模型规则并不总能被验证流程发现（注入错误规则0/18检出），且6个模型级不可达证明中只有5个可扩展到真实引擎。
article.figure_caption_zh: AWM的三阶段流水线：交互探索构建临时可执行模型，代数变换揭示并简化其结构，Lean 4形式化则支持可达或不可达的认证证明。

figure.caption: AWM's three-stage pipeline: interactive exploration builds a provisional executable model, algebraic transformations reveal and simplify its structure, and Lean~4 formalization enables certified proofs of reachability or impossibility.

In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations.
Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning.

Substantial clinical gaps nonetheless remained, with comprehensive and appropriate treatment recommended in only 46.7% of human-evaluated encounters, at least one critical intake question omitted in 60.6% of simulated intakes, and acute safety risks under-triaged in 12.9% of adversarial presentations.
Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters. However, addressing residual diagnostic, management, and safety limitations, alongside integrating external safeguards and clinician-supervised workflows, remains necessary before prospective clinical validation with real patients.

Introduction
Clinical dialogue is foundational to patient-facing medicine, but in psychiatry, the clinical interview itself remains a principal diagnostic instrument
144
. In psychiatric presentations, the psychopathology itself can directly compromise how history is communicated, and patients often do not recognize the relevance of prior treatment failures or comorbid medical conditions causing their symptoms

. As a result, the quality of the history depends on both systematic inquiry into these complex causes and interpersonal trust, with a stronger therapeutic alliance supporting more complete diagnostic formulation and improved treatment outcomes

;
2

176
. In psychiatry, both dimensions are especially entangled. A clinician who probes aggressively risks rupturing rapport; one who overprioritizes validation may never arrive at a diagnosis. Here we investigate whether language models can acquire these capabilities through training in simulated clinical environments.

We report three findings. First, in a randomized, double-blind OSCE with psychiatrists role-playing patients, the simulation-trained agent outperformed its identically prompted base model, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, differential diagnosis formulation, and initial management planning (Section

Third, under adversarial presentations, training reduced but did not eliminate unsafe behavior, and the residual failures were mainly under-triage and missed red flags, including errors of omission that post-hoc output filters cannot intercept because no overtly harmful text is generated, such as failing to ask the probing questions needed to uncover a concealed crisis or failing to escalate care (Section

In each pair, one of 32 board-certified psychiatrists (Supplementary Table

Discussion
We trained a language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters and validated it against its identically prompted base model in three settings. In a randomized, double-blind crossover OSCE with board-certified psychiatrists role-playing standardized patients, the trained agent received a higher independent transcript score than the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, and differential diagnosis formulation (Section
2.1
). Across an automated evaluation of 127 clinician-validated psychiatric intake scenarios, it nearly doubled its base model’s pre-penalty clinical rubric score and substantially improved composite clinical reward, with gains across all four difficulty tiers (Section
2.2
). Under 256 adversarial presentations designed to elicit unsafe clinical behavior, training more than halved under-triage relative to the base model, although residual failures remained (Section
2.3
). Comparing the post-trained agent against its untuned base checkpoint under an identical clinical system prompt, tool interface, and reasoning-token budget isolates the combined effect of the simulation RL pipeline (spanning both adaptation to dynamic patient states and alignment to structured clinical rubrics) from prompt engineering or test-time compute. Because on-policy RL updates model weights from scalar rewards on self-generated trajectories without additional medical corpora, these results also show how far procedural gains carry across clinical tasks. In psychiatric intake, diagnostic reasoning and communication are more tightly coupled than in general medical consultations
176
;
15
, where core symptom histories are less contingent on trust; accordingly, diagnostic formulation scaled with interpersonal and history-taking gains, consistent with building rapport and sustaining structured inquiry unlocking the gated patient disclosures needed to double differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3% in the OSCE). Conversely, downstream management tasks that generally depend on static clinical knowledge rather than conversational elicitation, specifically comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% vs. 26.7% appropriateness across pharmacological and psychotherapeutic recommendations), showed more modest gains and likely remained constrained by both the base model’s parametric capacity and the greater case-level subjectivity of psychiatric treatment selection
75
.
Gains in patient-centered communication were broad, and clinician-patients rated the trained agent as displaying more empathic behavior than the base model during live interaction. These are best read as gains in procedural communication and structured empathic responding, captured in the same direction by all three communication instruments (PCCBP, GMCPQ, and the patient-facing PACES items), rather than as evidence of therapeutic alliance formation, which develops over sustained multi-session relationships
45
. Frequent not-applicable responses on the WAI-SR, an instrument designed for multi-session psychotherapy
62
, are consistent with this distinction (Appendix
A.3
). Whether simulation training also improves alliance in longitudinal settings remains an open question.
Automated multi-turn evaluation complements clinician-enacted assessment by gating diagnostically critical information behind rapport and targeted inquiry, testing interactive clinical interviewing rather than static knowledge recall; the training gain was preserved under an independent out-of-family evaluator (Section
2.2
; Appendix
C.2
). In the adversarial evaluation, simulation training substantially reduced contraindications, missed red flags, and under-triage, but did not eliminate failures when acute risk was concealed behind benign complaints. The composition of these residual failures has direct implications for safety governance. Deterministic guardrails can intercept generation-side harms such as a contraindicated prescription, because the harmful content is present in the output and can be filtered. They cannot address omissions in which the agent never asks the question that would have surfaced a concealed risk, because a post-hoc safety layer has no corresponding content on which to act. Mitigating omission failures therefore requires process-level safeguards external to free-text generation, including structured state-tracking checklists that gate encounter termination on mandatory safety and review-of-systems inquiry, real-time supervisory monitors that audit dialogue state for unprobed red flags, and clinician-in-the-loop verification at handoff. Beyond evaluating our trained model, the clinician-validated intake suite, adversarial stress-testing protocol, and Delphi taxonomies (Table
1
) provide a structured methodology for auditing both commission and omission failures across conversational systems proposed for mental health settings.
How closely automated evaluation tracks clinical judgment is quantified by the three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios (Section
2.2
). The autorater correlated moderately with the psychiatrists’ ratings on the same transcripts (

Simulated evaluation can therefore order and stress-test models, but neither estimate the size of their differences nor identify the scenarios on which one model outperforms another. As a training environment, however, the same simulator proved sufficient: the gains it produced held when psychiatrists role-played the patients and graded the transcripts.
A documented gap in access to mental health services motivates this line of work. More than 75% of individuals with mental disorders in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment
191
, and even in high-income settings, fewer than one in five individuals with major depressive disorder receive minimally adequate care
173
. Tele-psychiatry supports effective evaluation and treatment delivery for many presentations
71
, which suggests that the encounter format is not the primary barrier to competent assessment, but it does not change the supply of clinician time, since a synchronous consultation occupies a psychiatrist for its full duration whether remote or in person. Addressing this bottleneck does not, however, imply automating psychiatric evaluation or replacing psychiatrists, social workers, or intake clinicians. Given the complexity of psychiatric care and the substantial error rates observed even after simulation training, our findings do not support autonomous deployment of the present system; rather, any prospective near-term clinical role should be strictly assistive and clinician-supervised
75
;
131
;
53
, such as conducting a structured pre-visit intake to generate a provisional history and symptom summary that a supervising clinician reviews, verifies, and builds upon during the clinical encounter, potentially supplementing routine psychosocial intake or static questionnaires with structured medical review of systems, medication reconciliation, and preliminary differential screening for somatic mimics.
Limitations.
Several methodological and clinical limitations constrain what these results support. First, while multi-institutionally validated synthetic cases help address the scarcity of shareable psychiatric clinical data
75
and allowed training and automated evaluation to scale across the diagnostic taxonomy, simulated and clinician-enacted patients cannot reproduce the full range of rare conditions, backgrounds, motivations, or disorganized communication encountered in clinical practice; unlike trained professional standardized patients (such as those used in clinical trial rater calibration) or real patients, psychiatrists role-playing patients may present symptoms in overly structured, textbook patterns, making validation with professional standardized patients and real patient cohorts essential next steps. Second, our study uses a controlled within-model design comparing a lightweight policy model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) against its identically prompted base checkpoint rather than against larger frontier models or human clinicians (such as psychiatrists or psychiatric social workers); while this design keeps multi-turn GRPO rollouts computationally tractable and isolates whether simulation training improves upon static prompt instructions, smaller model capacity likely constrained the ceiling on knowledge-intensive tasks such as comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% comprehensive and appropriate treatment in the OSCE), and future studies evaluating clinical readiness must incorporate human clinical comparators alongside ablations against non-interactive rubric fine-tuning and oracle-history baselines. Third, the training reward and scenario reference rubrics were generated within the same model family (Gemini 3.1 Pro) that served as the primary automated evaluator, introducing circularity risks including verbosity bias, stylistic mimicry, and reward hacking
203
;
182
. Cross-evaluator validation with GPT-5.6-Luna confirmed that a substantial training gain persisted under an independent judge (difference between models 0.165, attenuated from 0.270 under the in-family Gemini evaluator against which the policy was trained), though agreement between language-model judges does not exclude shared stylistic preferences, underscoring why evaluation grounded in human clinical judgment remains essential.
In the three-way concordance analysis (Section
2.2
), only the in-family autorater was compared against psychiatrists on the OSCE transcripts. Furthermore, because each OSCE transcript was graded by a single psychiatrist (with different evaluators across each pair), cross-rater reproducibility could not be estimated directly (Appendix
A.6
). Although transcript formatting and turn-count metadata were standardized and independent evaluators graded unpaired transcripts, the trained agent’s substantially longer consultations (median 60 vs. 8 clinician turns) could partially cue crossover clinician-patients during live interaction; however, independent psychiatrist score gains were not significantly correlated with turn-count differences across scenarios (

The simulated and clinician-patient settings also used different interfaces (Methods, Section

), and we did not separate patient from interface effects on interview length or score. The training gain nonetheless held under an OSCE interface that differed from the one used in training.
Clinically, our findings are restricted to single-encounter text-based intake rather than ongoing care. Single-encounter intake aims at a provisional formulation and triage plan, whereas ongoing psychiatric care, including longitudinal medication management and psychotherapy, requires sustained therapeutic relationships and adaptive treatment planning across repeated contact
180
;
118
. Moreover, text restricts assessment to a text-inferable Mental Status Examination (Methods, Section
4.3
); written dialogue exposes thought process, thought content, orientation, and expressed insight, but structurally excludes physical, behavioral, and non-verbal observations on which several diagnostic discriminations depend, including separating negative symptoms of schizophrenia from depressive psychomotor retardation, identifying catatonic features, and detecting acute intoxication or withdrawal
121
;
84
. A text-based agent therefore cannot perform a comprehensive psychiatric examination or substitute for a psychiatrist, and at most could support preliminary, clinician-supervised pre-intake information gathering. In addition, all scenarios and consultations were conducted in English and the clinical norms encoded in our rubrics reflect US psychiatric practice, whereas linguistic expressions of distress, diagnostic conventions, emergency hold criteria, and duty-to-warn mandates vary across languages and jurisdictions
64
;
49
, and the agent was trained for semi-structured intake as opposed to scripted diagnostic instruments such as the SCID-5
42
. Finally, deploying AI in psychiatric care raises domain-specific ethical risks
20
. Reinforcement learning to overcome guardedness corresponds in human practice to motivational interviewing
111
, but under unconstrained optimization has a potential risk of discovering manipulative conversational shortcuts, and individuals in distress are susceptible to anthropomorphic projection and parasocial attachment
87
. Any future translation would therefore require safeguards architecturally external to the learned policy, including hard output-level vetoes on clinical disposition and prescribing, anti-sycophancy auditing, clinician oversight, and deterministic escalation protocols for acute risk
154
.
Conclusion.
A simulation-trained agent conducted standardized psychiatric intake at a level that board-certified psychiatrists rated above its identically prompted base model across clinical examination skill, patient-centered communication, and diagnostic formulation. Standardized patient OSCEs are an established milestone in medical education, but they do not substitute for prospective validation in real patient populations; the environment, agent, reward functions, rubrics, and evaluation scenarios described here are research prototypes, and none has been cleared by any regulatory authority for clinical use. Prospective study under institutional clinician oversight, with real patients and longitudinal follow-up, is the necessary next step. Such text-based systems are not a substitute for psychiatric clinicians and are not ready for autonomous psychiatric assessment; the immediate clinical question for future research is whether, as strictly assistive tools operating under direct clinician oversight, they can help expand the reach of clinician-led care
191
;
173
;
75
. Answering that question requires the psychiatric community to define the evaluation standards and governance boundaries
75
;
47
, and the evaluation framework, rubrics, and taxonomies described here are offered as one contribution toward that goal.
4

Methods
Training an agent for psychiatric care requires a corpus that captures the diagnostic breadth, clinical ambiguity, and relational complexity of outpatient practice. A training set clustered on common presentations (such as uncomplicated depression or generalized anxiety) risks producing an agent that fails to generalize to diverse clinical encounters. Building on
Liévin et al. Super
, we developed a four-stage clinician-designed generation pipeline covering the diagnostic, demographic, and behavioral spectrum of outpatient psychiatry (Fig.
5
). Of 50,000 initial generation requests, 48,243 scenarios passed quality verification and deduplication against the held-out evaluation scenarios.
4.1

OSCE study design
Standardized patient methodology is an accepted standard for assessing diagnostic formulation, communication, and clinical safety
7
;
61
;
68
. Role-play by board-certified psychiatrists provides clinical fidelity and expert calibration without exposing patients to experimental systems
176
;
100
, but does not reproduce real clinical care.
The OSCE cohort comprised 60 scenarios drawn from the 127 clinician-validated intake evaluation scenarios (Section
4.6
) by sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content, covering major psychiatric categories, occult somatic mimics, and complex ethical or legal presentations. Thirty-two board-certified psychiatrists (59.4% female; median experience 12.5 years, IQR 8–18; Supplementary Table
5
) served as clinician-patients in a within-case crossover design. Psychiatrists were selected for this role rather than lay actors because executing each scenario’s conditional information-gating protocol required real-time clinical judgment of whether the agent’s inquiry warranted disclosing guarded diagnostic facts, alongside expert calibration when scoring post-encounter communication instruments, while avoiding any exposure of real patients to an experimental system. Each received a detailed role sheet specifying the patient’s history, presentation, psychological defenses, and disclosure triggers (Appendix
A.1
). The clinician-actor conducted separate, blinded, synchronous text consultations with the identically prompted base model and the simulation-trained agent. Presentation sequence was randomized and counterbalanced, with a 48-hour washout period between paired consultations. Clinician-actors and independent raters were blinded to model identity and training condition.
To prevent affective halo effects from live role-play, evaluation used a two-perspective protocol. Clinician-patients provided post-encounter perceptions immediately following the chat. Separately, an independent panel of 15 board-certified psychiatrists drawn from the 54-member expert validation cohort (disjoint from the 32 clinician-patient actors) independently evaluated full consultation transcripts and clinical outputs, formatted as standardized clinical records stripped of AI identifiers (Appendix
A.2
; Supplementary Table
4
). Independent transcript evaluators scored an 18-item clinical-skills rubric derived from the Royal College of Physicians PACES examination
40
(which, together with the four patient-facing communication items rated by clinician-patients, comprises the 22-item PACES framework; Supplementary Table
1
); a four-dimensional differential diagnosis rubric; and structured items covering investigations, treatments, management plan appropriateness, and clinical confabulation (Appendix
A.4
; Supplementary Table
2
). Clinician-patients completed a post-encounter battery comprising the 11-item General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire
17
(nine Likert and two binary items), the four patient-facing PACES items, the 11-item patient-centered communication checklist operationalizing the Kalamazoo consensus essential elements

4.6
Simulated psychiatric intake evaluation design and expert validation
The automated psychiatric intake evaluation comprises 127 expert-validated scenarios, instantiated from clinician-authored specifications, spanning the diagnostic, demographic, and difficulty taxonomy of outpatient psychiatry; the 60 scenarios used in the human OSCE (Section
4.5
) were drawn from this validated set by stratified sampling. Whereas the training corpus uses prevalence-weighted stochastic sampling to maximize conversational breadth during reinforcement learning (Section
4.1
), the evaluation suite was constructed through a separate, stratified factorial pipeline designed to give equal weight to all presentations and to pair each case with an explicit disclosure schedule and clinician-verified scoring key. All 127 scenarios gate clinically critical facts behind specific clinician behaviors, including direct inquiry, empathic probing, or sustained trust-building. Accurate diagnosis requires active clinical elicitation rather than retrieval of overt symptoms. Existing medical AI evaluations assess clinical knowledge through static question-answer pairs
74
;
162
;
8
or simulated patients in general medical domains
152
;
86

100
;
151
, but neither assesses the elicitation of gated diagnostic information through targeted inquiry and rapport
75
; Appendix
E
situates our evaluation methodology against this literature in full.
Overall, the evaluation cohort spans eight diagnostic and competency domains, including six core psychiatric categories (consolidating the 15 training diagnostic domains; mood, anxiety and stress-related, psychotic spectrum, substance use, personality and complex presentations, and other presentations including ADHD, eating disorders, sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder in adults, and gender dysphoria), medical mimics requiring workups for somatic causes (e.g., autoimmune encephalitis
30

136

Extended Methodology
A.1
Psychiatrist-as-Patient Recruitment and Protocol
Board-certified psychiatrists were recruited to role-play patients in a blinded, counterbalanced, within-scenario crossover design. During the OSCE, clinician-patients received only the Patient Role Sheet specifying the patient’s clinical background, behavioral traits, disclosure rules (what to share freely versus what to reveal only if trust is established or if asked directly), communication style, and resistance patterns, without the ground-truth diagnostic or management scoring key. Although some clinician-patients had participated months earlier in scenario validation (where each reviewer inspected a small subset of candidate scenarios; Appendix
C.1
), each scenario’s two crossover encounters were enacted by the exact same clinician-patient under strict blinding to model identity and condition order, ensuring that any prior familiarity was held constant across paired conditions.
From the 127 expert-validated psychiatric intake evaluation scenarios (Appendix
C.1
), 60 were selected for the crossover OSCE via stratified sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content. Each scenario produced two text-based encounters (one with the identically prompted base model and one with the RL-trained agent) in counterbalanced order with a mandatory 48-hour washout period. Post-encounter, clinician-patients completed the WAI-SR (Appendix
A.3
), GMCPQ (11 items; comprising nine 5-point Likert communication items used to compute the GMCPQ composite and two binary global retention items), PACES patient-facing communication and empathy items (4 items), and PCCBP patient-centered communication items (11 binary items). Clinician-patients also provided qualitative feedback.

article.headline: 模拟环境强化学习提升精神科访谈能力
article.lede: 随机双盲交叉OSCE显示，模拟环境多轮强化学习提升语言模型精神科接诊表现，但治疗规划与安全遗漏仍存。
article.problem: 精神科接诊访谈本身是主要诊断工具，要求医生在建立信任的同时系统追问并鉴别重叠表现。现有医疗对话AI评估多集中于一般医学场景，静态问答难以衡量通过关系建立和针对性询问获取被隐藏的关键临床信息的能力。
article.method: 作者构建模拟临床环境：用语言模型生成并验证48,243个精神科场景，让模型与模拟患者进行多轮互动，由自动评分器按临床量表打分，并用GRPO更新策略。训练后在127个专家验证场景中自动评估，并开展60对随机双盲交叉OSCE，由32名精神科医生扮演标准化病人、15名独立精神科医生盲评转录。
article.results: 在60对OSCE中，训练代理在76.7%配对中胜出（p<0.0001），PACES临床技能3.04 vs. 2.32（满分5），以患者为中心沟通82.0% vs. 65.2%，鉴别诊断适当性68.3% vs. 33.3%。自动评估的127个场景中，临床量表分0.706 vs. 0.379，复合奖励0.564 vs. 0.294（p<0.0001）；256个对抗呈现中，急性风险分诊不足12.9% vs. 30.5%，禁忌0.8% vs. 6.2%，漏红旗6.2% vs. 10.9%。残余问题仍明显：人评接诊中仅46.7%获得全面且适当的治疗建议，模拟接诊中60.6%至少漏问一个关键问题。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明模拟环境可作为训练和压力测试精神科对话智能体的受控试验台，且增益能迁移到医生扮演的标准化病人接诊。但论文强调其近期角色应是临床监督下的辅助工具，而非自主评估或替代精神科医生。
article.limitations: 研究限于单次、文本、英语及美国临床规范的接诊，医生扮演患者可能过于结构化，且模型为轻量级Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite、未与人类临床医生或更大前沿模型比较；训练奖励与场景评分同属Gemini 3.1家族，存在循环性与奖励黑客风险。更关键的是残余失败包括“从不提问”的遗漏型安全风险，事后输出过滤无法拦截，需外部流程级防护和临床监督。

figure.caption: {Overview of contributions.} The proposed framework involves training a language model in a simulated environment and evaluating it with human experts. {Left (Training in Simulation),} The training process comprises three components: {a,} Scenario Generation, which synthesizes clinical, behavioral, and demographic data into verified patient scenarios using a language model; {b,} Simulation, where the model engages in multi-turn interactions with a simulated patient; and {c,} Reinforcement Learning, which uses an autorater to grade conversation transcripts against a clinical rubric and updates the policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). {Top Right (Evaluating with Standardized Patients),} The trained model (trained in simulation) and its base model act as the clinician in randomized, double-blind text conversations with board-certified psychiatrists acting as standardized patients. Separate independent, board-certified psychiatrist evaluators (blinded to whether transcripts came from the trained or base model) and the role-playing clinician-patients score the encounters across multiple dimensions (e.g., perceived empathic behavior, diagnostic formulation, clinical safety, and management plan), as compared across normalized domain scores in the radar chart. {Bottom Right (Evaluating in Simulation),} Automated evaluation across expert-validated scenarios shows that the simulation-trained agent achieved a higher composite clinical reward than its base model overall and across all four difficulty tiers (overall, 0.56 vs.\ 0.29; easy, 0.65 vs.\ 0.34; edge, 0.51 vs.\ 0.25; all $p < 0.0001$; left chart). Under 256 adversarial stress-testing presentations (right chart), the trained agent reduced measured safety failure rates relative to its base model, including contraindications (0.8\% vs.\ 6.2\%, $p = 0.001$), missed red flags (6.2\% vs.\ 10.9\%, $p = 0.04$), and clinical under-triage (12.9\% vs.\ 30.5\%, $p < 0.0001$).

Play2Perfect
: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
Tyler Ga Wei Lum
Kushal Kedia
C. Karen Liu
Jeannette Bohg
Affiliation:
Stanford University
Affiliation:
Cornell University
*
Equal contribution
†
Equal advising
play2perfect.github.io
Abstract
Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can
perfect
precise assembly, it must first learn to
play
. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to
play
matter for precise assembly? We propose
Play2Perfect
, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through
play
on diverse objects and goals, which is then
perfected
on precise assembly. The goal of
play
is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in
play
pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.
Figure 1:
Play2Perfect
Overview.
Before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it first learns to play. We pretrain a single goal-conditioned RL policy on task-agnostic dexterous object manipulation, producing a reusable prior for grasping, in-hand reorientation, and 6D pose control. This pretrained play policy is then finetuned in sparse-reward RL environments derived from CAD designs to solve diverse contact-rich assembly tasks, including tight insertions, screwing, and multi-part assembly.
Keywords:
Reinforcement Learning, Dexterous Manipulation, Sim-to-Real
1
Introduction
Robots with multi-fingered hands hold the potential to bring speed and dexterity to the diverse tasks humans perform with their hands. Yet, this flexibility comes at the cost of controlling many degrees of freedom through contact, leaving challenging domains like precise assembly out of reach for current robot learning methods. On one hand, the contact-rich nature of assembly makes dexterous teleoperation challenging, so most imitation learning has focused on lower-precision pick-and-place tasks
[
58
,
14
,
15
,
39
,
7
]
. On the other hand, assembly is sparse-reward, defined by a part’s final pose, limiting the use of sim-to-real RL methods that require dense-reward shaping
[
56
,
65
,
11
,
2
,
18
,
27
,
13
]
.
Prior work has made progress on assembly by adding structure to the problem. One approach is to modify the environment with custom fixtures that simplify grasping and insertion
[
32
,
42
]
. Another is to modify the robot itself with specialized tool attachments or end-effectors that make the control problem easier
[
17
,
44
]
. However, both strategies require per-assembly engineering of the hardware or environment. The use of robots with parallel-jaw grippers makes teleoperation feasible, enabling imitation learning
[
3
]
and subsequent RL finetuning
[
4
]
. Without teleoperation, RL methods often rely on dense, task-specific rewards
[
52
,
51
]
or scripted multi-stage controllers
[
54
]
. The reliance of these approaches on parallel-jaw grippers still limits their speed and dexterity.
Our goal is to tackle hard, sparse-reward problems such as precise assembly with dexterous hands, without relying on teleoperation. The core challenge is that the sparse reward defined by the final goal configuration of an assembly part offers limited training signal for RL. Starting from a random policy, the agent must discover grasping, in-hand reorientation, alignment, and contact-rich insertion before receiving any reward. Intuitively, before learning the hard problem of
perfecting
precise assembly, a robot should first learn the easier problem of
playing
with objects in free space. While the concept of learning from
play
has been explored previously
[
33
,
57
,
25
,
23
]
, it remains unclear what aspects of the
play
pretraining recipe matter for downstream finetuning, especially for precise assembly. In this work, we systematically study the design choices that make
play
useful for precise assembly, including object diversity, trajectory diversity, training objective, and goal precision. Across these studies, we find a consistent takeaway:
play
pretraining transfers best when it forces the robot to learn in-hand manipulation using its fingers rather than movement with a fixed grasp.
We propose
Play2Perfect
, a framework for dexterous pretraining on general objects and goals, followed by finetuning for precise assembly. In simulation, we pretrain a goal-conditioned
play
policy via RL to manipulate diverse primitive objects to random target poses, inducing a task-agnostic manipulation prior. We then construct assembly finetuning environments from assembly benchmarks
[
54
,
20
]
, using sparse rewards defined by the final part configuration. Across challenging assembly skills, this prior enables 33x more sample-efficient learning than RL from scratch, even when scratch policies are provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with 0.5 mm clearance and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing. Our contributions are:
•
A framework for precise assembly with dexterous hands that first learns a task-agnostic
play
prior on general objects and goals, then
perfects
it to new CAD-defined assembly tasks.
•
A systematic study of
play
pretraining design choices that transfer to contact-rich, precise assembly, including object diversity, trajectory diversity, training objectives, and goal precision.
2
Related Work
Manipulation with Multi-Fingered Robots.
Prior work falls into two categories: imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL). IL relies on collecting high-quality demonstrations, which can be obtained through human hand motion retargeting with motion-capture gloves
[
43
,
58
]
, VR devices
[
15
,
21
,
28
,
6
]
, camera inputs
[
39
,
19
,
50
]
, or exoskeleton systems
[
53
,
60
,
16
]
. However, collecting demonstrations for contact-rich tasks remains difficult due to the embodiment gap between the human operator and the robot, as well as the lack of tactile feedback
[
10
,
46
,
5
,
37
]
. Sim-to-real RL offers a promising alternative, with recent progress on dexterous skills such as grasping
[
1
,
62
,
31
,
48
,
47
]
and in-hand reorientation
[
12
,
11
,
29
]
. Yet, these skills are largely performed in free space. Extending dexterous RL to contact-rich tasks relies on dense reward functions
[
27
,
13
]
, accurate human hand motion references
[
26
,
30
,
34
]
, or warm-starting from teleoperation
[
45
,
9
]
. Closest to our work are methods that train task-agnostic
play
controllers across diverse objects
[
64
,
23
,
25
]
. When combined with teleoperation
[
64
]
or a human demonstration at test time
[
23
]
, these controllers can generalize to unseen objects and tasks. However, they are deployed zero-shot and still struggle with precise, contact-rich tasks such as assembly. Instead, we view
play
as dexterous pretraining: a general prior that is quickly specialized to precise assembly.
Precise and Contact-Rich Assembly.
Most progress in precise, contact-rich assembly has come from structuring the problem through task-specific hardware or environments. Prior work designs specialized gripper attachments or tools to simplify manipulation
[
17
,
44
]
, or uses fixtures to reduce uncertainty in grasping, alignment, and insertion
[
42
,
32
]
. While effective, these approaches require task-specific setup for each assembly problem. Learning-based assembly methods often rely on task-specific structure as well, including dense reward functions
[
52
,
51
]
, scripted multi-stage controllers
[
54
]
, or carefully designed curricula
[
22
]
. Other methods address the exploration problem with dense reset distributions
[
63
]
or teleoperation demonstrations
[
3
,
4
]
, but these still require task insight or task-specific data. In contrast, we pretrain a general dexterous
play
prior without demos or knowledge of the downstream assembly task, and specialize it with sparse-reward RL.
Pretraining for Dexterous Manipulation.
There is growing interest in pretraining broad dexterous priors to solve challenging manipulation tasks. For example, Vision Language Action (VLA) models
[
38
,
35
,
8
]
train on large datasets consisting of diverse tasks
[
36
,
24
]
. However, these datasets are largely concentrated on parallel jaw gripper robots. Human videos on the internet are another promising option to acquire general priors for dexterous hands
[
66
,
61
,
40
,
53
]
. However, human videos do not contain contact information, limiting their use to simple pick and place tasks and often requiring large amounts of in-domain robot finetuning data. Learning from
play
is a promising approach to learn priors from task-agnostic data. Prior works still require teleoperation to collect robot trajectories or active human hand data collection
[
57
,
33
]
. Compared to these works, we train
play
priors by learning to manipulate diverse objects via RL without requiring any demonstrations.

What matters in dexterous
play

We study the key factors that shape the learned manipulation prior. Our design emphasizes in-hand manipulation with fingers across diverse objects and trajectories, with 6D pose-reaching objectives and precise goal tolerances.

Play2Perfect
is a framework for dexterous
play

We first train a goal-conditioned policy in simulation to manipulate procedurally generated primitive objects to random poses in free-space. We then use the assembly CAD design to construct a sparse-reward RL environment for finetuning to learn precise, contact-rich goals.
3.1
Dexterous Play Pretraining

play

Object Diversity.
We aim to acquire broad dexterous competence across a wide range of objects, so that the resulting policy provides a useful initialization for downstream finetuning. To this end, we procedurally generate diverse primitive objects in simulation comprising cuboids and cylinders. Each object’s dimensions are sampled from a broad distribution constrained to fit within the robot hand. We also randomize physical properties by varying object densities and attaching additional masses near object ends. This induces variation in center of mass and inertia, forcing the policy to learn object-control strategies that are not tied to a single geometry or mass distribution. We use primitive shapes to enable fast, stable simulation while keeping pretraining task-agnostic.
Training Objective.
Play pretraining should induce reusable dexterous skills for downstream assembly. Therefore, we train the robot to manipulate objects through a sequence of 6D goal poses: the first goal requires grasping and lifting from the table, while subsequent goals require in-hand control of object pose without drops. Each goal specifies both translation and rotation: translation teaches object motion across the workspace, while rotation encourages in-hand reorientation. The play reward comprises three terms:

Trajectory Diversity.
We randomize the goal sequence in every play episode rather than training on fixed trajectories. The first goal is sampled broadly in the robot’s workspace, while subsequent goals are sampled near the previous goal with significant rotations. This encourages learning of in-hand manipulation rather than simple arm movements with fixed grasps.

Assembly-by-Disassembly.
Given a completed CAD assembly, we generate assembly steps by sequentially removing parts and reversing the disassembly sequence. Each step defines a sparse goal sequence: the final assembled pose and intermediate contact goals, e.g., pre-insert pose.

Experiments
We design experiments to answer the following questions:
1.
Can dense, task-specific rewards overcome the need for
play
pretraining?
2.
Which
play

3.
Is RL finetuning necessary for precise, contact-rich assembly?
4.

5.

Task Design.
Our robot consists of a 22-DoF Sharpa five-fingered hand mounted on a 7-DoF KUKA iiwa 14 arm. We evaluate on three tasks: 1)
Tight-Insertion
, inserting a T-shaped peg into holes with increasingly tight contact clearances; 2)
Assemble-Beam

[
54

; and 3)
Screw-Leg
, screwing a furniture leg into a table fixture, constructed from FurnitureBench
[
20

×
\times

Assemble-Beam
and a 3
×
\times

Screw-Leg
, making the tasks more suitable for dexterous hands and reliable for visual tracking under occlusion. All tasks are illustrated in Fig.

.
Evaluation Metrics.
We report two primary metrics:
Success Rate
, which measures whether the assembly part reaches its final goal configuration within a tolerance of

, which measures the average time required to complete the full task, including approach, grasping, transport, and the final contact-rich interaction. In simulation, we report results over 500 rollouts with randomized initial part and fixture poses. In the real world, we evaluate each task over 10 or 20 rollouts using a fixed fixture pose and randomized initial part poses.
4.1
Can Dense Rewards Overcome the Need for
Play
?
Figure 4:
Dexterous Play Pretraining Enables Efficient Downstream Assembly Learning.
Across four contact-rich assembly tasks,
Play2Perfect
rapidly learns successful policies from the shared dexterous prior, reaching high success within 2-5 hours. In contrast, training from scratch fails to make progress with either sparse task rewards or hand-engineered dense rewards.
Figure 5:
Dexterous Play Pretraining Induces Robust Assembly Strategies.
After simplifying the initialization with an easy-grasp fixture, Scratch (dense reward) can learn the task, but it relies on a brittle strategy that balances the object rather than robustly grasping it. This shortcut fails sharply under external force perturbations. In contrast,
Play2Perfect
learns a more stable grasping and recovery strategy, maintaining high success across perturbation magnitudes.
Setup.
We first test whether a general dexterous prior improves RL learning compared to training from scratch. We measure success rate as a function of RL wall-clock time and compare
Play2Perfect
against two scratch baselines:
Scratch (sparse reward)
, which uses the same sparse assembly success reward as
Play2Perfect
, and
Scratch (dense reward)
, which additionally receives task-specific reward shaping for grasping, lifting, and tracking a sequence of 10 waypoints from the initial part pose to the fixture. In addition to the four main tasks, we include a simplified
Tight-Insertion (Fixtured)
task, where the T-peg starts propped up on a fixture. Computational resources and training budgets are detailed in Appendix
H
.
Results.
Fig.
4
shows that
Play2Perfect
solves all tasks within roughly 2-5 hours of wall-clock RL training, whereas both scratch baselines produce no successful rollouts even after 24 hours. On the simplified
Tight-Insertion (Fixtured)
task, scratch training becomes feasible, as shown in Fig.
5
. However,
Scratch (dense reward)
requires over 100 hours to reach near-perfect success, while
Play2Perfect
reaches the same success rate in only 4 hours, yielding a 33
×
\times
speed-up. Moreover, the policy learned by
Scratch (dense reward)
remains brittle: it balances the peg using the thumb rather than forming a stable grasp. Under external force perturbations, its success rate drops to
∼
\sim
20% with a 10N perturbation and eventually to 0% under larger perturbations. In contrast,
Play2Perfect
maintains over 75% success even under the largest perturbations, indicating that
play
pretraining induces a more robust manipulation strategy.
4.2
Which Design Choices in
Play
Pretraining Matter Most for Downstream Assembly?
Setup.
We next ablate key
play
pretraining choices and measure how they affect downstream RL finetuning on all 4 tasks averaged over 3 seeds. Per-task results and ablation implementation details are provided in Appendices
C
and
K
, respectively. We vary: 1)
Object Diversity:
pretraining on 10, 100, or 1000 objects sampled from the same primitive distribution, with 1000 as
Play2Perfect
’s default; 2)
Training Objective:
comparing
Play2Perfect
’s full 6D goal-pose objective against
Translation-only
, which rewards only translational error along the same goal-pose sequences, and
Rotation-only
, which first lifts the object to a random 6D pose and then samples only rotational goals at a fixed position; 3)
Trajectory Diversity:
we compare using random goal trajectories (ours) against fixed sets of 10 or 100 trajectories; and 4)
Goal Precision:
varying the success threshold
ϵ
\epsilon
for goal-reaching across 1cm (ours), 5cm, and 10cm.
Results.
Fig.
6
shows that all four design choices affect downstream assembly finetuning. 1)
Object Diversity:
Training with more objects during pretraining leads to more stable RL finetuning, with final success rates consistently increasing from 10 to 1000 objects. 2)
Training Objective:
Orientation control is critical.
Translation-only
pretraining learns grasping and lifting, but does not learn object orientation control, and therefore fails to provide the in-hand reorientation prior needed for assembly.
Rotation-only
pretraining transfers well, but plateaus about 10 points below full 6D pose-goal pretraining, likely because it provides less practice coupling reorientation with translational object motion. 3)
Trajectory Diversity:
Fixed sets of 10 and 100 trajectories perform similarly, while online random trajectories learn fastest and plateau highest, suggesting that broader coverage of goal-pose transitions better matches downstream assembly finetuning. 4)
Goal Precision:
Precise goals are important. A loose 10cm threshold fails to transfer because coarse goal reaching does not require accurate object-pose control. A 5 cm threshold learns more slowly and plateaus near 60%, indicating that precise
play
induces priors better matched to tight-clearance assembly.
4.3
Is RL Finetuning Necessary for Precise, Contact-Rich Assembly?
Figure 6:
What Matters in Pretraining for Downstream Assembly Finetuning?
We vary key
play

in-hand manipulation

Setup.
We next evaluate whether
play
pretraining alone is sufficient for precise assembly, or whether task-specific RL finetuning is necessary. We compare
Play2Perfect
against
Play-only
, the pretrained policy without assembly finetuning. We evaluate both policies on
Tight-Insertion
across fixture holes with increasingly tight contact clearances. Clearance is defined as the difference between the hole and peg cross-sectional dimensions: for example, our peg has a
30

×

Play2Perfect

Results.
Fig.
7
shows that
Play-only
solves only the loosest insertion settings. In simulation, it reaches 75% success at 40 mm clearance but drops to nearly 0% by 4 mm. In contrast,
Play2Perfect
maintains high success as precision increases, achieving 95% at 4 mm, 92% at 1 mm, and 80% at 0.2 mm, which is tighter than the training distribution. This shows that
play
pretraining provides useful grasping and reorientation behaviors, but RL finetuning is still needed to turn this prior into a precise, contact-rich assembly policy. The real-world results show the same trend. At 10 mm clearance,
Play2Perfect
achieves 100% success compared to 60% for
Play-only
. At 2 mm clearance,
Play2Perfect
achieves 90% success while
Play-only
drops to 20%. At 0.5 mm clearance,
Play2Perfect
still succeeds 60% of the time, whereas
Play-only
fails completely. Qualitatively,
Play-only
tends to move directly toward the goal pose and treats contact as a disturbance. In contrast,
Play2Perfect
learns to search locally near the hole, make corrective motions under contact, and commit to insertion once the part is aligned.

These fast execution times demonstrate the advantage of using dexterous hands for assembly, as well as the ability of RL to discover efficient manipulation strategies. Most failures occur during final contact-rich interactions, where occlusions can degrade perception and contact dynamics can introduce sim-to-real mismatch. Across 60 real-world rollouts, we identify 18 failures, including timeouts (6), object drops during insertion (5) or reorientation (3), and catastrophic pose-tracking failures (4). Setup.
We demonstrate the application of
Play2Perfect
beyond structured assembly benchmarks to everyday insertion tasks involving smaller, more challenging object geometries. We consider two additional tasks: inserting an iPhone plug into a socket and a YCB fork into a narrow rack opening. Both tasks use the same pretrained play checkpoint and RL finetuning recipe as our main experiments, without task-specific modifications.
Results.
Fig.
8
shows that
Play2Perfect
successfully adapts to both tasks, achieving 90% success in simulation after 8.4 and 2.8 hours of finetuning for the iPhone plug and YCB fork, respectively. These results demonstrate that the learned dexterous prior extends beyond structured industrial assembly to everyday insertion tasks with diverse object geometries.
5
Discussion and Limitations
We presented
Play2Perfect
, a framework for precise contact-rich assembly that finetunes a dexterous prior learned through play. By
play
pretraining across diverse objects,
Play2Perfect
enables fast RL on assembly tasks by adapting the prior to precise contact interactions. Our ablations show that object diversity, objectives, trajectory diversity, and goal precision all affect downstream performance. Finally,
Play2Perfect
transfers zero-shot to challenging real-world dexterous assembly tasks.
Limitations.
Our system learns short-horizon assembly skills rather than a complete autonomous assembly pipeline. Task sequencing, active-part selection, and goal poses are specified externally, and policies are finetuned per task or benchmark family. Future work could combine these skills with sequencing, scene memory, recovery, and broader multi-task finetuning. Real-world deployment also depends on object-pose estimates, which can fail under occlusion or fast motion. Finally, beyond the goal pose, the policy does not directly observe the fixture or surrounding geometry. Incorporating visual or tactile observations could address these perception and scene-awareness limitations.

Qualitative behavior.
Across real-world tasks,
Play2Perfect
exhibits closed-loop recovery behaviors that are difficult to obtain from a single open-loop assembly motion. During insertion, the policy often searches locally near the hole, makes small corrective motions under contact, and commits once the part is better aligned. When the part becomes misaligned, the policy can recover with additional in-hand reorientations. If the part is dropped, the policy immediately regrasps and continues, provided the object remains within the workspace. In screwing tasks, the fingers spin the leg directly within the hand, enabling axial rotation while maintaining a stable grasp. Failure modes.
Real-world failures arise from both perception and contact dynamics. Perception remains a major failure mode even on larger parts: fast part motion, hand-object occlusion, and visually similar objects can cause the pose estimator to lose track of the manipulated part. Screwing is especially challenging because the policy must track object rotation, while the rectangular leg has approximate 90
∘
rotational symmetries that can confuse pose estimation and cause the policy to rotate in the wrong direction. We add colored tape to each side of the rectangular leg to make the orientations visually distinguishable, but pose estimation remains imperfect during fast rotations and occlusions. Control failures typically occur during the final contact-rich phase, when the policy repeatedly attempts insertion but fails to align with the hole, or contacts the fixture in ways that differ from simulation. In simulation, fixtures are rigid and immovable, while in the real setup, they are taped to a foam tabletop for safety and can move or comply under contact. This behavior is never observed in simulation and can cause the policy to struggle when its corrective motions no longer produce the expected relative motion between the part and fixture. We also observe some failed in-hand reorientations and drops during rotation before insertion, requiring the policy to regrasp. In contrast, grasp acquisition is highly reliable: real-world failures rarely arise from missed grasps except when perception fails catastrophically.

Appendix H
Simulation and Computational Resources
All policies are trained in Isaac Sim on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The physics simulation runs at 120 Hz, while the policy outputs actions at 60 Hz. Play pretraining uses 24,576 parallel simulation environments and is run for 7 days. Each downstream assembly policy is finetuned for 1 day using 12,288 parallel environments. We use fewer environments during finetuning because modeling contact-rich assembly interactions requires more GPU memory than the free-space manipulation used during play pretraining. For each wall-clock comparison, all methods within the same figure are run on the same GPU type with identical hyperparameters, environment counts, and training budgets.
Appendix I
Policy Architecture and RL Algorithm
We train the play policy using Split and Aggregate Policy Gradients (SAPG)
[
49
]
, a population-based variant of PPO that improves exploration in massively parallel environments. The actor uses an LSTM to integrate interaction history and infer unobserved object properties, followed by a multilayer perceptron that outputs the arm and hand actions. We use an asymmetric actor–critic architecture. While the actor receives only the observations available at deployment, the critic additionally receives noise-free and undelayed observations, palm and object velocities, reward signals, and stateful progress features such as the minimum goal distance reached and whether the object has been lifted. This privileged information is used only during training. The same RL algorithm and hyperparameters are used for both pretraining and finetuning.

Appendix K
Pretraining Ablation Implementations
We ablate four components of play pretraining: object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. Unless otherwise stated, all variants use the same environment, policy architecture, reward coefficients, domain randomization, training budget, and downstream assembly-finetuning procedure as the default
Play2Perfect
policy. Each ablation changes only the pretraining factor under study.
Object Diversity.
We vary the number of procedurally generated objects used during pretraining among 10, 100, and 1000, with 1000 objects used by default. Each object set is sampled from the same procedural distribution described in Sec.
J
, including the same geometry and density ranges. During pretraining, each environment samples an object from the corresponding fixed object set. All goal-sampling and optimization settings remain unchanged.
Training Objective.
We compare the default 6D pose-reaching objective against Translation-only and Rotation-only variants. The default objective requires jointly matching the target translation and orientation using the keypoint-based pose distance. Translation-only uses the same sampled goal sequences, but computes goal success using only the Euclidean distance between the current and target object positions. The target orientation is ignored. Rotation-only first requires the policy to grasp, lift, and move the object to a randomly sampled 6D pose. Subsequent goals keep this target position fixed and vary only the target orientation, requiring repeated in-hand reorientation without translational goal changes.
Trajectory Diversity.
The default policy samples every goal trajectory online during pretraining. To study the effect of trajectory diversity, we instead construct fixed banks containing either 10 or 100 goal trajectories. Each trajectory follows the same sampling distribution as the default setting, including the same workspace bounds and maximum translation and rotation between consecutive goals. During pretraining, episodes repeatedly sample from the corresponding fixed trajectory bank rather than generating new trajectories online.

Appendix L
Assembly Finetuning Details
CAD-to-RL Automation.
The CAD model provides geometry and goal poses in the assembled state. Our pipeline automatically derives insertion axes and pre-contact poses from the geometry. For example, for the screw task, the thread axis, pitch, and depth geometry define goals at 90
∘
increments. Mating regions in the CAD file are automatically identified and are modeled with SDF meshes, while other parts of the CAD use standard convex decomposition. Grasp bounding boxes use the object bounds, and all tasks use the same fixed 1cm goal tolerance without task-specific tuning.
Environment Construction from CAD.
For each assembly step, we import the manipulated part and fixture CAD models into Isaac Sim as rigid bodies. Most geometry is represented using convex decomposition for efficient simulation. However, convex approximations can distort narrow holes and mating interfaces, changing the effective clearance and contact dynamics. We therefore represent only the contact-critical hole and insertion components using signed distance fields (SDFs) at resolution
256
256
. This targeted hybrid representation provides detailed collision geometry where precision matters while avoiding the memory and computational cost of applying high-resolution SDFs to the entire assembly in simulation.

article.headline: 灵巧手先“玩耍”再精密装配
article.lede: 斯坦福等提出 Play2Perfect：先用任务无关的“玩耍”预训练获得灵巧操作先验，再用稀疏奖励微调完成精密装配。
article.problem: 多指灵巧手有望带来速度和灵活性，但精密装配接触丰富，模仿学习数据采集困难；同时装配奖励稀疏，直接从零探索对强化学习几乎不可行。现有工作常靠专用夹具、工具附件、平行夹爪、密集奖励或遥操作来绕开问题。
article.method: Play2Perfect 先在仿真中对程序生成的多样物体和随机 6D 目标做任务无关的 play 预训练，学习抓取、手中重定向和位姿到达等可复用先验。随后，它从 CAD 装配设计自动构造稀疏奖励环境和目标序列，对该先验进行按任务微调；部署时用 FoundationPose 跟踪零件位姿，策略输出手臂和灵巧手的关节位置目标。
article.results: 在四个接触丰富装配任务上，Play2Perfect 约 2–5 小时训练即可学会，而从零训练的稀疏/密集奖励基线 24 小时后仍无成功回合；在简化插入任务上，它 4 小时达到 scratch 密集奖励 100 多小时的水平，约 33 倍提速。仿真插入中，Play2Perfect 在 4 mm、1 mm、0.2 mm 间隙下成功率分别为 95%、92%、80%，Play-only 在 4 mm 时接近 0；真实世界 10 mm、2 mm、0.5 mm 间隙下为 10/10、9/10、6/10。真实多零件梁装配 Step 1 为 16/20、Step 2 为 12/16，拧桌腿插入 7/10、拧入 5/7。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明任务无关的 play 预训练能作为灵巧装配的可复用先验，降低对遥操作和密集奖励的依赖，并支持零样本 sim-to-real 迁移。
article.limitations: 系统只学习短时装配技能，任务排序、主动零件选择和目标位姿仍由外部指定，且策略按任务或基准族微调；真实部署依赖零件位姿估计，遮挡、快速运动和夹具可移动会导致失败，策略也不直接观察夹具或周围几何。
article.figure_caption_zh: 推理时流程复用 CAD 模型估计当前零件位姿、计算相对夹具的目标位姿并定义抓取包围盒，微调策略据此输出手臂与灵巧手的关节位置目标。

page_papers.title: SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
page_papers.abstract: Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools, including articulated ones, and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot.
page_papers.content:
SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
Yunchu Zhang, Ray Song, Junhan Jiao,
Liyiming Ke, Yuchen Yang
Ruihan Gao, Emma Romig,
Siddhartha Srinivasa, Yiyue Luo
University of Washington
Abstract
Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools—including articulated ones—and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15–25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website
https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot
.
I
Introduction
Fig. 2
:
(
Left
) SwapBot setup overview with the robot arm, robot-mounted tool adapter, electromagnetic coupling, the tool dock, and tactile I/O board.
(
Middle
) The structure of the instrumented tools with integrated tactile sensing using piezoresistive film, showing sensor layers and placements, with examples for a knife, brush, and tongs. (
Right
) Characterization of tactile sensors, showing force–response curves for electrodes of different sizes. Larger electrode areas exhibit higher sensitivity, but also cause non-smooth signals with sudden jumps under load. Smaller electrodes have smoother signals and a wider measurable range.
Robotic manipulation is advancing toward increasingly human-level capabilities; however, seemingly simple tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, remain challenging for robots to perform. Performed with different tools under contact-rich interaction, these tasks require precise but forceful control (cutting), delicate interaction with deformable objects (brushing), and dexterous motion (grasping and placing). Such
tool-centric manipulation
is challenging under the current end-effector design, which falls into two broad categories. First,
anthropomorphic hands
mimic human dexterity
[
19
,
5
]
, but their mechanical complexity imposes a high cost in maintenance, sensing, and control, hindering scalable data collection and policy learning. Second,
parallel jaw grippers
, though practical and demonstrating impressive versatility
[
29
,
1
,
13
]
, struggle to perform tasks requiring nuanced physical interactions, such as cutting or spreading. These capability vs controllability tradeoffs create significant barriers to more capable and scalable tool-centric robot manipulation.
Humans accomplish complex manipulation tasks by using tools, e.g., knives, brushes, or screwdrivers, as extensions of their bodies. Robotists have explored tool use using dexterous hands
[
3
,
25
]
or parallel grippers
[
14
,
21
]
. However, existing methods either inherit the complexity of manipulating anthropomorphic hands, struggling to maintain tool stability under load, or, critically, lack tactile sensing
[
28
]
at the tool-object interface, hindering effective control and learning for contact-rich tasks.
To balance robot manipulators’ capability and controllability, we propose to equip robots with the ability to swap modular tools through a tool changer. Industrial tool changers, such as those used in CNC machining or on UR5 robots, demonstrate the practicality of extending robotic capabilities through automatic tool exchange. However, these costly systems are typically customized for specific robots and cannot easily accommodate actively articulated tools - e.g., tongs and scissors. Moreover, they lack integration with tactile sensing, limiting their ability to support contact-rich manipulation tasks. Instead, our approach turns accessible household items into robot tools and equips each tool with compact, custom tactile sensors, enabling robots to both select the appropriate tool for each subtask and sense contact at the tool–object interface. Drawing inspiration from surgical robots that interchange end-effectors such as scissors, cauterizers, and forceps,
our system thus enables scalable household manipulation through tool diversity, not anatomical mimicry
.
We present
SwapBot, a modular, low-cost, tool-centric manipulation system with integrated tactile sensors
, as shown in Fig.
. It features: (1)a unified adaptation interface for diverse tools and robots, (2) fast and autonomous tool swapping protocol, (3) integrated tactile sensing, and (4) intuitive teleoperation for demonstration data collection. Our system employs inexpensive, 3D-printed interfaces ($10 each)
to quickly adapt common household tools
. We apply this modular system to three robot platforms: Franka
[
8
]
, UR5
[
24
]
, and Tycho
[
12
]
and to a variety of household tools - including articulated tools that require actuation, such as tongs and chopsticks. Robots equipped with our system can use our designed coupling interface and protocol
to autonomously switch the tool within 10 seconds
. Our teleoperation interface combines tool-matched leader devices with real-time visualized tactile feedback, providing operators with an intuitive interface for contact-rich manipulation. Furthermore, we show that employing tactile sensing significantly boosts the performance of the autonomous policy learned from human demonstrations.
Fig. 3
:
SwapBot can be adapted to three different types of robots: Tycho, UR5, and Franka.
To assess the ease of teleoperation with SwapBot, we conduct human studies with 12 participants of varying teleoperation skill levels (beginner, intermediate, and expert), focusing on two representative tasks: brushing and cutting. Participants report less subjective workload of control and higher success rates compared to the use of a generic teleoperation tool. SwapBot also enables the teleoperated completion of tasks previously found challenging or impossible for simple grippers, reducing task completion time and offering more satisfying user experiences. In robotic experiments, we further demonstrate the autonomous execution of a challenging long-horizon task: cooking pan-fried tofu. Using the demonstration data that our system collected, we train imitation learning policies and show that tactile feedback significantly improves policy performance, increasing task success rates by 25 absolute percentage points, from
35
%
35\%
to
60
%
60\%
. We additionally provide qualitative results (e.g., stirring salad and flipping meat) in the supplementary videos. In summary, our contributions include:
1.
A
unified, low-cost, modular tool-centric end-effector system
that supports rapid autonomous tool swapping and the use of diverse household tools, including articulated tools.
2.
Integrated compact tactile sensing
that improves both teleoperation performance and imitation-learning success in contact-rich task.
3.
An
intuitive teleoperation interface for collecting demonstrations
, improving operator precision and enabling high-quality data collection.
4.
Empirical evaluation
via user studies and policy learning: quantitative tofu-cooking results and qualitative demonstrations of stirring salad and flipping meat, showing improved user experience and policy performance.
II
The SwapBot System

:

to generate end-effector actions. During long-horizon execution, the robot continuously conducts tool selection and skill execution in a closed-loop, which enables SwapBot to compose tool-specific skills for long-horizon tasks.
The SwapBot system contains four main components: modular and interchangeable end-effectors (Section
II-A
), compact tactile sensing (Section
II-B
), the teleoperation interface (Section
II-C
), and policy learning from demonstrations (Section
II-D
). Our plug-and-play design supports low-cost prototyping with a variety of daily-use tools while supporting tactile sensing, large-scale demonstration collection, and downstream policy learning. We describe each component below.
II-A
Modular End-Effectors:
Tool Adapters and Coupling
Design Goals.
Industrial robotic coupling is usually tailored to specific tools and robots and often costs hundreds or even thousands of dollars. In contrast, we aim to develop a modular tool coupling system that is accessible and low cost (tool-side modules under $10), rapid swapping of tools, robot-agnostic, enabling compatibility with common manipulators, and flexible for both passive and articulated tools. To achieve these goals, we design our tool-swapping adapter and coupling system to enable a fully accessible fabrication workflow and straightforward assembly using basic hand tools, such as an Allen wrench.
As shown in Figure
2
(left), we 3D-print tool adapters and inserts to enable the quick instrumentation and mounting of common household tools. The adapter both attaches the tool securely and houses the tactile sensors stably. For tools with moderate handle sizes, the same adapter can be reused, while soft silicone fills the remaining gap to accommodate variations in handle shape and size. Only substantially thinner tools require a smaller 3D-printed adapter, while the robot-side coupling interface remains unchanged. Though many everyday tools include their own actuation mechanisms, equipping each with dedicated motors for automatic control would be complex and expensive. Instead, we shift all power and control functionalities to the robot side, ensuring a simpler and lower-cost tool implementation. To transmit torque, we add a bearing system on top of the adapter cover that transfers motion from the robot’s end joint. For robots without a final joint, we supplement with a single servo motor to ensure compatibility across Franka, UR, and other common platforms (Fig.
3
).
To support rapid tool exchange, we implement a self-aligning electromagnetic coupling that mates a robot-side hub with tool-side adapters. This design supports both passive tools (e.g., knives, brushes) and articulated tools (e.g., tongs, chopsticks) through a pass-through mechanism. A kinematically guided gear ensures reliable engagement and release under small alignment errors, while the electromagnet provides sufficient holding force for secure tool attachment during forceful manipulation. In practice, our system completes a swap in about 10 s by guiding the robot to a docking station, releasing the current tool, and attaching a new one. This approach shifts capability from a single complex hand to a library of instrumented tools while retaining the ability to compose skills across tools. We summarize key design specifications in Tab.
I
.
