II-B
Compact Tactile Sensing: Instrumented Tools
We design compact, tool-specific piezoresistive tactile sensors that provide task-relevant contact information for teleoperation and policy learning. By tailoring the sensor layout to each tool, we capture force information without adding bulk or compromising usability.
The piezoresistive tactile sensors consist of a three-layer structure, shown in Fig.
2
(center), where a force-sensitive material layer (Velostat) is sandwiched between top and bottom electrodes (conductive fabric) for signal transmission. These sensors
[
22
]
convert real-time normal force pressure information into an electrical signal via the drop of resistance. The electrodes are made from copper-nickel conductive fabric, laser-cut to precise dimensions for optimal fit considering the sensitivity they need for tasks. To accommodate the limited surface area of tools, we implement the sensors in a matrix layout, where sensing nodes are formed at the intersections of orthogonal electrode rows and columns. This configuration enables an n
×
\times
n sensor array using only 2n electrodes. Our approach is low-cost, relies on only off-the-shelf materials, and supports easy customization through digital fabrication.
We show the design and placement of tactile sensors for each tool in Fig.
2
(center). For tools with larger surfaces, we place sensors on both the handle and the blade or tip (e.g., tongs, spoons, knives). For smaller or thinner tools, such as chopsticks, brushes, and forks, it is impractical to mount sensors directly on the blade or tip. In these cases, we instrument only the handle, providing indirect measurements of tool–object interaction. This strategy ensures that tactile information is captured where feasible while keeping the modules compact and lightweight. For blade or tip instrumentation, we mount the fabricated tactile sensors directly onto the tool surface. To accommodate handles of varying sizes, instead of attaching sensors directly, we install them between the TPU layer and the PLA adapter cover and fill the gap between the handle and TPU shell with soft silicone. This approach allows the sensors to comply with different handle shapes, stabilizes the installation process, and ensures consistent reflection of sensor readings during interaction.
Fig. 5
:
Tool-centric teleoperation for two challenging and complex long-horizon cooking tasks: Dish 1: Celery Beef and Dish 2: Potato and Pepper Stir-Fry.
II-C
Teleoperation Interface: High-Quality Demonstration Collection
We design the teleoperation interface to maximize operator intuitiveness and data quality, both of which are critical for downstream policy learning. Our interface maps the intuitive leader device’s 6-DoF pose and actuation commands directly to the corresponding tool on the robot side. By using similar tools on both sides, e.g., chopsticks to control chopsticks or a knife to control a knife, operators interact with familiar household tools, making control feel natural. This reduces the re-targeting effort common in teleoperation and lets operators focus on task execution rather than compensating for mismatched dynamics. For each leader tool, we estimate the 6-DoF pose using an Intel RealSense T265 tracking camera, and use the result to drive the robot during teleoperation. For articulated tools, we infer the actuation command from the relative motion measured by two IMUs, providing accurate correspondence between human and robot tool motion.
During demonstration data collection, all data streams are synchronized at 20 Hz, including multi-view RGB images, tactile signals, robot joint states, actions, and task labels. This ensures that multimodal inputs remain temporally aligned for learning. We also provide visual overlays that display the live contact forces and tactile maps to help operators anticipate and refine contact-rich interactions. As we will show in Fig.
6
, tactile information is visualized on-screen to indicate contact information. This immediate feedback provides operators with additional information about contact, improving both control precision and the quality of collected demonstrations.
To evaluate the interface, we conduct controlled human studies to measure task completion time, success rate, and the subjective workload (see Sec.
III-B
). Integrated tactile feedback emphasizes subtle events, such as first contact or changes in load distribution, which are often ambiguous in vision alone. This design reduces cognitive load and improves operator precision for long-horizon tasks such as cutting, grasping, and transporting.
II-D
Policy Learning: From Demonstrations to Long-Horizon Manipulation

[
21
]
and shown in Fig.
4
, we train hierarchical policies from demonstrations that scale to long-horizon tasks. The policies are divided into two components: (1) the
high-level tool-selection policy
π
sel
\pi_{\text{sel}}
determines which tool to use at each stage of the task, and (2) the
low-level, tool-specific control policies
π
tool

III
Experiments
Fig. 6
:

Overall, the SwapBot interface yields faster completion times, higher success rates, and lower subjective workload than the general teleoperation tool baseline.
Our experiments aim to answer the following questions.
(1) Characterization of tactile sensing:
How well do our compact, tool-specific tactile sensors perform in terms of sensitivity and detection range, and does our design achieve the right balance for integration into diverse tools?
(2) Intuitive teleoperation:
Does our tool-centric teleoperation interface provide a natural, user-friendly experience that improves demonstration efficiency and data quality compared to standard baselines?
(3) Policy learning with tactile feedback:
Does integrating tactile sensing into imitation learning policies improve performance on complex, long-horizon tasks?
III-A
Characterizing Tool-Specific Tactile Sensing
Directly applying the tactile sensors without considering their size and sensitivity can lead to saturated and inconsistent signals during data streaming. To ensure smooth and reproducible sensing, we characterize the performance of our resistive tactile sensors made with electrodes of varying widths. Signals were recorded under controlled pressure using a force gauge, from which we extracted both sensitivity and detection range. These measurements provide valuable insights into how the electrode design impacts sensing quality and guides our choice of parameters.
As we show in Figure
2
(right), electrode size has a direct impact on both sensitivity and signal quality. Larger electrodes provide higher sensitivity, with identical forces producing stronger responses due to increased overlap between the conductive layers. However, these larger electrodes also generate non-smooth signals with sudden jumps under load, and can saturate the 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC), making them less reliable for continuous feedback. Smaller electrodes, by contrast, sacrifice sensitivity but produce smoother, more stable signals with a wider measurable range. To balance sensitivity, detection range, and signal fidelity within ADC limits, we select a 2 mm electrode width, which provides sufficient sensitivity while maintaining smooth, stable responses.
III-B
Evaluating Intuitive Tool-Centric Teleoperation
To evaluate the interface, we conduct a controlled human study with 12 participants spanning three teleoperation skill levels (beginner, intermediate, and expert), with four participants in each group. Each participant performs both brushing and cutting tasks under three teleoperation conditions: a general VR-style tool, SwapBot without tactile feedback, and SwapBot with visualized tactile feedback. Each participant performs 10 trials per task–condition pair, terminating upon success or a 60-s timeout. Completion time is computed over successful trials, while failures contribute only to the success-rate metric. The order of teleoperation conditions was counterbalanced across participants to reduce learning and fatigue effects, while task order was randomized. We measured task completion time, success rate, and subjective workload using NASA-TLX, normalized to a 0–10 scale. For completion time and success rate, we first aggregate the 10 trials for each participant and then report the mean performance across the four participants within each expertise level.
As demonstrated in Fig.
6
, the SwapBot interface generally improves teleoperation performance over the baseline across both tasks. The visualized tactile feedback provided operators with direct information about contact forces and load changes, enabling more effective manipulation during teleoperation. This interface also supports demonstration collection for more complex tasks, as illustrated in Fig.
5
.
Quantitatively, participants consistently achieved higher task success rates and reported lower cognitive load with our system compared to the baseline general teleoperation tool. These results suggest that our teleoperation design supports efficient and intuitive demonstration collection.

III-C
Policy Learning with Tactile Feedback for Long-Horizon Tasks
We then evaluate whether tactile sensing improves imitation learning for complex, long-horizon manipulation. As a testbed, we use the challenging real-world task of preparing pan-fried tofu for quantitative experiments. The tofu is fragile and easily breaks if mishandled, requiring both gentle and dexterous manipulation. The robot must (1) gently brush sauce onto the tofu, (2) transport it to a pot using tongs for frying, and (3) return it to the cutting board and slice it into two pieces without damage. A trial is successful if the tofu is placed back on the board and cut cleanly into two pieces. Additionally, we provide qualitative demonstrations of other tool-mediated behaviors (e.g., stirring salad and flipping meat) in supplementary videos.
We used our teleoperation interface to collect 100 demonstrations for each stage, i.e., brushing, transporting to the pot, and cutting. The reverse transport back to the board was not evaluated quantitatively since it mirrors the forward motion, but we collected the same number of demonstrations to train the policy for completeness and composition. We then used these demonstrations to train tool-specific imitation learning policies under different input modalities. As baselines, we compared against policies trained without tactile sensing. We also performed ablations using: tactile only, top-down RGB + tactile, and egocentric T265 RGB + tactile. For all policies, we used a CNN feature extractor concatenated with proprioceptive state and tactile signals (when available) as inputs to the policy network. We evaluated each tool-specific policy across 20 trials in a 20 cm
×
\times
20 cm workspace. Policies trained with tactile sensing achieved consistently higher success rates and were robust to small tofu shape changes and variations on initial position. RGB-only policies, in contrast, frequently failed due to partial observability of the tool–object interaction—especially at the tong tips where contact onset and incipient slip are often occluded in RGB—leading to poor contact regulation, slipping, or damage. Egocentric RGB + tactile performed poorly, reaching at most 40% success even with 100 demonstrations and staying near zero in tong picking and knife cutting tasks. Top-down RGB + tactile achieved moderate success (up to 50% in brushing and cutting), but it lagged significantly behind our full RGBs + tactile method.
Though the top-down view offers reliable localization of the tofu on the cutting board, it lacks local visual detail for fine control. Conversely, the egocentric T265 view provides local information but suffers from its angled viewpoint (greater than 45°), which reduces localization accuracy compared to the near-vertical top-down camera. Most failures were due to tofu slippage or encounters with out-of-distribution states not covered in the demonstrations, highlighting the need for broader training data and more systematic recovery strategies. Nevertheless, within the demonstration coverage, we qualitatively observe recovery from external perturbations: when the tofu is pushed away during execution, the visuotactile policy re-approaches it and continues the task, as shown in the supplementary video. Overall, these results show that tactile sensing plays a crucial role in scaling imitation learning to long-horizon daily activities. SwapBot successfully integrates tactile-enhanced policies to execute tasks such as cooking pan-fried tofu, where precision, robustness, and tool coordination are essential.
IV
Related Work
IV-A
Tool Manipulation
To enable robots to understand and manipulate tools, prior work has explored task-oriented grasping and functional affordances through self-supervised learning
[
6
,
23
]
. However, these works mainly focus on how to utilize a single tool’s different parts, i.e., how the tool should be grasped.
[
14
]
,
[
21
]
further demonstrate long-horizon manipulation involving diverse tools through planning and learning.
In contrast, our work focuses on an integrated hardware and learning system that converts everyday household tools into interchangeable, tactile-instrumented end effectors, combines tool-matched teleoperation with tactile feedback for demonstration collection, and learns visuotactile policies for contact-rich manipulation.
Moreover, previous works
[
6
,
18
]
try to learn the synergy between different tool grasping points and tasks using self-supervised learning methods. The learned latent representations could provide a structured and condensed understanding of tool objects. However, our method does not rely on tool-affordance representations; instead, it uses a mechanically simple custom tool changer to directly focus on the interaction and manipulation parts of the task.
IV-B
Tool Design for Robot Tool Usage
Several works aim to extend the range of tasks a single robot can perform by improving tool design and switching mechanisms. Industrial robots such as the UR5 employ dedicated tool changers that provide robust
and precise switching performance. However, these systems are typically tailored to specific robots and tools, are expensive, and cannot easily accommodate actively articulated tools.
Previous works have explored interchangeable surgical instruments
[
17
]
and mechanically actuated tools compatible with parallel grippers
[
10
]
. In contrast, SwapBot provides a unified, low-cost system that supports both passive and articulated household tools, ensures secure coupling and reliable torque transmission for forceful, contact-rich manipulation, and integrates tactile sensing with tool-matched teleoperation for demonstration collection and downstream policy learning.
IV-C
Tactile Sensing for Manipulation
Tactile sensors capture real-time force information and have been widely applied for dexterous, real-world manipulation.
Visual-tactile systems, such as GelSight
[
26
]
, use a soft reflective layer paired with an embedded camera to detect force magnitude and direction through subtle surface deformation. These systems provide high-resolution tactile feedback and have been demonstrated for a variety of robotic tasks, including fine-grained manipulation
[
20
]
, material identification
[
7
]
, and pose estimation
[
9
]
. To extend tactile coverage over larger areas of a robot’s body, capacitive and resistive tactile skins are often used
[
16
]
. These skins typically use a three-layer stack of orthogonal electrodes with a dielectric/resistive layer, where electrode intersections act as pressure-sensing nodes. This scalable design supports seamless integration onto customized robotic components, such as grippers
[
30
]
, arms
[
15
]
, and full-body surfaces
[
2
]
, enabling broader and more versatile tactile sensing in complex environments. Our system adopts scalable tactile sensor designs and customizes them to diverse tools via digital fabrication. Tactile data has also been integrated into policy training for a variety of manipulation tasks, often showing substantial performance gains. For example, sensors mounted on parallel grippers
[
11
,
27
]
provide valuable contact information that improves grasp stability and task success. However, such approaches are typically limited to specific gripper designs. In contrast, SwapBot enables more flexible measurement at the tool–object interface.
V
Conclusion
We presented SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric manipulation system with integrated tactile sensing that improves demonstration collection and policy learning for long-horizon tasks. Tactile feedback proved crucial for both teleoperation quality and imitation learning robustness, especially with limited data. However, the current system has limitations: tactile sensors remain low resolution and prone to wear, sensor placement is fixed by human intuition, and policy learning depends on predefined task segmentation. Future work will explore more durable, higher-resolution sensing, data-driven strategies for sensor placement, and autonomous policy sequencing without manual subgoal definitions. We will also open-source the system to promote reproducibility and community adoption.

article.headline: SwapBot：可换工具与触觉的机器人操作
article.lede: 研究者提出模块化末端执行器系统，让机器人快速更换家用工具，并用触觉提升接触密集任务表现。
article.problem: 日常操作常需借助刀具、刷子、夹钳等工具完成接触密集任务，机器人需要自主更换并使用合适工具。拟人手复杂昂贵，平行夹爪难以完成切割、涂抹等动作；工业工具更换器多为特定机器人定制、成本高，且不易支持铰接工具与触觉传感。
article.method: SwapBot 采用统一的机器人侧电磁耦合接口和低成本 3D 打印工具侧适配器，把家用工具变成可快速更换、带压阻触觉传感器的末端执行器，并兼容 Franka、UR5、Tycho 等平台。策略上，高层工具选择器根据顶视观测和目标图像选工具，低层工具专用扩散策略以多视角图像、触觉和本体状态为输入输出动作，形成长时任务闭环。
article.results: 在真实豆腐烹饪任务中，使用触觉示范的策略将整体成功率从仅 RGB 的 35% 提升到 60%，即提高 25 个百分点；分阶段最高成功率为刷酱 85%、夹取 70%、切割 90%，论文还报告触觉相较仅 RGB 在接触密集技能上提升 15–25 个百分点。高层工具选择器测试准确率为 96.8%，工具切换约 10 秒，电磁耦合保持力最高 50 N，工具侧模块成本低于 10 美元。12 名参与者的用户研究显示 SwapBot 遥操作完成时间更短、成功率更高、NASA-TLX 负荷更低，但正文未给出这些指标的精确数值。
article.why_it_matters: 它把工具多样性而非单一通用夹爪作为扩展机器人能力的路径，并把触觉、遥操作数据采集和模仿学习串成可复现流程，对家庭长时操作有参考价值。
article.limitations: 局限包括触觉传感器分辨率低且易磨损，传感器位置由人工经验固定，策略依赖预定义任务分段和人工指定子目标。模态消融多为单种子结果，完整任务 20 次 rollout 的失败主要来自豆腐滑落或分布外状态，恢复策略仍不系统。

figure.caption: Overview of the hierarchical policy learning framework. The high-level tool-selection policy $ _{ {sel}}$ takes top-view observations $ {O}_{top}$ and a goal image $ {O}_g$ as input and outputs a distribution over candidate tools. The selected tool index $ $ activates the corresponding low-level tool-specific control policy $ _{ {tool}}^ $. Each policy conditions on visual observations $ {O}_t$, tactile feedback $ {T}_t$, and proprioceptive state $s_t$ to generate end-effector actions. During long-horizon execution, the robot continuously conducts tool selection and skill execution in a closed-loop, which enables \ to compose tool-specific skills for long-horizon tasks.

1,3

Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

1   Introduction
Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with a computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As a result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on a

Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence

[
19

Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. A token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while a token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what a token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can a token’s output role also determine how it should communicate?
SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations:
Read
,

K
K
indexed slots, with each slot assigned a disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. A spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add a local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure
2
illustrates this design.

At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Diffusion and pixel-space generation.
Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis

It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. The communication literature provides the other half of the problem by restricting how tokens exchange information. Swin uses local windows with shifted boundaries, Longformer combines local windows with a few global tokens, and Perceiver routes information through a small latent bottleneck

SpecSlot organizes pixel-space generation around one idea: tokenization as allocation—assigning each token a fixed output role and dividing a fixed token budget between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global attention is then spent only on the role that needs it; the rectified-flow state, target, and loss remain in pixel space.

7   Conclusion
SpecSlot recasts tokenization as allocation: a fixed token budget is split between anchor density and spectral subdivision, while global attention is assigned by role. On ImageNet-256, it reaches a comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models a new way to trade detail for communication.

article.headline: 频谱槽位解耦像素生成细节与全局注意力
article.lede: SpecSlot 按 DCT 频带把锚点分槽，仅低频槽位进全局注意力；ImageNet-512 少算力降 FID 2.8
article.problem: 像素空间生成 Transformer 通常一个图像 patch 对应一个 token，因此细节越细就需要越多 token，全局注意力的二次成本随之上涨。现有方法虽在压缩或限制通信，但大多仍把输出细节与 token 通信绑在同一空间网格上。
article.method: SpecSlot 把每个空间锚点扩展成 K 个槽位，每个槽位负责一组不重叠的径向 DCT 系数，从而把锚点密度与频谱细分拆开。只有最低频槽位作为载体进入全局注意力，所有槽位在锚点内做局部交互；空间头再用槽位状态在像素空间加局部修正，而生成状态、目标和损失仍留在像素空间。
article.results: ImageNet-256 上 W256/K4 的 FID 为 6.59，与 FLOPs 匹配的 JiT-CM（6.68）相当且早期收敛更快。ImageNet-512 上 FID 比 JiT-CM 低 2.84、FLOPs 少 3.9%，与 JiT-B/16 仅差 0.69 FID 而成本低 38.2%。文本到图像 DPG-Bench 得分 62.21，超过 JiT-B/8 的 61.15，前向成本低 40.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 把 tokenization 变成锚点密度与频谱细分的显式预算分配，并让通信资格由输出角色决定，为像素空间生成在细节与全局注意力成本之间提供新的折中点。
article.limitations: 消融仅在固定 N=2048 等有限配置内观察到增加锚点密度更划算，作者未声称该规则可外推；此外 K 从 2 增至 8 时有效槽位比例由 0.803 降至 0.495，且文本到图像 GenEval 仍落后 JiT-B/8（26.99 对 29.78）。
article.figure_caption_zh: SpecSlot 生成的文本到图像示例；更多带提示词的样本见附录图 10。

Abstract
Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same
transformer, or parts of it, to token representations, effectively making the
model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful
depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or
autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense
decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model
are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between
loops. Our experiments span models with up to
1B parameters
, trained on
up to
155B tokens
using up to
1.07
×
𝟏𝟎
𝟐𝟏
\mathbf{1.07\times 10^{21}}
training FLOPs
, with up to
𝟑𝟐
\mathbf{32}
loops
. We find that
looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed
parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return
when training FLOPs are constrained. These trade-offs also depend on the number
of loops: adding loops is not uniformly beneficial, and gains eventually
saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This saturation motivates asking whether
forcing every loop to use exactly the same weights limits the benefit of deeper
looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that
improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. A separate practical
concern for looped transformers is the sequential dependency during
autoregressive generation, which causes a slowdown proportional to the number
of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this limitation by passing
information between loops across adjacent token positions via hidden states,
allowing loop stages to run concurrently during decoding. However, in our
experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality
gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding
and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before
combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training
budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching
the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.

Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or selected parts of it, to token representations, allowing the model to behave like a deeper network without storing a new set of parameters at every ‘depth’
(
Dehghani et al., 2018
;
Saunshi et al., 2025
;
Geiping et al., 2025
)
. This makes looping attractive when model size is constrained, but the additional depth is not free: every extra loop must still be executed. As a result, a design that uses parameters efficiently may not use training compute efficiently.
Prior work reflects this trade-off, showing that repeated shared computation can recover some of the benefits of additional depth, while adding independently parameterized layers can be preferable when training compute is constrained
(
Schwethelm et al., 2026
;
Prairie et al., 2026
)
. The same weight reuse, however, raises another question as more loops are added. In ordinary looping, every loop applies the same weights, even though later loops operate on representations that have already been transformed several times. This suggests that exact weight sharing may
give diminishing returns
with deeper looping. Prior work has relaxed this constraint by giving each loop iteration a different low-rank adapter while keeping the main transformer weights shared
(
Bae et al., 2025
)
.
Looped transformers also suffer from a separate issue during autoregressive generation: each loop for a token still depends on the output of the previous loop, so the model must execute them one after another, increasing the sequential computation required to generate each token. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize this dependency by passing hidden states from one loop to the next across adjacent token positions, allowing multiple loop stages to be evaluated in parallel during decoding
(
Wu et al., 2025
)
. This change alters the information available to each loop, and recent work reports that gains can decrease as more parallel loops are added
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
. This leaves open what information the shifted transition must preserve for parallel looping to remain effective at greater loop depth. Together, these studies show that looping is not a single design choice but a set of coupled trade-offs. Repeating more of the model can make better use of a fixed parameter budget but requires more training compute; reusing the same weights across more loops can make exact sharing increasingly restrictive; and changing the dependency between loops can parallelize sequential looping while also changing the information available to each loop. These trade-offs may also change with model scale and training budget. Despite prior work studying these choices in different settings, it remains unclear which conclusions generalize and how the choices interact. We therefore study them within a common training from-scratch setting across model scales and training budgets, and ask:
How should transformer layers be looped under constraints on model size, training compute, and autoregressive inference?
We address this question through a controlled study of dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch. Our experiments span models with up to
1B parameters
, up to
155B training tokens

1.07

Main Contributions.

Background and Methods
2.1

Experiments

We train models with 70M, 100M, 200M, 300M, 500M, and 1B parameters,
containing 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 16 stored transformer layers, respectively.
Training budgets range from 10 to 160 tokens per parameter (TPP). All models
use the same pretraining mixture of natural language, code, mathematical, and
scientific content, with the data sources, sampling distribution, preprocessing,

(

primary measure of language-modeling quality and report bits per byte (BPB;
lower is better). To test whether the trends observed on DCLM hold across
datasets, we additionally evaluate on other language-modeling corpora and a
broader set of mathematical, code, reasoning, and question-answering
benchmarks. These results, together with the full model configurations,

Conclusion and Future Directions
We show that looping is a multidimensional design
problem that must jointly account for stored parameters, training FLOPs, data
efficiency, and inference efficiency. A promising future direction is to
find ways of combining PLT with speculative decoding to further reduce inference latency.
Another is to develop a theory of how normalization and current-token
embedding reinjection affect stability in both the cross-token recurrence of
PLT and the same-token recurrence of standard looping, and to identify which
regimes favor each approach.

Parameter efficiency, compute efficiency, and inference latency are therefore distinct objectives. This observation motivates the next question we study: whether the benefits of repeated computation can be retained while relaxing the serial dependency imposed by conventional looping.
B.2
Low-Rank Adaptation and Relaxed Weight Sharing
A looped Transformer repeats the same layer, or group of layers,
L
L
times.
Normally, every loop uses the same attention and MLP weights. Sharing the
weights in this way keeps the model small, since adding loops does not require
storing new Transformer layers. However, the loops do not all receive the same
kind of input. The first loop processes the initial representation, while later
loops process representations that have already passed through the shared
layers one or more times. It may therefore be useful for different loops to
learn slightly different transformations.
One option would be to give every loop its own attention and MLP weights. This
would provide complete specialization, but it would also make the loops
equivalent to separately parameterized Transformer layers. The number of
stored parameters would then grow with the number of loops, removing much of
the motivation for weight reuse. We instead use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
to place a small loop-specific correction around a larger
shared weight matrix.

datasets. We first evaluate additional pretraining corpora: C4

subsubsection E.3.1

subsubsection E.3.8

subsubsection E.3.9

on DCLM generally persists. At smaller model scales and lower TPP,
full-stack and Middle-Stack Looping are often competitive, while full-stack
looping becomes more consistently favorable as model scale and TPP increase.
When training compute is considered, shallow Middle-Stack Looping remains an
attractive alternative because it can achieve substantial quality gains
while repeating only part of the network. The mathematical and code
datasets exhibit more variation across looping designs, but broadly retain
the tendency for Full-Stack Looping to become more favorable at larger
scales and higher TPP. Across both groups of datasets, the gains from
increasing the loop factor

Additional Results for Parallel Looping
This appendix provides the additional experiments supporting
Subsec. 3.4
. As described in
Subsec. B.3
, Parallel
Loop Transformers (PLTs) reorganize looping so that, after a short warm-up,
the computations for different loops can be evaluated together during
autoregressive decoding. Evaluating several loop inputs with the same weights
can increase
arithmetic intensity
, the amount of arithmetic performed
for each byte read from memory, because one set of weights can be reused
across those inputs. PLT does not remove any of the loop computations. During
training, the model still runs all
L
L
loops, and the training FLOPs increase
accordingly. We evaluate model quality and account for training FLOPs here;
we do not measure wall-clock decoding latency or throughput.
Our analysis follows a single diagnostic sequence. We first reconstruct the
original PLT design and identify the quality loss introduced by its shifted
transition. We call the rule that combines the current-token representation
with the shifted state the
re-injection rule
. We then measure these two
representations, normalize them before they are combined, and test whether the
combination needs a learned gate or additional sources of context. Finally, we
evaluate the resulting design across model scale, loop count, training budget,
evaluation corpus, stored parameters, and training FLOPs. Unless stated
otherwise, quality is teacher-forced bits per byte (BPB) on the DCLM
validation set, and lower is better. We do not fill in missing observations or
connect curves across missing points.
Throughout this appendix,
Vanilla (No Looping)

denotes ordinary same-token looping.

shifted recurrent inputs and combines them with a rank-8 linear gate. Its
same-token counterpart is the
unshifted control

run its loops concurrently and is included only to measure the modeling cost

design. The figures label the same method as Matrix LoRA; throughout the text,

corrections are added to the attention and MLP projections and trained jointly

Full-Stack Looping
is ordinary looping, in
which each token passes through the complete Transformer repeatedly.

Limitations
Our experiments establish consistent looping trends across dense decoder-only
transformers trained from scratch at scales up to 1B parameters. We do not
evaluate larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, or post-trained
models; future work can test how broadly these trends extend. We study a diverse set of looping strategies, low-rank specialization
methods, training budgets, and evaluation datasets, but do not exhaust the
space of possible designs. We also focus primarily on likelihood-based
evaluation rather than free-form generation. Future work can broaden both the
architectural and evaluation settings. Our normalized shifted PLT performs particularly well at

4

substantially larger loop counts and model scales. Closing the remaining gap
to the unshifted control and developing a theoretical account of how
normalization and current-token embedding reinjection affect stability are
promising directions for future work.

article.headline: 循环Transformer：全栈、中栈与并行的取舍
article.lede: 在从头训练的稠密解码器上，如何循环、循环多少次、如何跨循环传信息，取决于参数、算力还是解码效率是瓶颈。
article.problem: 循环（looping）通过反复对同一组权重施加于token表示，在不增加参数的情况下让模型“变深”，因此当模型尺寸受限时很有吸引力。但每多一次循环就多一次实际计算，参数效率高不等于训练算力效率高；同时普通循环在自回归解码时存在串行依赖，而并行循环Transformer（PLT）虽然能并行解码，却改变了每个循环可见的信息。已有工作在不同设定下分别研究这些选择，哪些结论可推广、各选择如何相互作用仍不清楚。
article.method: 作者在统一的从头训练设定下做受控实验：稠密解码器模型规模70M至1B，数据量最高155B token、训练算力最高1.07×10²¹ FLOPs、循环次数最高32次，TPP（每参数token数）覆盖10至160。实验系统变化“循环什么、循环几次、循环之间如何传递信息”，包括全栈循环、中栈循环、逐层循环以及注意力与MLP分别循环，并用约4100万token的DCLM验证集BPB作为主要指标。作者还比较了循环专属低秩适配（Loop LoRA、Loop Matrix、Loop Softmax），并修正PLT：保留当前token嵌入，先将其与上一token隐藏状态分别归一化再组合（rank-8线性门）。
article.results: 固定参数量与数据预算时，全栈循环（Full-Stack Looping）总体质量最好，且在更大模型与更高TPP下优势更稳定；训练FLOPs受限时，中栈循环（Middle-Stack Looping）用更少的额外计算获得更大收益。循环次数并非越多越好：70M与100M的扫描延伸到L=32，BPB的边际下降随L增大而变小，并出现饱和、反转甚至不稳定（200M–500M只扫到L=8，1B只到L=4）。加入循环专属低秩适配可提升质量，且收益随循环数增加更明显（L=4时比L=2更清楚）。1B模型上，循环在八个推理与问答任务上保持或提高了平均NLL排名准确率。并行方面，作者发现在其复现中原始PLT配方并不能稳定保留普通循环的质量增益，而修正后的移位PLT（shifted PLT）通常优于普通全栈循环且保留并行解码；无移位PLT质量最强，但解码仍是串行的。
article.why_it_matters: 工程上，这篇论文提供了明确的选择规则：部署时受参数预算、训练算力还是解码时延约束，就应选不同的循环位置与循环方式；而作者对PLT的归一化与当前token重注入修正，让“并行解码不牺牲质量”更接近可用。
article.limitations: 实验只做到1B参数、稠密解码器、从头训练，未涵盖更大模型、MoE与后训练模型，评估也以BPB、teacher-forcing似然为主，而非自由生成的实际质量。修正版PLT主要在L=2、4上验证，更大循环数与更大规模是否成立未确定，作者也未测量实际解码延迟或吞吐。

figure.caption: {Loop-specific specialization preserves the ordering among ordinary and parallel looping designs.} DCLM BPB for 300M and 500M models. The figure compares ordinary Full-Stack Looping, shifted PLT, and unshifted PLT with shared weights and with Loop Matrix. Unshifted PLT gives the strongest quality but remains sequential during decoding. Shifted PLT generally improves over Full-Stack Looping while retaining parallel decoding. Lower BPB is better.

Robotic Data Inoculation
Qiyang Li   Zhiyuan Zhou   Charles Xu   Sergey Levine
UC Berkeley
data-inoculation.github.io
Abstract
Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover.
Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it.
In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves
during data collection
to collect more useful data.
We propose
Data Inoculation (DI)
, a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make.
These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human’s continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, “inoculating” the dataset against the learner’s future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
Figure 1
:
Data inoculation (DI).
Left
: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human’s closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human’s corrective feedback, “inoculating” the dataset against such mistakes.
Right
: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.
1
Introduction
Modern robot learning systems have shown promise in acquiring complex manipulation skills (
e.g.
, shirt-folding
[
7
]
, tea/juice-making
[
28
]
) from demonstration data.
While there has been extensive recent research on the design of these models, the quality of the data the models are trained on is every bit as critical. Good data should have high coverage: it should contain a wide range of states to maximize the chance that the policy generalizes to the states that it actually visits at test time. In practice, coverage is determined by the scenes where data is collected and the behaviors of the teleoperators, which must strike a balance between consistency and variety. Improving data quality and coverage through task design and operator instruction is largely heuristic and ad hoc. Can we instead directly modify how the robot behaves
during
data collection to provide for more useful data?
Existing solutions largely sit at the two extremes of how the robot is being controlled. Aside from the human-driven teleoperation which exhibits obvious drawbacks above, a learned policy may control the robot autonomously and collect data. While this allows us to run RL online which improves the policy upon its own experience overtime, real-world exploration can be sample inefficient and unsafe. DAgger-style methods partially address this by using learned policy to drive the robot until it makes a mistake, where a human intervenes and corrects it, often through teleoperation. This is reactive: each intervention requires a failure to occur naturally, and rare failure modes may take many rollouts to appear, and for many tasks (
e.g.
, that require working with delicate objects that may break) failures cannot be corrected once they occur.
In this paper, we argue that autonomous policy rollout and human control should
not
be mutually exclusive, and a shared-control framework in which a learned agent and the human drive the robot together allows for better data collection. Our framework is simple: the human retains closed-loop teleoperation of the robot that supplies the demonstration signal as usual in the form of control commands, but these commands are perturbed by a residual policy, which is trained online on the growing dataset, in a way that mimics the mistakes a policy trained on the current data might make. We call this residual policy an
inoculative policy
because it exposes data collection to controlled, human-corrected “doses” of the learner’s expected mistakes, so that the policy learned from the collected data is already robust to them. The human can therefore correct policy-like deviations continuously throughout every data collection episode rather than only after a visible failure while ensuring safety because they are always in control of the robot. The resulting data collection strategy, which we call
Data Inoculation (DI)
(
Figure
1
), produce data that are favourable for downstream policy extraction—it contains near-failure states paired with actions that allow recovery from these states, which is exactly the good coverage data that would help behavior cloning (BC) to learn the recovery behavior directly but also help offline RL to learn better value functions.
Our main contribution is the new data collection strategy (DI). We evaluate DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks and show that DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of the policies extracted from both behavior cloning (BC) and offline RL. These results demonstrate the benefits of proactively
inoculating
data collection so that the policies become more robust at deployment time.
2
Related Work
Human-in-the-loop learning
methods address a common failure mode of imitation learning on passive data, where the learned policy may visit states different from the training distribution and suffers from compounding errors. They typically work by alternating between executing the current policy and collecting human correction data in the form of action re-labeling
[
21
]
or intervention trajectories
[
9
]
. Interventions can be triggered automatically by the model
[
30
,
2
,
18
]
or initiated by human
[
9
,
16
,
15
,
13
,
4
,
6
]
. In real-world robotics, intervention-based approaches are often more convenient and natural to human because the corrective trajectories are collected under human’s continuous, closed-loop control of the robot. However, this also comes with a limitation: once the control is switched to human, the trajectory may quickly go out of the learned policy’s state distribution. As a result, only the first few transitions right after the switching point provide direct supervision to the mistakes made by the policy.
In contrast, rather than using a binary switching from the learned policy’s distribution to the expert’s distribution after intervention, our method constructs a controlled distribution by combining human demonstrator actions with residual actions from an
inoculation policy
, allowing the human to provide corrections of the policy’s mistakes throughout a data collection trajectory.
Prior work trains assistive residual policies in simulation, using a model trained on a fixed set of demonstrations to approximate human control, then deploys them with human operators
[
23
,
22
]
.
In contrast, our method doesn’t depend on simulation and directly train the residual inoculation policy online as data accumulates. This also yields a broader range of corrective demonstrations as updates to the residual policy expose humans to different errors during its training.
Data perturbation
approaches broaden the distribution of observations
[
26
,
11
,
29
,
31
]
, actions
[
31
,
8
,
3
,
17
]
, or even environment and its dynamics
[
5
,
27
,
20
,
25
]
during training so that the model is robust. These approaches typically directly perturb either a simulator (
e.g.
, domain randomization) or previously collected data (
e.g.
, data augmentation), but do not directly interact with how a human demonstrator collects trajectories, which our method does. The closest line of work injects zero-mean Gaussian noises during data collection, exposing human demonstrator to random mistakes and thereby eliciting recovery behaviors
[
10
,
19
,
24
]
. In contrast, our method injects directed residual actions produced by a state-dependent
inoculation policy
trained online to approximate the mistakes that a policy learned from the growing dataset would likely make. This allows the collected trajectories to target policy-specific failure modes like DAgger-style approaches, rather than relying on symmetric random perturbations. Furthermore, while prior approaches mostly focus on improving imitation learning performance, we additionally demonstrate that our technique allows for improved offline RL performance and the quality of learned value functions.

Data Inoculation
In this section, we describe in detail how we use a residual policy in a shared-control framework to continuously inject controlled perturbations such that the collected data is favorable for downstream policy training.
We start by discussing how a residual policy alongside closed-loop human control can address the failure mode of vanilla human teleop data collection, and then detail how such a residual policy can be learned online during data collection with online RL.

Injecting purely random noises without any guidance inefficient, because perturbations along axes that barely influence task success (
e.g.
, yaw rotation in a simple cube pick-and-place task) are uninformative to the downstream learner. Intuitively, the data collection budget is best spent on the critical perturbation axes that influence the task success the most, and elicit recovery behavior as a consequence of these perturbations. However, finding informative perturbations is not simple as they are highly task-dependent and non-stationary, requiring a form of fast adaptation that vanilla zero-mean random noises (as often used in prior work
[
10
]
) cannot provide. How should we best implement an algorithm that can quickly adapt and find the perturbation axes that are most informative? It turns out that we can achieve this altogether by simply optimizing the inoculative policy along with human data collection using standard online RL to
maximize task success
.
In particular, we train our inoculative policy using standard TD-based off-policy RL, concurrently with collection, on the growing dataset from the data collection itself. While the data collection loop runs on the robot at the normal control frequency, an asynchronous RL training loop updates

cooperative
policy produce informative perturbations and elicit recovery behaviors?
This answer is two-fold. First of all, when the inoculative policy is optimized using the same reward-maximizing objective as a downstream offline RL algorithm later uses for policy extraction, its deviations are expected to closely mirror those a downstream learned policy would produce. Furthermore, early in collection, the critic is barely trained and inaccurate which causes the residual policy to exploit the critic’s errors, steering the robot into suboptimal states that require explicit recovery behaviors. Aside from eliciting recovery behaviors, our inoculative policy can sometimes also improve data collection efficiency (as we will show in
Figure
3
) because it is optimized to cooperate with human to improve task success rates.
We have thus far described how training our residual inoculative policy with online RL leads to more informative data collection with the teleoperator maintaining closed-loop control of the robot. Experimental Setup
We empirically evaluate our method across three different challenging precise manipulation tasks in the real world. We first describe the experimental setup, then the results in
Section
6
.
Robot setup and tasks.
We evaluate our method on three real-robot tasks that require precise manipulation. We focus on these tasks because successful executions require precise control of the robot, making it a challenging testbed for data collection and policy learning.
We use a Franka robot arm with a Robotiq gripper and two wrist cameras attached near the end effector. We use a spacemouse to control the robot’s end effector position and rotation during data collection at a frequency of
10
10
Hz.
Illustrations of the three tasks are shown in
Figure
1
, and we describe them in detail below:
1.
t-cube
requires the robot to pick up two colored cubes and carefully balance them on top of another yellow cube, resulting in a T-shape
[
1
]
. While this seems like a simple pick and place task, this in fact requires very precise manipulation skills and is arguably the most demanding task of the three: the robot needs to stack the two top cubes diagonally on top of the yellow cube with the centers of the three cubes roughly aligned, and any misalignment would cause one or two of the top cubes to fall off.
2.
cable
is a precision insertion task where the robot needs to pick up a USB-C cable and insert it into a port hole on a desktop machine that is barely bigger than the cable itself. Without changing the difficulty of the task, we only use the side plate of the desktop machine for ease of task setup.
3.
keycap
tasks the robot to use a keycap puller to remove the Q keycap from a keyboard. The robot must pick up the tool, locate the Q key, position the puller over the keycap, and lock its two hooks onto both sides of the keycap. Successful removal requires precise, directionally controlled force rather than a large brute force pull, which could cause the keycap to fly off. The robot must therefore learn a sequence of small lateral wiggling motions to loosen the keycap before pulling it out and placing it on the table.
Data collection procedure.
Since data collection through tele-operation is unavoidably a subjective process and can vary across different operators and collection trials, we conduct experiments on all tasks and data collection strategies with multiple operators and trials, which we refer to as “seeds”. For all experiments, three different operators conduct data collection for a total of
9
9

5
5

t-cube
because it is the most difficult task.
Before data collection, each operator spent time to practice on the task to achieve a sufficient level of expertise before collecting any data.

The observations for the policy consist of the two wrist RGB images, as well as proprioceptive state consisting of the end-effector position, rotation, and gripper position.

Discussion
In this paper we introduce Data Inoculation, a data collection strategy that trains a residual RL policy online to aid human teleoperated data collection in a shared-control framework. The residual inoculative policy perturbs the human’s control of the robot to a wider range of states and can elicit recovery demonstrations in critical phases of the task, and eventually lead to higher data collection success rate as the residual policy is trained. Data collected with DI also improves the success rate of downstream policy learning.
Our work serves as a step towards a new paradigm of robot learning where data collection is shared between humans and autonomous policies, each helping the other.
Several challenges remain and is promising for future work. First, our approach trains the residual policy from scratch using online RL, which offers near-random perturbations at the beginning of training. A natural next step is to develop mechanisms for directed exploration that can more quickly provide useful perturbations, such as boostrapping training from an existing offline dataset.
Second, our approach assume the human operator to be fully in-the-loop during data collection, which is expensive in human time. One interesting direction is to explore whether we can automate parts of data collection to be autonomous gradually during training and leave only important correction for human operators.

article.headline: 用在线RL扰动遥操作，给数据集「接种」
article.lede: 伯克利提出 Data Inoculation：在人类遥操作时叠加一个在线训练的残差策略，让演示数据自带纠错片段。
article.problem: 机器人模仿学习的效果高度依赖演示数据的覆盖度：熟练操作者的遥操作轨迹往往又快又一致，状态分布狭窄，缺少从偏离状态恢复的示范，策略一旦出错就难以纠回。纯在线 RL 探索代价高且不安全，DAgger 式干预又必须等策略偶然失败才能获得纠正，对易损物体的任务甚至无法事后补救。论文要问的是：能否不改变任务与操作者指令，而是直接改造采集时机器人的行为，从而收集更有用的数据。
article.method: DI 采用共享控制框架：人类操作者保持闭环遥操作，每一步给出控制命令，一个残差「接种策略」在同一观测和该命令的基础上输出 L∞ 有界的扰动量，叠加后执行，人类随即对偏差做出纠正，扰动与纠正天然配对成恢复示范。该残差策略与数据采集异步并行，用同一份不断增长的数据以标准 TD 离线式（off-policy）RL 在线训练，优化目标与后续策略提取所用的奖励最大化一致；因此其扰动会模仿「用当前数据训出的策略」可能犯的错，早期评论家网络不准时的利用行为还会把机器人带到需要显式恢复的次优状态。实现上每 0.5 秒（10 Hz 下 5 个控制步）采样一次扰动并保持，评论家直接估计扰动后动作的价值，并用一个流匹配 BC 模型近似 TD 目标所需的「干净」人类动作。
article.results: 在三个真实 Franka 精细操作任务上，t-cube、cable、keycap 分别用 9、5、5 个采集种子，每个种子评估 20 次。BC 策略成功率由 clean 的 0.37/0.38/0.63 提升到 DI 的 0.66/0.50/0.72；离线 RL（BFN 取 N=4）由 0.35/0.42/0.81 提升到 0.67/0.59/0.84。随机噪声基线在 cable 上有提升（BC 0.48、RL 0.56），但在 t-cube 几乎无益（0.40/0.42），在 keycap 上反而拖累 BC（0.69 对比 clean 0.63 尚可，RL 0.67 明显低于 clean 0.81）。采集过程本身，DI 的初期成功率低于对照，约进行到全程四分之一时追平 clean 和 random，最终反超；残余动作幅度随训练持续下降。纠正行为分析显示，DI 的纠正集中在 t-cube 最关键的 place/release 阶段，而随机噪声的纠正多发生在较简单的 retreat 阶段。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「数据采集」本身当成可学习对象：人类负责安全与意图，学习策略负责生成有针对性的扰动，得到接近失败的状态，以及配套的恢复动作，这正是 BC 学恢复、离线 RL 学值函数都需要的覆盖度。相比 DAgger，它不必等真实失败发生，也不改动最终策略的算法。
article.limitations: 残差策略从零用在线 RL 训练，采集初期扰动近乎随机，t-cube 上 DI 的整体采集成功率 54.4% 仍低于 clean 的 57.7%（keycap 94.0% 对 95.8%，cable 94.2% 对 96.9%），且需要人类全程在环，人力成本高。keycap 上三种方法差距很小（RL 0.84 对 0.81），说明任务本身对精确恢复要求不高时收益有限；实验仅覆盖三个桌面操作任务、单一机械臂平台，跨任务泛化性尚未验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 左：采集时用在线 RL 训练残差接种策略，扰动人类的闭环遥操作命令；右：在三个需精细操作的真实机器人任务上，DI 提升 BC 与离线 RL 策略的成功率。

figure.caption: {dmc}{ {Data inoculation (DI). }} {Left}: During data collection, we train a residual inoculative policy with online RL to perturb the human's closed-loop teleoperation commands. The perturbations steer data collection towards the mistakes the policy trained on the data would make, and elicit human's corrective feedback, ``inoculating'' the dataset against such mistakes. {Right}: We test DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks that require precise manipulation, and DI consistently improve success rate of policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL.

page_papers.content:
ScheduleGen: Demonstration Generation via Skill Scheduling for Multi-Arm Imitation Learning
Neel Jawale, Stephan Pleines, Soha Pouya, Yuke Zhu, Ajay Mandlekar, Caelan Garrett
NVIDIA  The University of Texas at Austin
†
Equal advising
Abstract
Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks
with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints.
The paradigm of training generalist robot policies from massive datasets is a promising approach to address general-purpose multi-arm manipulation, but the acquisition of large multi-arm manipulation datasets remains a bottleneck.
Automated demonstration generation can alleviate this burden by synthesizing new demonstrations from a handful of source demonstrations, but existing algorithms ignore multi-arm constraints and as a result often induce unsafe and unsuccessful behaviors.
We address this limitation by introducing ScheduleGen, an integrated planning & scheduling algorithm for multi-arm demonstration generation.
We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 simulation task variants, including seven externally authored RoboDojo tasks and settings inaccessible to prior systems; it achieves 79.6% mean data-generation success and trains policies with 65.5% mean success.
ScheduleGen policies outperform those trained on a state-of-the-art data generation baseline, and achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants through zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real transfer.
Videos and more at:
schedulegen.github.io
.
keywords
Imitation Learning, Demonstration Generation, Multi-Arm Manipulation, Planning and Scheduling
Figure 1:
ScheduleGen overview.
Top:
From a few source demonstrations, ScheduleGen adapts contact-rich skill demonstrations, plans collision-free connecting motions, and jointly schedules multiple arms to generate simulation data for multi-arm imitation learning that transfers to the real world.
Bottom:
ScheduleGen can handle long-horizon contact manipulation, challenging reset distributions, cluttered layouts, and multi-arm scenarios.
\abscontent
1
Introduction
Generalist robot policies
[
1
,
24
]
hold the promise of seamlessly solving a wide range of manipulation tasks across diverse robot embodiments. There is substantial interest in applying this paradigm to multi-arm embodiments, especially bimanual and humanoid robots, due to their ability to address a wider range of tasks compared to single-arm embodiments. Such embodiments make it possible to address tasks requiring multi-arm coordination and larger manipulation workspaces, and also have the potential to carry out tasks more efficiently due to simultaneous operation.
However, the predominant method for training generalist robot policies requires large-scale data collection, usually obtained through months of human teleoperation effort
[
8
,
16
]
. Collecting such datasets is already painful and costly for single-arm embodiments, but these problems are exacerbated in the multi-arm setting, due to the need for special teleoperation interfaces
[
29
,
32
,
5
]
, and the resulting increase in operator burden. It can furthermore be difficult to capture desirable multi-arm coordination characteristics due to the limitations of the teleoperation interface
[
15
]
.
Synthetic data generation in simulation is a compelling method to address this need. Prior methods allow for the generation of large-scale datasets with minimal human effort
[
21
,
6
]
but fail to address some key challenges of generating data for multi-arm scenarios.
Some works use planning-based approaches
[
22
,
4
,
6
]
, but contact-rich tasks remain difficult for such methods, and generating data for diverse multi-arm coordination characteristics remains challenging. DexMimicGen
[
15
]
is able to handle different contact-rich tasks, but the coordination behaviors that it can generate are entirely dictated by the human demonstrations used to seed the process, limiting data diversity. Furthermore, the absence of planning means that it cannot handle situations where arm-arm or arm-object collisions are prevalent, such as wide object distributions or cluttered workspaces.
To address these shortcomings, we present ScheduleGen, a multi-arm manipulation data generation method that can encompass diverse multi-arm coordination strategies, long-horizon and contact-rich manipulation, and a wide range of workspaces and embodiments, including challenging object initializations and cluttered scenes. Given a small set of annotated demonstrations, ScheduleGen preserves object-relative contact skills, replans collision-free transitions, and jointly schedules the arms under task and collision constraints.
The contributions of this paper are:
•
ScheduleGen, a new automated demonstration generation algorithm for multi-arm systems that integrates planning, scheduling, and demonstration adaptation.
•
ScheduleGen utilizes a novel planning formulation that first plans single-robot behavior to adapt object-centric skill demonstrations and then safely coordinates the robots by framing scheduling as a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) with constraints evaluated using GPU-accelerated collision checking.
•
We demonstrate ScheduleGen’s applicability to long-horizon contact-rich tasks, challenging resets, cluttered workspaces, and configurable coordination strategies across bimanual, four-arm, and humanoid systems. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 task variants across 3 simulation frameworks. On comparable tasks, ScheduleGen-trained policies outperform prior work DexMimicGen
[
15
]
. In zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real evaluation, the learned policies achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants.
Figure 2:
ScheduleGen methodology.
(a) Contact-skill segments
τ
ψ
\tau_{\psi}
are adapted to the initial state and connected by planned motion
τ
m
\tau_{m}
, producing partially ordered paths for each arm. (b) Collision checking identifies conflicting path segments. (c) ScheduleGen implicitly inserts waits to form a joint schedule that preserves task order, avoids collisions, and enforces synchronization when required. It minimizes makespan with optional soft costs, like summed robot execution times. (d) Scheduled motions are replayed across parallel simulation environments, and successful rollouts are retained as demonstrations.
2
Related Work
Imitation Learning from Human Demonstrations.
Manipulation demonstrations are often collected via robot teleoperation
[
31
,
20
]
, and
Behavioral Cloning (BC)
[
25
]
is a common method for training manipulation policies on such datasets.
Recent efforts have scaled this paradigm to months of demonstration data using large teams of human teleoperators
[
8
,
16
]
, and train expressive policy architectures on this data, resulting in capable generalist robot policies
[
1
,
24
]
.
However, data sourcing remains a key bottleneck for this paradigm.
The problem is exacerbated for bimanual robots and humanoids, which can require specialized teleoperation interfaces to support multi-arm teleoperation
[
29
,
32
,
5
]
.
Automated Demonstration Generation.
Synthetic data generation in simulation is a promising way to address the data bottleneck.
TAMP-based approaches
[
22
,
4
,
10
]
fully automate generation but are limited to single-robot prehensile manipulation.
MimicGen
[
21
]
and DexMimicGen
[
15
]
instead adapt a few teleoperated demonstrations to new initial states for single-arm and bimanual tasks, but adapting full demonstrations without accounting for collision or kinematic constraints limits their robustness to substantial initial-state variation.
SkillGen combines demonstration adaptation with motion planning to preserve contact-rich behavior while accommodating environmental and state changes
[
11
]
, but is limited to single-arm systems.
GLIDE
[
17
]
and HumanoidMimicGen
[
18
]
also incorporate motion planning and support some bimanual tasks, but independently planned arm motions compromise safety and success on complex bimanual tasks.
In contrast, ScheduleGen frames demonstration generation as a collision-aware scheduling problem to directly plan safe and efficient multi-arm manipulation.
Multi-Arm Manipulation.
Planning for multiple arms as a single composite robot can be intractable due to high-dimensional, combinatorial search spaces.
Multi-robot planners therefore factor the problem into interacting single-robot subproblems
[
7
]
, reconciling pairwise constraints through backtracking over action timing
[
12
]
.
Prior work includes domain-specific planners for assembly
[
2
]
and construction
[
13
]
, as well as single-robot TAMP frameworks extended to simultaneous multi-robot manipulation
[
28
,
30
,
9
]
.
ScheduleGen also uses factorization for efficient multi-arm planning, but it introduces demonstrations as schedulable skills and analyzes how scheduling decisions affect end-to-end visuomotor policy learning.

5.2
ScheduleGen Features
ScheduleGen generates demonstrations across diverse tasks and robot embodiments.
Across 17 Isaac Lab variants, ScheduleGen achieves 61.1-98.0% data-generation success, exceeding 85% on 10 variants. All policies trained on this data reach 30-100% success (Fig.
3
). These results span bimanual YAM and DROID
[
16
]
, a four-arm DROID setup, and a GR1T2 humanoid. Data-generation success also remains high (75.5-100.0%) across seven RoboDojo tasks on X5 (Fig.
5
).
On four robosuite variants in MuJoCo, BC-RNN-GMM policies reach 60-100% success over 50 episodes from data generated at 24.7-84% success (Table
1
).
ScheduleGen generates collision-free demonstrations even in scenarios with inter-arm overlap, unlike prior work.
The Cross-Arm variants introduce overlapping arm workspaces and broader object resets while reusing the Normal task demonstrations. DexMimicGen transfers each arm independently, while the manually selected holds in DexMimicGen-Tuned apply fixed timing across resets. ScheduleGen instead replans connecting motions and schedules collision-free waits for each reset. Across the four bimanual Cross and Cross-Bin variants, it reaches 64-88% data-generation success and 70-86% policy success. Two-Arm Cube Stacking uses a state-based BC-RNN, while Four-Arm Cube Stacking uses state-based flow-matching policies. DexMimicGen generates no valid trajectories on these variants, while DexMimicGen-Tuned remains below ScheduleGen throughout (Fig.
3
).
ScheduleGen scales data generation and policy learning to multi-arm systems.
Four-Arm Cube Stacking uses motion-planned pick-and-place segments as source skills rather than teleoperation. ScheduleGen jointly schedules them across four arms, checking all six arm pairs while building a five-object tower on a table or in a narrow bin. We train a separate state-based flow-matching policy for each layout and reset distribution. Across eight settings, data-generation success is 63.4-95.1% and policy success is 30-90% (Fig.
3
). DexMimicGen is not applicable because its interface supports only bimanual generation.

ScheduleGen scales released demonstrations to externally authored tasks.
Agentic annotation converts five released RoboDojo demonstrations per task into seeds with per-arm contact boundaries, object-relative frames, and task constraints; ambiguous cases retain human review, and all annotations must pass replay and task-success checks. ScheduleGen then generates 500 successful training demonstrations per task at 75.5-100.0% success (89.1% mean). The resulting flow-matching policies complete all seven tasks under both conditions, averaging 47.9% success on held-out Nominal layouts and 25.0% under doubled pose perturbations over 20 episodes per task and condition (Fig.

5.3
ScheduleGen Analysis
ScheduleGen reduces the task-specific data collection and tuning needed for difficult layouts.
We separately collect Cross-Arm demonstrations for YAM Bowl and Dishware Stacking. Each set takes the operator about 20 minutes, with additional work for annotation and hold tuning. To generate 1,000 demonstrations, DexMimicGen reaches 32.1% and 11.2% data-generation success and 30% and 20% policy success evaluated over 50 episodes. ScheduleGen instead reuses the five Normal demonstrations, reaching 66.7% and 68.0% data-generation success and 80% and 76% policy success. Task-matched teleoperation alone therefore does not close the gap: ScheduleGen retains the contact skills while replanning and scheduling free-space motion for each reset.
Policies trained on ScheduleGen data outperform the best DexMimicGen baseline across tasks and embodiments.
Across nine variants supported by DexMimicGen, ScheduleGen policies improve success on eight and match the best baseline at 94% on Normal Two-Arm Cube Stacking. Policy success rises from 42-78% to 76-100% on Bowl and Dishware Stacking, 0-74% to 70-86% on the Cross-Arm and Cross-Bin cube variants, and 20-90% to 48-96% on Humanoid Nut Pouring. ScheduleGen policies also use fewer steps whenever a baseline policy succeeds (Fig.
3
).
ScheduleGen shortens RoboDojo trajectories by scheduling more arm motion in parallel.
Across the 3,500 trajectories used for policy training, ScheduleGen reduces mean execution length by 2.3-11.1% per task relative to the released RoboDojo trajectories, with a 7.5% average reduction across tasks. Both arms are active together for 31.5% of execution steps, compared with 15.5% in the released demonstrations. To measure scheduling alone, we also apply the scheduler to all 700 released trajectories while keeping their paths and task order fixed. It finds valid schedules for 98.3% of these trajectories and reduces total steps by 14.98%
without replanning or physics replay. The mean reduction per episode is 16.44% (Fig.
5
). Appendix

gives the per-task measurements.

5.4
Real-World Evaluation
We evaluate two transfer routes on the real YAM setup. In sim-to-real, policies are trained only on ScheduleGen simulation data. In real-to-sim-to-real, calibrated real demonstrations seed simulation data generation for Cube Stacking and Trash, and the resulting policies are returned to the same robot. All policies are trained in simulation without real-world fine-tuning. We use calibrated robot, camera, workspace, and object geometry, and randomize object pose, appearance, lighting, camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and background. Policies observe three RGB views and both arms’ joint and gripper states, and predict joint-position and gripper targets.

6
Conclusion
We presented ScheduleGen, an automated demonstration generation system for multi-arm imitation learning. It combines object-centric skill adaptation, motion planning, and joint scheduling to preserve contact-rich behavior while satisfying task order, synchronization, and collision constraints. Experiments across 28 simulation variants show that ScheduleGen supports diverse embodiments and challenging layouts, and trains policies that outperform prior bimanual methods on most comparable tasks. The learned policies also transfer to eight real-world variants without real-world fine-tuning. These results show that adapting both motion and coordination can reduce task-specific data collection while supporting long-horizon, contact-rich multi-arm manipulation.

article.headline: ScheduleGen：多臂演示生成与调度
article.lede: NVIDIA 等提出 ScheduleGen，用规划与调度从少量示范生成多臂机器人训练数据，并验证真实迁移。
article.problem: 多臂机器人（双臂、人形、四臂）能并行完成复杂操作，但大规模示范数据采集成本高、遥操作接口负担重。现有自动演示生成方法往往忽略臂间碰撞与协调约束，容易产生不安全或失败的轨迹，尤其在接触丰富、杂乱场景和宽初始分布下。
article.method: ScheduleGen 先把源示范切分为以物体为参照的单臂技能，按新初始状态做技能适配，并用运动规划连接各段。随后把多臂执行顺序建模为带时序约束和碰撞约束的混合整数线性规划（MILP），用 GPU 加速碰撞检查，隐式插入等待以生成无碰撞的联合调度。生成轨迹在仿真回放成功后才保留为训练示范。
article.results: 在 28 个仿真任务变体上，ScheduleGen 平均数据生成成功率为 79.6%，训练策略平均成功率为 65.5%，并在可比任务上优于 DexMimicGen 基线。零样本 sim-to-real 与 real-to-sim-to-real 在 8 个真实世界变体上取得 50–80% 成功率；RoboDojo 七个任务生成成功率为 75.5–100.0%（均值 89.1%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把多臂协调纳入数据生成环节，减少为每个新布局重新遥操作采集示范的需要，并为双臂、四臂和人形平台的模仿学习提供可扩展的数据来源。
article.limitations: 调度公式未显式约束加速度，且若任一机械臂的起止状态发生碰撞，MILP 会不可行。真实世界评估每个变体仅 20 个回合，RoboDojo 策略在物体位姿扰动加倍时平均成功率降至 25.0%。

page_papers.title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
page_papers.abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.
page_papers.content: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

article.headline: 给离散扩散模型补上概率流ODE
article.lede: 作者提出指数残差流（ERF），为离散扩散构造确定性ODE采样轨迹，并证明其保持原扩散的边缘分布。
article.problem: 连续扩散模型的边缘分布可由概率流ODE复现，这一确定性表述是加速采样与一致性蒸馏的基础。离散扩散模型此前缺少对应的确定性形式，采样主要依赖祖先式随机过程。论文追问：离散情形是否也存在类似的ODE表述。
article.method: 作者为每个 token 和位置引入一个连续残差变量，将离散状态扩展为混合状态；残差按分段定义的 ODE 确定性演化，其向量场取决于当前离散状态以及给定扩散模型的前向、后向速率矩阵。当某个残差到达零时，对应离散状态发生跳变，作者证明该构造保持原扩散模型的边缘分布。随后给出该采样器的实用离散化，并专门化到 masked 与 uniform 两类扩散。
article.results: 论文未给出具体数字：摘要仅报告在包括代码与文本生成任务在内的多个基准上相对既有方法取得经验性提升，未列出任何指标数值。配图显示在 TinyGSM 设置下，跨全部评测的 NFE 预算比较 GSM8K 准确率随采样温度的变化，各面板给出逐点 95% bootstrap 置信区间，虚线为祖先采样、实线为 ERF。
article.why_it_matters: 确定性轨迹把离散扩散接到连续扩散已有的加速采样与一致性蒸馏工具链上，可能让少步数生成在离散文本、代码场景中变得可行。
article.limitations: 摘要未报告任何定量结果、基准规模或与基线的具体差距，提升幅度无法核验；同时为每个 token 与位置引入连续残差使状态维度上升，额外的采样开销与离散化误差也未在文中摘要层面量化。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.
