closes the gap between NCA and the no-PPT baseline.
2.
Additive compute: PPT can help at small natural-language budgets.
When each method is tuned over initialization schemes,
k
k
-Dyck and NCA improve over the best no-PPT baseline at 50M and 100M natural-language tokens (budgets reported to parallel the amount of language humans may learn from,
Warstadt et al., 2023
). However, by 1B tokens the advantage disappears. This suggests synthetic PPT can instill useful inductive biases, but its benefits diminish at larger natural-language budgets.
3.
Compute-matched: natural-language training performs as well as or better than PPT across all compute-matched regimes.
This includes the strongest scarcity case, where multiple epochs on 100M unique natural-language tokens beat every synthetic curriculum. The same holds on most of our downstream evaluations, both DCLM CORE
(
Li et al., 2024
)
and BLiMP
(
Warstadt et al., 2020
)
, with exceptions confined to our smallest compute budget (Table
1
).
4.
Mechanism: learned PPT priors may not survive the phase transition to natural language.
We find that gains acquired during PPT on the PPT distribution disappear over the PPT-to-PT phase boundary. Uniformly interleaving the same data throughout training instead preserves performance on those distributions, but we do not find significant improvement in natural-language validation loss.
These findings highlight the surprising effectiveness of naturally occurring data as a training signal: even when unique natural-language tokens are scarce, repeated training on them remains more useful than training on the synthetic corpora we test. Importantly, we do not take this to imply that synthetic data cannot help. Instead, our results point to front-loading synthetic data as a poor way to use it, since what is learned during PPT is progressively lost once natural-language training begins. It may instead be better integrated gradually, through interleaving that avoids the abrupt distribution shift between PPT and PT. Our results therefore motivate rethinking the PPT phase, rather than ruling out synthetic data as a training corpus.
2
Background & Related Work
2.1
Pre-pretraining
All prior work in synthetic pre-pretraining shares a common hypothesis: training on certain synthetic distributions can instill language-modeling priors that transfer to natural language. Designed to encourage in-context learning, these distributions can be generated procedurally in effectively unlimited quantities.
PPT corpora in prior work can be divided broadly into three categories: formal languages
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Mita et al., 2026
)
, algorithmic tasks
(
Wu et al., 2022
;
Jiang et al., 2026
)
, and data sampled from randomly initialized neural networks
(
Lee et al., 2026
;
Guo et al., 2026
)
. Of these, we focus on
k
k
-Dyck and NCA, for which prior work reports the largest improvements in natural-language perplexity.
Hu et al. (2025)
introduce PPT on
k

k

Lee et al. (2026)
instead use NCA for PPT. A cellular automaton is a grid of cells, each holding a value from a finite vocabulary—for example, one of ten symbols. The grid evolves over discrete time steps: at each step, every cell takes a new value as a function of the cells in its immediate neighborhood, using a single update rule applied identically to every cell. This can be defined as follows: let

To construct an NCA PPT corpus,
Lee et al. (2026)
sample a random initial grid, with each cell assigned a value drawn from the fixed vocabulary, together with a randomly initialized convolutional neural network as the update rule. They then run the simulation forward for a fixed number of time steps. At this point, the resulting rollouts range from low-entropy static grids to more complex, visually interesting ones. Hence, each rollout is further filtered by a proxy-complexity metric, the gzip compression ratio, and only those falling within the highest compression band are kept. Each grid in a retained rollout is then flattened exactly as a 2D image tensor would be, and the flattened grids are concatenated in time step order into a one-dimensional token sequence for training.
The experimental protocol is largely shared across the PPT methods in the literature. The natural-language token budget and training recipe are fixed, and a synthetic data phase is prepended, with the number of PPT tokens varied to optimize the downstream natural-language loss after PT. The usual control replaces the synthetic tokens with an equal number of natural-language tokens, and a gain is reported if PPT reaches a lower downstream loss than this control. Methods are therefore compared at equal total tokens and equal model size.
In their largest-scale experiment, training a 1.6B-parameter model,
Lee et al. (2026)

Yamaguchi et al. (2026)

k

However, like prior work, they also keep the weight-initialization scheme fixed. We find that ablating it significantly improves the natural-language baseline, enough to close its gap with PPT.
2.2
Training regimes
How a compute budget should be spent depends on which resource is scarce. When natural language is the constraint, additional compute buys only repeated passes over the same tokens.
Muennighoff et al. (2023)
characterize this setting and find that, for their models and data, up to four epochs of repetition are close to lossless, after which the gains from additional compute rapidly diminish and new data is more useful. The slowrun benchmark
(
Vegesna et al., 2026
)
isolates the regime in its extreme form, fixing a 100M-token sample of FineWeb and leaving compute essentially unconstrained. Work in this setting has shown that heavy regularization and ensembling continue to buy substantial data efficiency well past the point at which ordinary training overfits
(
Kim et al., 2025
)
. PPT is motivated by the same scarcity, so these are competing answers to one question: what to do with compute once the natural-language data has run out. When data is instead plentiful, compute becomes the constraint, which is the setting where
Hoffmann et al. (2022)
show that model size and token count should be scaled together. Deployed models, however, are rarely trained at that ratio, because training compute is not the only cost; once inference is accounted for, this moves the optimum toward smaller models trained on more tokens
(
Sardana et al., 2024
;
Touvron et al., 2023
)
. These are the three compute-matched regimes we study: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and over-Chinchilla, a comparison that prior PPT work has not explicitly made. Because the compute-optimal model size may itself depend on data quality and curriculum
(
Bi et al., 2024
)

Although the previous section shows that PPT can improve performance when compute is added on top of a fixed natural-language budget, this does not establish that synthetic data is the best use of those resources. In practice, the same compute could instead be spent on further natural-language training, including repeated epochs when unique language is scarce. We therefore turn to compute-matched experiments, asking whether PPT can justify diverting part of the training budget away from natural language.

One reason PPT may fail to improve over the baseline is that what it learns does not carry over into PT. The shift from PPT to PT is abrupt: the PPT data differs substantially from natural language, and is seen only at the start of training and never again.
Ibrahim et al. (2024)
show that even a shift between two natural languages causes forgetting. Their work shows that continued pretraining on German, after 300B tokens of English, causes forgetting on the original English distribution. The shift from a synthetic distribution to natural language is even larger.

Holding 5% of every batch as PPT data throughout training instead improves performance on the PPT distribution over the entire run. This is despite both schedules spending the same total compute on the PPT distribution. Forgetting at the boundary is therefore preventable by simply mixing in the synthetic distribution throughout PT. Interleaving improves FineWeb BPB for the PPT methods, though not significantly for all, and as these runs are not hyperparameter-tuned at this scale, how large the gain could be remains open.

Limitations
Hyperparameter search at larger scales.
We could not run a full hyperparameter search above
9
×
10
18
9\times 10^{18}
FLOPs, where each trial becomes expensive; the over-Chinchilla runs, for instance, sweep only the peak learning rates and use other hyperparameters from the smaller budgets (Appendix
D.6
). However, the baseline and PPT methods receive the same reduced sweep, so the comparison between them remains matched. Similarly, the share of compute given to PPT is itself a hyperparameter, which we fix at 1% and 5% in the data-unconstrained setting rather than tune, leaving shares in between, or ones that change with the total budget, untested.
Effect sizes relative to prior work.
The differences we report between PPT and the baseline are small, and in some settings smaller than those previously reported. One reason is that we use NanoChat, which uses a different tokenizer, model architecture, and natural-language dataset than prior work. The tokenizer alone has been shown to change the effect of PPT
(
Riazhskykh et al., 2026
)
. However, within our own experiments, the setup is held fixed across the baseline and the PPT methods, so any difference between them is attributable to PPT rather than to these details. Another reason for discrepancies with prior gains is the metric we report. In order to make our results easily comparable for future work, we evaluate using validation BPB. Prior work often reports results in perplexity, which is the exponential of the loss and hence yields larger relative differences than BPB. Hence, our BPB differences are not directly comparable to the perplexity ones shown in prior work.
8
Discussion
We set out to test whether PPT improves PT efficiency. Across three synthetic corpora and multiple training regimes, allocating compute to PPT never outperforms spending it on natural language. This holds even under a multi-epoch setting over 100M tokens. However, in the additive setting at the smallest natural-language budgets, a benefit persists even against a well-initialized baseline. Prior studies hold the initialization scheme fixed while varying the curriculum, a natural design choice for isolating the curriculum effect. Our results suggest that future robustness checks should additionally vary this axis for both PPT and no-PPT methods.
Previous work argues that the priors learned during PPT persist through to the PT phase
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2026
)
. In our experiments, however, models do not retain their ability on the PPT distribution after the transition (Section
6
). If such priors are indeed kept after PPT, we would expect the model to keep at least part of this ability. One could argue that losing this ability is expected, and that it may not matter how well the model does on the PPT distribution, as long as the priors survive. Once the PPT data is no longer present in training, the model no longer needs to assign probability to the PPT tokens, so it is likely that the performance on the PPT distribution degrades. However, if this were the sole reason for the drop in performance, degradation on the code distribution would not occur. Unlike the synthetic distributions, most tokens seen during the code PPT phase are also seen during the PT phase, since comments and variable names carry natural-language semantics. Hence, the model keeps learning to predict them during PT, albeit outside of code contexts. Yet, even in this case, loss on the code distribution rises after the phase boundary. This suggests that the priors learned on code-specific data are not fully kept, and are instead progressively overwritten once the distribution shifts abruptly to natural language. We therefore recommend that future work on synthetic data schedules also measure the model’s ability on the synthetic distribution throughout training, as a proxy for whether the inductive biases learned from it are retained.
A natural question is whether PPT could pay off at scales beyond those tested in this work. Though our largest models stay below one billion parameters, our over-Chinchilla experiments train an 881M-parameter model on 50B tokens, a compute budget comparable to or larger than experiments in prior PPT work
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Yamaguchi et al., 2026
)
. Even so, we show that neither NCA nor
k
k
-Dyck improves on the baseline at this scale. We also approach the question from a scaling-law perspective, which motivates our data-unconstrained experiments. Such a perspective has not been explicitly analyzed in prior work. There, we search for each method’s compute-optimal recipe at three budgets and fit a power law to each, and find no evidence that any PPT method scales better than the baseline (Section
5
, Appendix
E.2
). Taken together, these results suggest that these PPT recipes would not overtake natural-language training at larger scales.
Next, our main conclusions concern natural-language validation loss. On downstream benchmarks, where prior work highlights gains
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Yamaguchi et al., 2026
)
, for example on specific BLiMP phenomena
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
and on reasoning benchmarks after fine-tuning
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
, the picture is less clear. In our experiments, aggregate BLiMP and DCLM CORE scores mostly match the baseline. However, exceptions exist on individual sub-tasks, including BLiMP phenomena, which shift in both directions, though without a clear pattern across methods or settings (Figure
11
). Hence, PPT may still shape narrower capabilities that aggregate benchmarks do not capture, which more targeted evaluations could bring out. Where it does, integrating synthetic data gradually rather than front-loading it could help better retain these capabilities. PPT could similarly prove more useful in other data modalities, which our study, limited to language modeling, does not examine.
Moreover, our findings leave open questions for future work. As natural-language data is increasingly constrained relative to available compute
(
Kim et al., 2025
)
, synthetic data is a compelling prospect. That said, our results motivate rethinking whether such data should be integrated via an explicit PPT phase. For such a phase to be worthwhile, the forgetting across the phase boundary must first be solved. Alternatively, this forgetting can be avoided by interleaving synthetic data throughout training. We therefore recommend that future work investigate better interleaving schedules. However, whether such schedules make synthetic data a better use of compute than natural language remains an open question.

Appendix C
FLOP Measurement
To convert a FLOP budget into a training configuration, we measure the FLOPs of
one forward and backward pass (one optimization step) for the model using the
FLOP-counting utilities in PyTorch
(
PyTorch, 2026c
)
. We then divide the
total budget by the FLOPs per step to determine the number of optimization steps
and tokens consumed by each phase. Working backwards from a FLOP budget to a configuration is the
standard framing of compute-optimal PT
(
Hoffmann et al., 2022
)
,
and it is what allows a PPT method and its baseline to be compared on
equal terms for the compute-matched experiments. We measure FLOPs directly rather than matching token counts for compute matching because the synthetic corpora use much smaller vocabularies than natural language, so the language-modeling head, and with it the FLOPs per token, is smaller during PPT. Given its smaller vocabulary size, the PPT phase is therefore afforded extra steps. However, this difference shrinks as models grow, since the language-modeling head makes up a decreasing share of the total parameters. For the over-Chinchilla configuration, our largest model, we therefore simply allocate tokens directly, 0.5B to PPT and 49.5B to FineWeb against the baseline’s 50B, so that every method sees the same total number of tokens (Appendix
D.6
).
Appendix D
Hyperparameters
D.1
How LLMTuna works
LLMTuna
is a language-model-based hyperparameter optimizer that we release with this work. The approach is inspired by prior work that also used language models for hyperparameter optimization and autoresearch more broadly
(
Yang et al., 2024a
;
Jiang & Zhao, 2026
;
Karpathy, 2026a
)
.
LLMTuna
maintains an ordered history of configurations tried so far and their corresponding scores, which in our experiments are validation BPB. At each step, a language model uses this history together with any additional context provided, such as training code, notes on hyperparameter behavior, or constraints on the search, to propose the next configuration. This gives the model semantic context from the codebase that can inform which hyperparameters are likely to matter. The search space is specified using three parameter types,
Float
,
Int
, and
Choice
, each with a name, a natural-language description, and optional bounds and initial value.
Following the API design of Optuna
(
Akiba et al., 2019
)
, the optimization loop consists of two calls.
suggest
provides the accumulated context to the model together with a tool whose schema is generated from the search space, so the proposal is returned as JSON in a fixed shape rather than as prose.
observe
then records the configuration and its resulting score, adding the trial to the history available to subsequent calls to
suggest
.

The system prompt for a study tuning all eight hyperparameters begins:
You are a hyperparameter optimizer minimizing val_bpb (validation

Most of the result at a given scale comes from three knobs: depth, matrix_lr,
and ppt_lr. Each has its own optimum, and each optimum shifts with scale.
Getting them near their minimum for THIS scale matters more than refining the

Appendix E
Full results
This appendix collects the complete results for each setting in turn. For our reported
BLiMP results, we score BLiMP following the released evaluation code of
Hu et al. (2025)
. Each of the 67,000 minimal pairs is scored by total
sentence log-probability, and a pair is counted correct only if the grammatical
sentence scores strictly higher than the ungrammatical one, so ties count as
errors. No beginning-of-sequence token is prepended, which means the first token of each sentence
is unscored. DCLM CORE is evaluated with the
NanoChat evaluation code
(
Karpathy, 2025
)
.

article.headline: 计算匹配下合成预预训练未胜自然语言
article.lede: 在计算匹配的多种训练机制中，把算力分给合成预预训练（PPT）始终不如直接训练自然语言；小预算下的增益也随规模消失。
article.problem: 合成预预训练被提出作为语言模型正式预训练前的阶段，试图用k-Dyck、神经细胞自动机等合成分布注入可迁移的归纳偏置。但此前报告的增益是否稳健、在总算力固定时是否值得从自然语言训练中分走算力，仍缺乏系统检验。
article.method: 作者在四种PPT课程（k-Dyck、NCA、DeclRef和代码）与三种训练机制（数据受限、数据不受限、高token-to-parameter比）下，比较“加法算力”和“计算匹配”两种分配方式。实验还消融权重初始化方案，并追踪模型在PPT分布上的表现以及将合成数据均匀交错到训练中的效果。
article.results: 在NCA复现中，原始初始化下PPT带来5.4%的困惑度改善；但把嵌入初始化改为N(0,0.02)后，无PPT基线自身改善9.0%，两者差距消失。计算匹配实验中，数据受限设置固定100M自然语言token和1×10^18 FLOPs，over-Chinchilla设置训练881M参数模型、50B token，PPT均未超过自然语言基线；到1B自然语言token时，小预算下的加法收益也消失。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明把合成数据前置为独立PPT阶段可能不是划算的算力用法；更值得探索的是在训练中渐进或交错地整合合成数据，并重新评估其保留机制。
article.limitations: 作者未能在9×10^18 FLOPs以上进行完整超参搜索，且PPT算力占比固定为1%和5%而非调优；效应量整体较小，并与先前工作因NanoChat的tokenizer、架构和数据不同而不可直接比较，BPB与困惑度的差异也需谨慎解读。
article.figure_caption_zh: 合成预预训练数据的词元化：NCA的每个网格按2×2图块切分并随时间拼接，k-Dyck的括号类型各自成词元，DeclRef的关键字、作用域括号、名称和值均为独立词元。

figure.caption: {Tokenizing synthetic pre-pretraining data.} For NCA, each grid of a rollout is split into $2 2$ patches that each become one token, and grids are concatenated in time order with start and end tokens. For $k$-Dyck, the opening and closing bracket types are each their own token. For DeclRef, keywords, scope brackets, names and values are unique tokens. In the example shown, a reference inside the opened scope retrieves the value of a name declared in that scope, and after the scope closes a reference retrieves the value of a name declared before the scope. Generation and tokenization details are given in Section~ {sec:related} and Appendix~ {app:data}.

Abstract
While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality.
In this paper, we introduce
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (
MoBA
) attention.
Mix Forcing
jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training.
In self-attention,
Mix Forcing
leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors.
To support online text interaction,
Mix Forcing
further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk.
Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator.
Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.
Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts.

Introduction
Interactive video world models
[
19
,
34
,
10
,
49
,
53
,
33
,
14
,
47
]
, which predict future states conditioned on historical context and user inputs, have shown great potential for world simulation, video gaming, and embodied intelligence.
Since users act based on past observations, each video chunk must be generated without access to future frames or future instructions, which calls for causal autoregressive generation.
Recent works
[
34
,
53
,
14
]
build upon pretrained video diffusion models to leverage their strong visual priors.
However, these priors are learned for bidirectional generation, where all frames are jointly denoised with access to both past and future frames.
Some methods
[
16
,
43
]
directly distill bidirectional models into few-step causal generators via ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialization and distribution matching distillation (DMD), but the trajectories of the bidirectional teacher depend on future information, preventing the causal student from converging to the target flow map.
To address this, other methods
[
54
,
50
]
first adapt pretrained models into many-step causal models with teacher forcing before few-step distillation, making this causal pre-training stage the foundation of the final generator.
However, teacher forcing departs from the pretraining setting of bidirectional video diffusion models in two aspects.
In attention, each chunk attends only to its history rather than the full video; in noise level, each noisy chunk is predicted from clean historical context rather than jointly denoised with other chunks at a shared noise level, which encourages velocity prediction to over-rely on clean context.
Both deviations disrupt pretrained visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality.
Moreover, causal pre-training methods typically condition the whole video on a single global prompt, which exposes future events to the current chunk.
Streaming methods
[
40
]
support prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt, which rewrites the context of past frames.
In this paper, we introduce
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the
Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (
MoBA
)
attention block.
The key idea of
Mix Forcing
is to mix teacher forcing and bidirectional training: teacher forcing learns causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while bidirectional training retains the pretraining setting in both attention and noise level, preserving pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation.
In addition,
Mix Forcing
conditions each teacher forcing chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, enabling online text interaction without exposing future instructions to the current chunk or recomputing the KV cache of past chunks.
Based on
Mix Forcing
, we build an interactive video world model with camera control and online text interaction (
Fig.
1
).
Starting from a 14B image-to-video model, we perform causal pre-training with
Mix Forcing
, and then apply consistency distillation (CD)
[
31
]
and DMD to obtain a four-step generator for KV-cached autoregressive rollout (
Fig.
2
).
Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control, and sustains high-fidelity generation over one-hour rollouts.
Ablation studies further show that
Mix Forcing
provides a stronger initialization for few-step post-training than teacher forcing alone.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We propose the
MoBA
attention block, which mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation, with chunk-wise prompt conditioning for online text interaction.
•
We build an interactive video world model through causal pre-training with
Mix Forcing
and few-step post-training with CD and DMD, supporting camera control, online text interaction, and four-step KV-cached autoregressive rollout.
•
Experiments on internal and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.

Self-Attention Design for Causal Pre-Training.
Using teacher forcing (TF) as the baseline, we evaluate the effects of adding diffusion forcing (DF)

As shown in

However, adding DF (rows 2 and 3) can reduce generation quality.
We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between training and inference, where DF uses noisy historical chunks during training, while KV-cached inference leverages fully denoised historical context.
Note that DF replaces the clean history with independently noised history, which matches neither the clean KV cache at inference nor the shared noise level of pretraining. In contrast,
MoBA
keeps the clean history in TF for inference consistency and recovers the pretraining setting in a separate BID branch.
We further study the effect of training chunk size under TF+BID.
As chunk size=1 (row 4) enables fine-grained causal modeling by assigning an independent noise level to each latent frame and outperforms the other settings (rows 5 and 6) in both generation quality and camera control accuracy, we combine TF and BID training with chunk size=1 in

5
Conclusion
We present
Mix Forcing
, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models.
Implemented with the
MoBA
attention block, it mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors, and uses chunk-wise prompts for online text interaction.
Combined with CD and DMD, our four-step model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with camera control over one-hour rollouts.
Limitations.
Our implementation targets video DiT architectures with separate self-attention and cross-attention modules, and its extension to unified attention
[
21
]
remains to be verified.
Moreover, our model is designed for chunk-wise local prompts, and its camera control is less precise when only a single global prompt is available, as observed on public benchmarks.
We leave these directions for future work.

A.1
Training Data
Data Acquisition.
We collect 100k video clips totaling 974 hours.
We collect egocentric recordings, videos from games and Unreal Engine environments, and web videos.
These sources cover first-person interactions, controlled synthetic scenes, and diverse real-world content.
Data Filtering.
We split videos at shot boundaries and remove clips with decoding errors or unsuitable duration and resolution.
We further filter clips using visual quality, exposure, text occupancy, and motion statistics.
A vision-language model assesses the remaining clips for editing artifacts, viewpoint, and interaction content.
Prompt Annotation.
For each clip, we generate a shared environment prompt describing the scene and a global prompt summarizing the entire video.
We separately annotate subject visibility, motion, interactions, and environmental changes, then combine the active annotations into local prompts.
We refine these prompts for consistent wording and temporal alignment, removing descriptions of future events or actions unsupported by visual evidence.
Each local prompt is shared by four consecutive latent frames, consistent with the cross-attention setting in the main paper.
Camera Annotation.
We estimate camera poses using COLMAP for 70% of the video clips.
The remaining 30% are used without camera annotations, with all-zero Plücker embeddings as the conditioning input.

B.3
User Study
We conduct a pairwise user study on InBench to evaluate visual quality, interactive following, and motion clarity.
Pairwise Comparison.
Each trial compares our model with one of five baselines: HY-WorldPlay, JoyAI-Echo-WM, LingBot-World-Fast, Matrix-Game 3.0, and SANA-WM-Streaming.
The two videos use the same initial image and source control sequence and are displayed side by side at the same size using the 480p evaluation outputs.
They are labeled only as
Video A
and
Video B
, with the left/right position of our model randomized independently for each trial.
Model identities and numerical evaluation scores are hidden from participants.
Case Allocation.
The study uses the full InBench case pool, comprising 96 cases: 64 roaming cases and 32 interactive cases.
Each session contains 20 pairs of videos (40 videos in total), corresponding to 10 interactive cases and 10 roaming cases, with no case repeated within a session.
Each baseline appears in four trials per session.
We shuffle the baseline assignments and select cases within each subset, prioritizing case–baseline pairs with fewer previous assignments.
The two subsets are presented in separate blocks, and no case is repeated within a session.
Evaluation Questions.
For each applicable question, participants select
Video A is better
,
They are the same
, or
Video B is better
.
The three evaluation dimensions are:
•
Visual quality (both subsets).
Participants compare overall appearance, temporal stability, natural motion, and visible artifacts.
•
Interactive following (interactive subset).
Participants compare how well the videos perform the requested events as the corresponding local prompts become active.
•
Motion clarity (roaming subset).
Participants compare scene detail during camera movement, focusing on blur, smearing, and ghosting. They judge frames during movement and select a tie when clarity is similar or no viewpoint change is visible.
Each trial therefore collects a visual-quality judgment and one judgment specific to its subset.

article.headline: 混合注意力因果预训练让交互世界模型稳定一小时
article.lede: 为交互式视频世界模型提出 Mix Forcing 因果预训练：自注意力混合教师强制与双向训练保住视觉先验，再用 CD 与
article.problem: 交互式视频世界模型要求按块自回归生成，每块只能看历史与当前指令；但把预训练的双向视频扩散模型直接改成教师强制训练，会在两方面偏离预训练设定：注意力上每个块只看自身与历史而非全视频，噪声水平上每块由干净历史预测而非与其他块在同一时间步联合去噪，从而破坏视觉先验、降低生成质量。此外既有因果预训练多用一个全局提示条件整段视频，等于把未来指令提前泄露给当前块；流式方法则按新提示重算历史 KV 缓存，改写了已生成帧的上下文。
article.method: 作者提出 MoBA（双向与自回归混合）注意力块：在同一次前向中，教师强制分支的每个噪声块通过稀疏掩码只注意自身与干净历史，另外追加的双向分支噪声 latent 之间相互全注意，从而在保持因果预测能力的同时复现预训练的注意力与噪声设定。交叉注意力采用块级提示条件，每个教师强制块只注意共享环境提示与自己当前的局部提示，双向分支仍用全局提示；推理时提示更新只影响后续块，过去块的 KV 缓存可直接复用。方法从 14B 图生视频模型 Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P 出发做因果预训练（相机位姿以 Plücker 嵌入经 AdaLN 注入），再用一致性蒸馏（CD，LPIPS 距离）与分布匹配蒸馏（DMD）压成四步自回归生成器。
article.results: 在自建 InBench 上，平均质量 75.1 为对比方法最高，事件遵循 EA=94.4、1.5 秒内及时准确率 OT1.5s=96.8，相机旋转/平移误差 0.296/0.316、CMC=0.539；同表最强的 LingBot-World-Fast 对应为 72.4、86.5、87.3 与 1.065、0.433、1.312。SANA-WM-Bench 的 60 秒简单/困难轨迹上平均质量 74.8/74.7、SIQ 66.7/66.4。一小时 rollout 按每五分钟窗口统计的质量均值在 67.3–71.6 之间，末段 69.3、首段 71.0；WBench 的 Navi-158 子集上平均质量 78.5、Setting 遵从度 80.3、Interaction 84.3。消融显示，同样经 CD→DMD 的四步模型，Mix Forcing 预训练对比仅教师强制：质量 70.9 vs 64.1、EA 55.1 vs 33.7、OT1.5s 64.3 vs 19.8；块级提示对比全局提示把 EA 从 23.4 提到 50.0、OT1.5s 从 18.3 提到 62.1。
article.why_it_matters: 交互式视频世界模型被视为游戏、具身智能与世界模拟的基础设施；用因果预训练把双向扩散先验低成本转成自回归生成器，再经四步蒸馏与 KV 缓存实现实时交互，是一条可直接通往可部署实时世界模型的路线。一小时生成质量基本不衰减，说明长时一致性不必依赖不断重算历史。
article.limitations: 作者承认相机控制在只有单一全局提示时精度下降：SANA-WM-Bench 硬轨迹上旋转误差 1.214，不及 Matrix-Game 3 的 0.914，且方法依赖自注意力与交叉注意力分离的视频 DiT 架构，能否推广到统一注意力尚未验证。主要结果建立在自建 InBench 与自采 100k 片段（974 小时）训练集上，第三方复现与横向比较成本较高。
article.figure_caption_zh: 给定初始图像与环境提示，模型依据 KV 缓存的历史上下文、相机位姿与局部提示自回归生成每个 latent 块，再由 VAE 解码器输出视频片段。

figure.caption: {Pipeline of our interactive video world model.} Given an initial image and an environment prompt $ {p}_{e}$, an interactive world is simulated by our four-step causal video model. Based on the KV-cached history context and user inputs, including the camera pose $ {e}_{i}$ and the local prompt $ {p}_{i}$, each latent chunk is generated autoregressively and decoded into a video clip by the VAE decoder.

Abstract
We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents.
While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities.
Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization.
To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues.
The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data.
Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality.
Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time.
By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

16
]
.
However, existing generated scene representations primarily capture geometry and appearance, while lacking an explicit understanding of their content. Downstream applications in embodied AI and physical simulation cannot interact with an collection of colored primitives; they require structured scene elements with semantic roles and discrete instance boundaries to support collision reasoning, physical manipulation, and interactive scene editing.
A natural solution might seem to generate an appearance-only scene first and recover semantic and instance representations post-hoc.
However, this two-stage route breaks down in the single-view generative setting. Existing post-hoc methods either attach 2D foundation-model predictions to an existing reconstruction through per-scene optimization
[
67
,
105
,
87
,
100
]
, or jointly infer geometry and understanding from multiple captured views
[
117
,
26
,
88
]
.
The former requires expensive scene-specific foundation model preprocessing and optimization.
The latter relies on captured multi-view inputs and is constrained by the limited scale and domain diversity of multi-view training data.
Neither route directly yields a structured 3D scene that has been generated from a single image.
Scaling these capabilities is not merely a matter of attaching a feature head to a reconstruction model. Generated regions lack paired ground-truth supervision, so estimated geometry, semantics, and object boundaries can drift and disagree across views. Predictions from 2D vision models compound this, as their semantics and masks are not guaranteed to be view-consistent. The central challenge is to turn complementary but imperfect generative and perceptual signals
into a consistent 3D representation while balancing geometry, appearance, semantics, and instances without compromising generation quality.
An integrated model should let semantic priors and geometry reinforce each other, rather than tagging an isolated reconstruction with semantic or object information.
We introduce LucidLyra, a framework that unifies feed-forward generative 3D reconstruction and scene understanding in an explicit Gaussian representation (
Fig.
1
).
Our central insight is that a video generator provides a unified foundation for structured 3D scene generation, serving both as the shared backbone and as the source of training data.
Building on Lyra’s latent-to-Gaussian formulation
[
2
]
, LucidLyra learns a 3D scene representation from camera-controlled video latents through multi-task distillation. Given a single input image, we denoise the corresponding video latents across camera trajectories, and process them through two parallel branches. The teacher branch decodes the latent into an RGB video and applies frozen vision-language, segmentation, and tracking foundation models to obtain semantic and instance supervision. The student branch incorporates vision cues of the input view into the video latents and directly maps the shared latent into a 3D Gaussian scene. We consolidate the teacher predictions across the generated views and distill them into persistent semantic and instance fields on the Gaussian primitives, jointly with geometry and appearance.
A single shared representation can therefore support novel-view rendering,
open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping.
As an initial exploration toward generative 4D scene
understanding, we also extend the formulation to monocular video inputs and predict
semantics- and instance-aware dynamic 3D scenes.
For this novel task, we introduce an evaluation protocol with benchmarks covering static scenes, real-image domain transfer, and dynamic scenes.
On our static LucidLyra-SDG benchmark, LucidLyra improves semantic mIoU and
class-agnostic instance mTrackPR over the strongest comparable baseline by
31.7
31.7
and
9.8
9.8
percentage points,
while maintaining reconstruction fidelity, with a modest PSNR gain of
0.53
0.53
dB over Lyra.
More broadly, this formulation turns pretrained video generation into a
scalable source of supervision for structured 3D learning, opening a path from
renderable but unstructured outputs to queryable 3D worlds that downstream
systems can reason about and interact with. In summary, our contributions are:
•
We introduce a unified generative 3D model that produces an explicit
Gaussian scene representation with geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantic, and class-agnostic instance features from a single image in a feed-forward fashion.
•
We develop a multi-task distillation strategy that transfers
2D generative, semantic, and object-level knowledge through aligned generated
views into a consistent 3D representation. This enables task-specific training
without captured multi-view data or manual 3D annotations, and avoids
per-scene optimization at inference time.
•
We jointly evaluate reconstruction and understanding on static and dynamic scenes. LucidLyra consistently outperforms two-stage baselines across optimization-based, mask-lifting, and feed-forward 3DGS segmentation methods, while maintaining novel-view reconstruction fidelity on static scenes with a small reconstruction trade-off on dynamic scenes. We further demonstrate downstream applications including robotic simulation, 3D scene editing, and 3D asset mining.

The former requires a pre-existing reconstruction, precluding single-view generation, while post-hoc lifting decouples semantics from geometry, leaving fusion vulnerable to cross-view inconsistencies. Crucially, both rely on an expensive preprocessing stage with a 2D vision foundation model.

LucidLyra instead unifies scene understanding with generative reconstruction. 5
Conclusion
We presented LucidLyra, which turns generated scenes into queryable 3D worlds by distilling generative and perceptual knowledge into a feed-forward Gaussian decoder.
A camera-controlled video model supplies both latent representations and training data, enabling joint reconstruction and understanding without captured multi-view data, manual 3D annotations, or per-scene optimization.
Experiments demonstrate improved semantic and instance understanding over the compared two-stage baselines while preserving Lyra’s reconstruction quality.
Furthermore, we demonstrate initial results on dynamic scenes and applications in 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and physical-AI simulation.
Future work could scale our approach by accelerated video generation
[
48
]
with larger-scale joint training for generation and scene understanding
[
13
]
.

C.1
Qualitative Baseline Comparison
Figures
7
and
8
compare semantic and instance predictions across both static benchmarks.
Open-vocabulary semantics.
LangSplatV2
[
45
]
and SFS
[
100
]
recover broad semantic structure but exhibit class confusion and label leakage across object boundaries, with LangSplatV2 additionally showing flickering artifacts as the viewpoint changes. The feed-forward baselines Chorus
[
50
]
and IGGT
[
42
]
exhibit incomplete category coverage and noisy boundaries, respectively. We hypothesize that their reduced performance partly reflects a domain shift from real-world and synthetic 3D training data to our generatively reconstructed scenes. LucidLyra preserves coherent semantic regions across viewpoints, approaching the lifted-teacher reference while correcting some of its assignment errors. LucidLyra+ further refines semantic assignments without changing geometry or appearance.
Instance segmentation.
Unified-Lift
[
116
]
produces coherent instance regions but exhibits local label fragmentation and bleeding across object boundaries. IGGT shows blurred instance boundaries and a tendency to over-segment individual objects. Its reconstruction appears sensitive to cross-view inconsistencies in the generated videos, producing duplicated fine-scale structures that further blur segmentation predictions. Our methods preserve more coherent object-level partitions across viewpoints, while the lifted-teacher reference remains competitive. Since instance clustering is conditioned on predicted semantic classes, LucidLyra+ can modify instance partitions without changing the learned instance embeddings.

In the dynamic setting, LucidLyra better separates foreground objects from background surfaces and preserves finer semantic regions than 4D LangSplat
[
46
]
and IGGT4D
[
118
]
(
Fig.
9
). The dynamic baselines require different scene representations and cannot be directly applied to our independently decoded 3D Gaussian states. We therefore evaluate their respective reconstructions and report reconstruction and understanding metrics separately (
Table
4
).
For instance segmentation, LucidLyra maintains coherent foreground masks across queried times, with fewer local gaps and cleaner boundaries than IGGT4D. TRASE
[
51
]
also recovers coherent foreground regions but produces coarser background partitions. The lifted-teacher reference remains competitive, particularly in separating smaller objects, while our method preserves complete foreground regions with less fragmentation.

LucidLyra infers two levels of instance representations that we aim to analyze qualitatively in
Fig.

The main object-level instance features group scene
entities, while additional part-level features expose finer regions within the recovered objects.
The qualitative results reveal a consistent feature hierarchy across all examples: object-level instance features remain similar over the spatial extent of an object, enabling clustering to recover a single instance mask, whereas part-level features preserve finer variations that distinguish individual object components. Because these representations form continuous feature fields, occasional grouping errors may still occur. While open-vocabulary querying and object-level instance segmentation provide the foundation for interacting with our generated scenes, part-level features offer a lightweight extension that enables finer-grained control over individual object components.
Appendix D
Downstream Applications
LucidLyra generates structured, queryable scenes that support diverse downstream applications. In the following section, we demonstrate this capability through examples of robotic simulation, 3D scene editing, and 3D asset mining. See our project website for video demos.
D.1
Robot Simulation
We extract a mesh from the LucidLyra depth maps and camera parameters by computing a signed distance field on a hierarchy of sparse grids. We use the generated scene, extracted mesh and the semantic labels to set up a simulation in NVIDIA IsaacSim
[
60
]
. For navigation, the semantic labels partition the scene into free space and obstacles, over which we build an occupancy grid and plan a route to a semantically specified goal using a clearance-weighted Dijkstra search. A robot (Unitree G1 humanoid) then follows this route with a pure-pursuit controller while a learned rough-terrain locomotion policy drives its joints under full rigid-body physics.
The humanoid also carries a box rigidly attached near its torso to demonstrate loco-manipulation. For manipulation, the LucidLyra semantic labeling localizes a kitchen counter and sink in a separate reconstruction, from which we derive a mount pose and reach-constrained pick-and-place targets for a stationary Franka robotic arm. The arm is simulated with full articulated-body dynamics and a friction-based parallel-jaw grasp under differential inverse-kinematics control, picks a small synthetic object (a sphere) from the sink and places it on the counter. The extracted mesh serves as the collision proxy during simulation, while the original Gaussian-splat reconstruction
[
28
]
is rendered for visual fidelity.
Figure
11
visualizes the simulation examples.
Figure 11
:
Robot simulation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim using LucidLyra scenes.
Four different robot-simulation scenarios built on LucidLyra reconstructions.
Extracted geometry provides collision surfaces, semantic labels support task planning,
and Gaussian-splat rendering preserves the scene appearance.
Overlaid robot poses show motion over time, with increasing opacity indicating temporal progression.
D.2
3D Scene Editing
We implement a simple browser-based editor. The user can select objects through text queries or clicks. Text selection intersects the predicted semantic class with an instance ID, thereby separating objects of the same category, while click selection retrieves the semantic–instance pair of the Gaussian center nearest the camera ray. Users can further refine the selection using separate similarity thresholds for Gaussian semantic and instance features relative to prototypes computed from the initial support.
Translation, rotation, scaling, duplication, and deletion operate directly on the selected Gaussian parameters. Transformations are applied around the selection centroid and update positions, anisotropic scales, and orientation quaternions, while color, opacity, and learned features remain attached to each primitive. Duplication appends a transformed copy, whereas deletion removes the selected primitives.
Moving or deleting an object can expose unobserved regions. After the user commits all edits, OmniPaint
[
108
]
inpaints the original object support, and a subsequent LucidLyra forward pass reconstructs a clean background scene. We retain only reconstructed Gaussians near the edit whose projections fall within the exposed source support, excluding the transformed object’s footprint. Opacity tapering converts these Gaussians into a smoothly blended local background patch.

3D Asset Mining
Much like in 3D scene editing, we can make use of the generated appearance from multiple views, together with the instance and semantic segmentation masks, to mine high-quality 3D assets from the generated scenes.
For each selected object, we extract six segmented views, prioritizing viewpoint diversity and object coverage without occlusion. The segmented RGB observations together with the corresponding camera parameters are provided to the pretrained Pixal3D

article.headline: LucidLyra：单图生成可查询3D场景
article.lede: LucidLyra 将单图生成的3DGS场景变为可直接查询开放词汇语义与实例的三维表示，无需逐场景优化。
article.problem: 生成式3D重建已能从单张图像合成可渲染环境，但输出主要只有几何与外观，缺少语义角色和对象实例。现有3D理解方法通常需要捕获多视图，或依赖逐场景基础模型预处理与优化，难以直接用于单视图生成场景。
article.method: LucidLyra沿用Lyra的latent-to-Gaussian路线，把相机控制视频扩散模型的多视图latents、相机射线和输入图像C-RADIO特征送入统一3DGS解码器。训练时，冻结的视觉语言、分割和跟踪基础模型在生成视频上产生语义与实例伪标签，再通过多任务蒸馏写入每个高斯的语义与实例特征。模型无需人工3D标注、捕获多视图数据或推理时逐场景优化，并可扩展到单目视频动态场景。
article.results: 在LucidLyra-SDG静态基准上，LucidLyra取得mIoU 64.1、mTrackPR 21.5，LucidLyra+将mIoU提至67.9；相比Lyra，PSNR为25.02 vs 24.49 dB，LPIPS为0.186 vs 0.211。摘要报告相对最强可比基线，语义mIoU高31.7个百分点、实例mTrackPR高9.8个百分点，PSNR高0.53 dB。ADE20K条件场景上mIoU 49.8、LucidLyra+ 53.7；动态场景PSNR 21.88 vs 22.16 dB，mIoU 53.2（LucidLyra+ 62.6）。单场景分割耗时2.1/2.3分钟，逐场景优化基线需64至697分钟。
article.why_it_matters: 机器人仿真、物理AI和3D编辑需要的不是彩色基元集合，而是带语义角色和实例边界的结构化场景；LucidLyra把生成式重建输出变成可直接查询的3D世界，为这些下游应用铺路。
article.limitations: 局限在于语义和实例监督来自生成视频与冻结2D基础模型的伪标签，跨视图不一致或教师错误可能被蒸馏进3D表示。动态扩展存在重建折衷（PSNR 21.88 vs 22.16 dB），且评估基于25场景的 curated 基准和固定生成轨迹，单图多解问题仍未解决。

page_papers.content:
Abstract
One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution.
Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network.
We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision.
A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly.

Introduction
Diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality images, but their repeated network evaluations impose substantial inference cost
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Song et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
. One and few-step generation reduces this cost by learning a much shorter sampling process. The challenge is to accurately render the details specified in the prompt using only one or a few sampling steps. Long-text rendering makes this challenge concrete: many characters must remain legible and correct within a coherent image
(
Geng et al., 2025b
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. It therefore provides a demanding test of whether fast generation retains detailed conditional information.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains a fast generator to match a reference distribution
(
Yin et al., 2024b
;
Yin et al., 2024a
)
. A score describes the local direction of increasing log density. A pretrained teacher supplies the reference score, while an auxiliary fake-score network estimates the score of the current generated distribution. Their difference guides updates to generated samples. These updates are applied sample by sample, but their direction depends on both distributions. Distribution matching can complement trajectory-based training: rCM combines score regularization with continuous-time consistency training
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
.

article.headline: 用矩约束改进一步文生图蒸馏
article.lede: 论文在 DMD 蒸馏中加入生成器 EMA 特征空间的矩约束，试图改善一步/少步文生图的提示细节还原。
article.problem: 一步和少步文生图必须在很少的细化机会下准确呈现提示中的细节，长文本渲染是典型压力测试。DMD 通过分数差把生成分布拉向参考分布，但学习到的分数监督是否足够仍待检验。作者据此追问：显式的矩约束能否改进这一监督信号。
article.method: 作者把反向 KL 场分解为高斯矩分量与非高斯残差，指出可显式约束的统计量。方法在生成器的 EMA 特征空间中，将内部 DMD 损失与特征矩损失结合，并沿用内部速度分支估计分数差，避免单独的假分数网络。实验比较 L_pop 与内部 DMD、EMA 特征与外部编码器，以及速度/端点回归的选择。
article.results: 在单张 A100（BF16）上，论文报告 batch=10 的吞吐（样本/秒）和 batch=1 的延迟（秒）；GenEval 汇总六个类别，基线 Z-Image 约 100 NFE，Z-Image-Turbo 为 8-NFE 蒸馏模型，两个提示在 1 和 2 NFE 下评估。就所给材料而言，FID、CLIP 与 GenEval 的具体数值未给出，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 若矩约束确实补足 DMD 的分数监督，它可作为不增加假分数网络的轻量插件，降低一步/少步生成的推理成本。对长文本渲染等细节密集任务，这类约束尤其值得关注。
article.limitations: 作者强调，协方差收缩命题只适用于平方误差下实现条件均值的预测器，严格收缩还需存在未解释的条件方差，不能据此断言一步生成器普遍低估方差。所给材料缺少完整定量表格，系统级效率与质量优势仍需核对原文数据。
article.figure_caption_zh: 多步采样迭代细化样本，而一步生成学习从噪声到数据的直接映射；方法在生成器 EMA 特征空间联合内部 DMD 损失与特征矩损失，右图示意单次评估推理的理想对齐。

figure.caption: {Overview of for one-step generation.} Multi-step sampling refines samples iteratively, whereas one-step generation learns a direct noise-to-data map. combines an internal DMD loss with a feature-moment loss in the generator's EMA feature space. The right panel illustrates idealized alignment with single-evaluation inference.

article.headline: 学习率调度的后期阶段主导最终损失
article.lede: 两条学习率调度在峰值、终端与累积学习率匹配后互相交换训练阶段，后期交换几乎转移全部最终损失差距。
article.problem: 学习率调度是训练大模型时的标配组件，但究竟是调度曲线的哪一段真正决定最终损失，一直缺少受控的因果证据。以往比较不同调度时，往往整条曲线一起改变，峰值、终值与累积学习率等因素互相纠缠，很难把性能差异归因到某个训练阶段。
article.method: 作者先构造两条完整的学习率调度（其中一条为 Cycloid），并让两者在峰值学习率、终端学习率与累积学习率上相互匹配，排除这些混杂因素。随后做阶段交换干预：分别把早期、中期和后期片段从一条调度换到另一条调度上。评价指标为终端指数滑动平均（EMA-0.99）训练损失。
article.results: 交换后期阶段后，最终损失差距几乎被完整转移到任一调度上；而交换早期或中期阶段几乎没有影响。损失数值、交换点位置与重复次数论文未给出具体数字（材料仅给出 EMA-0.99 这一设置）。
article.why_it_matters: 如果最终损失主要由训练末段的学习率决定，那么调度设计与超参搜索的算力就应该更多投向后段，早期曲线的精细调优可能收益有限。这也为「调度形状重要还是末期学习率重要」这一长期争论提供了一个可检验的因果视角。
article.limitations: 现有证据只来自图中所示的一对调度与单一指标（训练损失而非验证精度），论文未给出具体数字，交换点定义与统计显著性也不清楚。结论能否推广到其他模型规模、数据集与优化器，仍需更多实验验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 在峰值、终端与累积学习率匹配的两条完整调度之间交换后期阶段，几乎能把最终损失差距完整转移到任一调度，而早、中期交换影响很小（柱高为终端 EMA-0.99 训练损失）。

figure.caption: {Late-stage scheduling dominates the final loss difference.} Starting from two full schedules with matched peak, terminal, and cumulative LRs, swapping the late stage between and Cycloid nearly transfers the full final loss gap to either schedule, whereas swaps of the early and middle stages have little effect. The bars use the terminal exponential moving average (EMA-0.99) training loss, as in Table~ {tab:multi_scheduler_compare}; the intervention and reporting details are given in Appendix~ {app:protocol_stage_swaps}.

article.headline: SMD：四步采样覆盖五类生成任务
article.lede: 作者称「简洁即可扩展」：同一套SMD在4-NFE下覆盖图像、视频、编辑、多教师与音视频生成。
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配模型生成质量不断提升，但推理需要较多采样步数，速度仍是实际部署的主要瓶颈。已有的少步蒸馏方案（如DMD2）大多在单一模态或单一任务上验证，尚不清楚同一套方法能否在图像、视频、编辑、多教师和音视频等差异很大的任务上同时成立。
article.method: 论文提出SMD，把采样预算压到4-NFE（每个样本4次函数评估），并在图像生成、视频生成、图像编辑、多教师蒸馏和音视频生成五类任务上统一评测。对比对象包括作者自行复现的DMD2以及PDD的结果。除图注外，材料未提供方法细节，SMD的具体蒸馏目标与训练流程论文正文未给出。
article.results: 提供的材料只有图注，论文未给出具体数字。可核实的设定是：所有任务统一在4-NFE下评测，指标均为越高越好，包含语义一致性（SC）与感知质量（PQ）两类；图中DMD2一栏标注为作者自行复现，PDD的结果也一并列出。
article.why_it_matters: 如果4-NFE能在模态与任务差异如此大的场景下同时成立，少步蒸馏就更可能成为通用的推理加速方案，而不必为每个任务单独设计蒸馏流程。
article.limitations: 材料仅含一条图注，标题、正文、基线配置与全部数值均缺失，无法核验「简洁即可扩展」这一主张。图注还说明径向轴按指标分别截断、柱状轴从零起，且自行复现的DMD2与PDD结果的对比条件未交代，跨任务结论需谨慎看待。
article.figure_caption_zh: SMD在4-NFE下于图像、视频、编辑、多教师与音视频生成五类任务上的表现对比，径向轴按指标截断，柱状轴从零起，指标均为越高越好。

figure.caption: {Simplicity scales.} SMD at 4-NFE across image, video, editing, multi-teacher, and audio--video generation. Radial scales are truncated per metric. Column scales start at zero. All metrics are higher-is-better. SC/PQ denote semantic consistency/perceptual quality. $^{*}$Our DMD2 reproduction. $^{ }$PDD results~ {pdd}.

{surveycover}
Video Generation Meets Agent Harness
Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
Liaoyuan Fan
∗
Yuhao Zheng
∗
Dongxing Mao
∗
Hangyu Ran
∗
Siyuan Hu
∗
Weijia Mao  Rui Zhao
Weijia Wu  Guian Fang  Yanzhe Chen  Zeyu Zhu  Yuxin Jiang  Yiren Song  Yuchao Gu  Junchao Yi  Qi Hu
Dan Kong  Alex Jinpeng Wang  Kevin Qinghong Lin
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Mike Zheng Shou
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Wei Liu
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Video Rebirth National University of Singapore Nanyang Technological University Hong Kong University of Science and Technology University of Science and Technology of China Central South University University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Abstract
Abstract:
Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the
agent harness
: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions.
First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development.
Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization.
We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.
Keywords
: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models, Recursive Self-Improvement
Webpage
:
https://agentic-videogen.github.io/
GitHub
:
https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen
Figure 1:
Video generation meets agent harness.
This report explores how agent harnesses revolutionize video generation across key areas: agentic video generation, agentic world modeling, and recursive self-improvement.
Contents
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally
coherent clips
[
kong2024hunyuanvideo
]
. A generator alone, however, does
not organize the decisions needed to complete a video task. A creative brief
must become coherent shots;
references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must
preserve what is correct
[
huang2026vimax
,
vista2025
]
. Interactive
video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not
just a finished clip
[
gao2026lingbotworld2
]
.
These requirements motivate a transition from video generation
to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results
inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference,
select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes
[
li2026videogenagent
]
.
Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator
architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions,
while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities.
Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots
[
chen2026cinecrew
]
,
actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt
temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a
narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality
score alone rarely specifies what to do next
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
,
ding2026playworld
]
. Effective control
requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining
project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.
The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a
foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an
LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation,
as demonstrated by ReAct
[
yao2023react
]
. Planning and memory extend
this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions
[
weng2023agents
]
.
Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness:
the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context,
exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions
and budgets
[
weng2026harness
,
ning2026code
]
(Section
).
For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an
interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors,
and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good
clip to reliably completing a video
task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two
concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks
can improve the system that will perform future tasks.
Figure 2:
Agent involvement across three directions of video generation.
Representative works branch from a shared video generation foundation into
agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development toward
recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video models to
sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the improvement of
models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects increasing agent
involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and Agent Guided
Improvement to Self Improvement.
Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision
or take replacement targets the current artifact
[
vista2025
]
;
retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
;
updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model
versions
[
liu2025videoalign
]
. These outcomes
should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by
itself establish improvement in future capability.
Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers
how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are
selected and organized for subsequent decisions
[
weng2026harness
]
.
Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a
structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model
weights
[
zhang2025ace
]
. Such work shifts attention from a current
response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the
mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.
Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model
development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments,
and reporting
[
lu2024aiscientist
]
;
autoresearch
runs a bounded
loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based
acceptance
[
karpathy2026autoresearch
]
. These workflows connect proposals
to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the
same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents,
exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive
Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the
agent’s own code or harness
[
zhang2025dgm
,
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate
subsequent improvements.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve
the procedures that produce further improvements
[
chen2026surveyr04
,
duan2026surveyn21
]
.
Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection,
supervision construction, update
selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training
pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally
allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers
and addresses weaknesses.
An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction.
Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing
workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized,
revised
[
weng2026harness
]
. This does not make every harness
self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on
later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints
[
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can
revise reusable production skills
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
, uncertainty can
guide data acquisition for adaptation
[
savov2025autoexplore
]
, and
validation can govern critic renewal for later training
[
yang2026dualipo
]
. These are
building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full
RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses
organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction,
and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first
two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines
persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it.
Figure
2
maps representative work from a shared video
generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions
below.
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness
on video generation (Figure
1
), each corresponding to
one core chapter.
How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation?
Agentic Video Generation (Section
) studies
how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and
watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such
systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes
generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency,
and efficiency.
How can the agent harness be integrated into video
world models?
Agentic World Modeling
(Section
) locates where a harness can intervene in
observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management,
and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state
while the video model renders it.
We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control
fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this
question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world
model.
How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement?
Toward RSI in Video Generation
(Section
) examines how advances in video
generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces
subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement,
agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through
which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data
curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms
and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that
can support next-generation video generation models.
These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction
can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into
changes deployed in later tasks. Section
compares the shared
agent capabilities that support all three settings.
Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys
Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation.
Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models,
representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the
mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences
[
yin2025spatiotemporal
]
.
Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video
generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation,
preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation
[
li2026videoposttraining
]
.
Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and
alignment with user instructions
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
]
.
Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved,
and assessed.
More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation
surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions
available to a controller across visual modalities
[
huang2026agenticvisual
]
,
or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of
stateful artifacts
[
xu2026ags
,
wang2026artifactcreation
]
. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single
capability ladder of visual generation
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
.
World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities
across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness
in sustained interaction
[
chu2026agenticworldmodel
,
liu2026interactiveworldmodel
]
,
or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to
continually improving agents
[
yang2026quovadis
]
.
Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding
agents
[
ning2026code
,
guo2026harnessdesign
]
.
Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets,
adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI
systems
[
gao2025surveyr02
,
chen2026surveyr04
,
wu2026rsisurvey
]
.
These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent
control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the
unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.
Table
1.2
compares related surveys and
adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design.
Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on
video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video
model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as
the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness:
agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide
interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model
development. Where capability ladders treat agentic
generation and world modeling as successive stages of the
generator
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
, we take the agent harness around the
generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production,
interaction, and development.
Our contributions are threefold.
•
A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness
execution loop (Section
) and apply it to
production, organized by workflow function
(Section
), and to world-model interaction,
organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes,
including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world
state (Section
).
•
An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current
output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and
evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels
through which an improvement could re-enter video development.
No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and
validates the generator (Section
).
•
Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness
supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and
world models (Section
), what the
evaluation of agentic production must separate
(Section
),
which capabilities video imposes on agents
(Section
), and which challenges remain
(Section
).

article.headline: 视频生成转向智能体运行时
article.lede: 一篇综述以“智能体运行时”为分析单元，串联智能体视频生成、世界模型交互与递归自我改进三条路线。
article.problem: 视频生成器能产出越来越逼真的片段，但本身不组织完成视频任务所需的决策：创意简报要变成连贯镜头，参考要在场景间保持，生成结果要检查，剪辑要保留正确部分。交互式视频还要求动作能基于观察持续进行，而不只是输出一段成品。现有综述多分别讨论生成模型、智能体或世界模型，较少把视频生成器外围的运行时作为贯穿生产、交互与模型开发的统一分析单元。
article.method: 综述定义了一个共同的“智能体—运行时”执行循环，并据此组织三类问题：智能体视频生成按脚本规划、素材管理、镜头生产、编辑等工作流功能展开；智能体世界建模按观察、控制、执行、状态等运行时接口展开；递归自我改进则区分当前输出修订、运行时状态/生成器参数/评估器更新，以及产生后续更新的流程变更。作者还比较了相关综述的覆盖范围，并提出评估要求与开放挑战。
article.results: 作为综述，论文未给出具体实验数字；其框架归纳了三个核心方向与三个问题，并提出四条改进可回流到视频开发的通道。作者同时指出，在所调研系统中，尚无系统能够修订训练和验证生成器的流程。
article.why_it_matters: 这把讨论重心从“生成一段好视频”转向“通过反馈可靠完成视频任务”，为生产流水线、世界模型交互和模型开发提供了共同词汇。它也有助于设计同时考察视频质量与任务表现的评测。
article.limitations: 论文是概念性综述，未提供实验或定量验证；其递归自我改进部分更像路线图，因为尚无调研系统跑通完整闭环。运行时框架覆盖面较广，具体系统未必实现图中所有组件，视频质量与任务表现如何联动评估仍待解决。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从视频生成到由智能体运行时介导的世界交互：条件生成仍是共同核心，运行时负责观察、决策、控制转换、调度生成并整合反馈与历史。

figure.caption: {From video generation to harness-mediated world interaction.} Conditional visual generation remains the shared core. In a video world model, one-shot conditioning becomes sustained control, temporal context must support continuing state, and output frames become observations for the next decision. Around this core, the harness observes, decides, translates controls, schedules generation, and incorporates returned feedback and relevant history. The central interfaces translate controls, coordinate execution, and interpret returned observations. External memory and tracking are distinct from model-side state or context. The diagram summarizes shared, adapted, and added components; a particular system need not implement every component. Abstract
Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM’s behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.
1
Introduction
As Large Language Models (LLMs) become deployed in more diverse and unconstrained applications, understanding and controlling their behavior is of increased importance. This paper focuses on activation space steering, which identifies an activation layer and a 1-dimensional vector within that layer, and at inference times applies a light-weight shift in that direction. In contrast to more diffuse effective of prompting
(
wei2022finetunedlanguagemodelszeroshot
)
or the more distributed and expensive finetuning
(
brown2020languagemodelsfewshotlearners
)
, the simple activation steering is often as powerful, with a finer level of control
(
wu2025axbenchsteeringllmssimple
;
turner2024steeringlanguagemodelsactivation
;
zou2023representation
)
.
Despite this promise, activation steering remain precarious to use in practice. There is no consensus or standard for what scale to apply a steering vector, or how to interpret the meaning of different steering magnitudes — the same nominal strength can produce wildly different effects across vectors. This makes it difficult to reason about steering in a principled way, and motivates our first goal: identifying the most steerable region for a given vector and introducing new methods for applying steering within only that range. A second, related problem arises when steering multiple traits at once, which can steer the generations out of distribution.
Figure 1
:
Steered text generations after adding sycophancy and warmth steering vectors to an LLM and where these generations lie in the representation space.
Consider one emerging application: using LLMs for psychotherapy, which offers a potentially useful and inexpensive alternative to traditional care, but also carries substantial risk
(
lawrence2024opportunities
)
. A therapist LLM should be warm toward patients, but not sycophantic
(
ibrahim2026warmth
)
. This is important to ensure LLM therapists are considerate of patients’ feelings, but still looking out for their best interests instead of blindly agreeing with them.
In Figure
1
, for example, the patient is feeling down and wants to feel better by indulging in ice cream. The unsteered baseline agrees that some ice cream is okay, but makes sure to warn the user to not over indulge. When we take out the warmth trait and only add sycophancy, the LLM just agrees with what the user wants and does not consider facts or warnings, but is also not overly comforting. Then, when we add the warmth trait back in, the LLM is much more understanding and encouraging towards the user while still agreeing with what they want. Finally, when we take away sycophancy but keep warmth, the LLM is still very understanding and wants to help the user, but more carefully considers the drawbacks of eating ice cream and suggests healthier alternatives.
We consider the geometry of these two traits and why it might be difficult to steer a model toward one without inadvertently inducing the other, as in
ibrahim2026warmth
. When we have correlated traits like warmth and sycophancy, they point in similar directions, so it can be difficult to interpret the space we want to steer to and can also cause issues like over- or under-steering. Our solution is to
orthogonalize
the steering vectors and transform the activation space to a parameterized space. This creates an interpretable grid that makes the steering vectors the axes and represent the controllable range that we steer on.
